title: What Philosophy Is and How It Differs from Science

lectureTitle: 1.1 What Philosophy Is and How It Differs from Science
body:
# What Philosophy Is and How It Differs from Science

## Philosophy as the delineation of categories

Philosophy studies the **categories** in terms of which we understand the world. A category, here, is not a genus in a taxonomic scheme, but a basic mode of understanding: **event**, **space**, **time**, **cause**, **persistence**, **thing**, **mind**, **perception**, **belief**, **knowledge**, **language**, **truth**, **value-judgment**, **law**, **justice**, **existence**, **impossibility**, **statement**, **fact**. These are not optional additions to thought. They are the forms through which thought about the world proceeds at all.

That is why philosophy’s function is sole and specific: it **delineates the structures** of these categories. It does not compete with the sciences in telling us what happened, when it happened, or what caused it. It asks instead what it is for something to be an event, what it is for one thing to cause another, what conditions must be met if a state counts as knowledge rather than merely true belief, what truth consists in, what it is for an action to fall under justice rather than merely under law.

The point becomes clearer if we start from some of our most ordinary beliefs. We believe that the world is not homogeneous, but articulated into events standing in causal and more generally spatiotemporal relations. We believe that some events involve persistent things such as rocks and trees; that some things have minds; that animate beings perceive; that percipient beings believe; that some beliefs are true and some false; that some true beliefs are knowledge; that language enables communication and reasoning; that rational beings make value-judgments; that systems of law are meant to secure justice. In making these pedestrian judgments, we are already employing the very categories philosophy studies. Philosophy therefore concerns neither a special region of reality nor an occult subject matter. It concerns the structural framework presupposed in all our understanding of reality.

## Expertise in use, ignorance in theory

We are adept with these categories and yet understand them poorly. That is the second essential point. Ordinary competence is not the same thing as explicit comprehension. We distinguish with great reliability between linguistic and non-linguistic behavior. We know who knows a language and who does not. But when asked to state the conditions a creature’s behavior must satisfy if it is to embody knowledge of a language, we find ourselves struggling. Our practical discrimination outruns our theoretical articulation.

The same is true mutatis mutandis of moral judgment. We know that rape is immoral and that donating money to charity for selfless reasons is moral. Yet when asked to identify the principles embodied in these judgments, we often produce theories that distort the very judgments from which we began. We can sort cases better than we can explain our standards of sorting.

Philosophy is therefore not first-order knowledge of the world; it is **meta-knowledge**. **Meta-knowledge** is knowledge about knowledge: knowledge of what it is that we know when we know anything through these categories. To delineate a category is to identify, as explicitly and clearly as possible, the conditions a thing must satisfy to fall under it. If one analyzes knowledge, one is not thereby learning that Smith knows this or Brown knows that. One is clarifying what must be true if anything is to count as knowledge at all. If one analyzes truth, one is not thereby determining whether this proposition is true, but what truth consists in.

This derivative status of self-understanding is important. The mind’s primary function is not self-inspection. A mind that thought about nothing other than itself would be incoherent. Hence any self-awareness is derivative of some more fundamental awareness of objects, facts, events, or propositions. Philosophy, because it is self-understanding of our own cognitive framework, is difficult precisely because it is reflective and second-order. It attempts to make explicit principles that guide thought without ordinarily becoming objects of thought.

## Philosophical puzzles and empirical puzzles

From this it follows that philosophical puzzles differ in kind from empirical puzzles. An **empirical** puzzle is settled by finding out more facts. If one wants to know what happened, when it happened, what caused it, or by what mechanism it occurred, one gathers evidence. One observes, measures, experiments, and infers. The puzzle is about which contingent fact obtains.

A **philosophical** puzzle is not of that type. It is not solved by learning one more fact among others. It is solved, if at all, by clarifying the concept or structure involved. Suppose one asks what it is for one event to cause another. No accumulation of examples of actual causation can by itself answer that question, because all such examples already presuppose that we can identify causation. Likewise for truth, knowledge, language, law, or justice. The issue is not which instances there are, but what makes them instances.

The source puts this with great precision: the philosopher does not want to know what in fact holds; he wants to know what it would even make sense to claim to hold. He wants the laws the laws cannot break. A scientist may discover a law; the philosopher asks what sort of structure something must have to count as a law, explanation, cause, or truth-condition in the first place. That is why no amount of empirical information can simply replace conceptual analysis. Facts instantiate categories; they do not by themselves explicate them.

## Not merely linguistic analysis

Because analytic philosophy proceeds by analysis, it is often confused with the analysis of words. That is too crude. Philosophy is not merely **linguistic analysis**, if that means an exclusive concern with sentences as strings of words. Often the real object of analysis is the **proposition**, that is, the **sentence-meaning**—what is meant by an utterance of a sentence.

The distinction matters. If I point at Smith and say “that man is a scoundrel,” the proposition is not the noise, not the inscription, not the sentence-type, but what is meant in that utterance. Different sentences can express the same proposition; the same sentence can express different propositions in different contexts. So when philosophy analyzes truth or logical structure, it is often analyzing propositions rather than mere sentences.

The chapter on propositions makes the point in a form directly relevant here. A proposition is treated as a set of properties, and truth as the jointly instantiatedness of those properties. Consider the proposition that Tommy is smoking. Its structure includes something individuative of Tommy, the property of smoking, and a third property that combines them: the property of being identical with something that is smoking and is identical with Tommy. The point is not, for present purposes, to rehearse the whole theory, but to note that philosophical analysis goes beneath surface grammar to the underlying structure of what is asserted. That is why philosophy cannot be reduced to cataloguing ordinary uses of words. Its concern is with the structure of what those uses mean.

This also explains why attention to logical form is indispensable. Surface language can mislead. What appears grammatically simple may conceal a more complex propositional structure. Philosophy must therefore analyze sentence-meanings, not merely sentence-shapes.

## Science and philosophy: contingent fact versus necessary structure

Science discovers **contingent** spatiotemporal facts. A truth is contingent if it could have been otherwise. Scientific inquiry tells us what events actually occurred, what mechanisms there are, what regularities nature exhibits, what objects exist in space-time, and how they are related. It investigates what is the case.

Philosophy, by contrast, clarifies **necessary** structural relations among properties and categories. A claim is necessary if it could not have been otherwise. Philosophy is therefore **a priori** conceptual analysis rather than empirical observation. **A priori** knowledge is knowledge not derived from observation of particular spatiotemporal facts. This does not mean it floats free of all thought about the world; it means that its justification does not come from observation, but from analysis of the categories in terms of which any observation is possible.

The distinction is sharpened by the treatment of properties. Everything in space-time is an instance of at least one property, but the properties themselves are not in space-time. I may have the property of liking to play tennis, but no search of the universe will encounter that property itself; one finds only its instances. Properties can be instantiated or uninstantiated. The property of being a square circle has the higher-order property of being uninstantiated. The property of having a perfectly triangular shape exists even though nothing instantiates it. These points are not discoveries about some hidden region of space-time. They are structural clarifications concerning what must be admitted if we are to make sense of predication, commonality, and truth.

Why is this philosophical rather than scientific? Because the question is not whether, as a matter of fact, we have found some strange non-spatiotemporal object. The question is what must be true if Sally and Fred are both intelligent. If that is true, then there exists some property of which both are instances. The analysis is compelled by the logical structure of our thought and discourse. Likewise, if uninstantiated properties such as being a perfect husband and being a perfect soldier are distinct, then properties cannot be identical with aggregates of their instances, since in both cases the aggregate is a nullity. The argument is conceptual, not observational.

## The laws governing the laws

The relation between philosophy and science is best understood through the hierarchy of interests the text gives us. The stranded motorist wants the car to work. He is concerned with the immediate practical result. The engineer wants to know enough of the laws of physics to build the right mechanism. The physicist, less parochially, wants to know the laws embodied in those mechanisms. The philosopher stands to the physicist as the physicist stands to the engineer and the engineer to the motorist.

This analogy is exact, not ornamental. The philosopher seeks the **laws governing the laws**. He wants to know what it is for one thing to cause another, what it is for a proposition to be true, what it is for a belief to count as knowledge, what it is for a system of norms to qualify as law, and what relation law must bear to justice if it is to be understood as law aiming at justice. The physicist may tell us that such-and-such law governs electromagnetic phenomena. The philosopher asks what a law is, what necessity is, how laws relate to properties, and what makes explanatory connection intelligible.

Thus philosophical concern with first-order facts is always instrumental. The philosopher wants to know what caused what and by what mechanism only insofar as this helps clarify the category of causation. He is interested in place and time insofar as this helps articulate the categories of space and time. He is interested in language use insofar as it illuminates what it is to know a language. His concern is structurally upstream from empirical inquiry.

## Philosophy as analysis of the preconditions of all knowledge

This is why philosophy is uniquely **metaknowledge**. It does not merely add one more domain of knowledge alongside botany, physics, or history. It analyzes the **preconditions of all knowledge**. To know anything empirically, one must already operate with categories such as object, event, cause, truth, belief, and evidence. To reason at all, one must already stand within logical structure. Philosophy turns back upon these enabling conditions and makes them explicit.

That is why Mill’s phrase, as reported in the text, is apt: philosophy is the “science of science.” The slogan should not be misunderstood as granting philosophy a quasi-empirical subject matter. It means that philosophy studies the framework within which the sciences are sciences at all. Hence the source’s formulations: philosophy is the **analysis of analysis**, the **logic of logic**, the **science of science**. Each phrase marks a second-order discipline. Analysis presupposes standards of implication, identity, structure, and category-membership; philosophy analyzes those. Logic governs inference; philosophy, in turning to logical categories themselves, becomes the logic of logic. Science discovers truths; philosophy clarifies the conditions under which there can be truths, propositions, laws, and knowledge of them.

The result is not a rival body of factual conclusions, but a clarified map of the conceptual terrain through which all factual inquiry moves.

## Clarifying logical form rather than multiplying entities

A central methodological rule of analytic philosophy now emerges. When a correct belief appears to entail absurdity, the proper response is to clarify its **logical form**, not to posit exotic entities or abandon the belief prematurely. Analytic philosophy is disciplined by the thought that absurdity often arises from misconstruing structure.

The chapter on properties offers a model. Take the true claim that Sally and Fred are both intelligent. One might resist the implication that there is a property they share because one wishes to avoid non-spatiotemporal entities. But the attempt to evade the consequence by identifying the property with an aggregate of its instances leads to absurdity. Uninstantiated properties would vanish; distinct uninstantiated properties would collapse into one null aggregate. The property of being a perfect husband would become indistinguishable from the property of being a perfect soldier. That is absurd not because we have encountered a bizarre object, but because a mistaken structural analysis has forced a collapse of distinctions our original correct beliefs require.

The analytic remedy is not to say that there are no properties, or that our talk is merely verbal. It is to analyze the proposition correctly: if several particulars are each said truly to be intelligent, then there must be something common to them in virtue of which the predication is true. Likewise with propositions and truth. Rather than treating truth as some mysterious additional ingredient attached to sentences, the text analyzes a proposition as a set of properties and truth as the instantiatedness of those properties. Whether one is examining predication, truth, or causation, the governing impulse is the same: uncover the structure already implicit in what we correctly believe.

This is the hallmark of analytic restraint. One neither indulges in nominalist eliminations that destroy the phenomenon nor in obscurantist metaphysical additions unmoored from logical necessity. One clarifies form.

## Explication: making latent implications explicit

Philosophy proceeds by **explication**. An explication does not import alien content into our beliefs. It makes explicit what was already latent within them. Because our ordinary and scientific judgments use categories expertly without understanding them theoretically, philosophy brings to light implications we were already committed to.

Again, the treatment of properties is exemplary. From the seemingly harmless statement that Sally and Fred are both intelligent, philosophy explicates a commitment to a shared property. From the distinction between instantiated and uninstantiated predicates, it explicates the existence of properties not identical with aggregates of instances. From the truth of “Tommy is smoking,” it explicates a structured proposition involving individuative and predicative properties plus a combining property. In each case, the philosopher does not invent a new doctrine arbitrarily. He teases out what must be true if our original statement is to be understood coherently.

This is equally true at the level of categories like language, morality, or knowledge. We already know who speaks a language, which acts are immoral, which claims are true, which beliefs count as knowledge better than we can say why. Philosophy’s task is to make explicit the conditions embodied in these judgments. Because self-understanding is derivative and difficult, this explication is often partial and hard won. But its aim is always the same: to render explicit the structure tacitly governing cognition.

So philosophy advances not by discovering new continents of fact, but by increasing explicitness. It says, in effect: here is what you were already presupposing when you judged, inferred, spoke, or knew.

## The possible over the actual

A final contrast with empirical inquiry concerns the relative importance of the actual and the possible. The botanist prizes the actual over the possible. He wants to know which plants there are, how they grow, where they occur, which properties they in fact exhibit. Possibility matters to him only insofar as it bears on actual botanical reality.

The philosopher reverses this priority. He prizes the **possible** over the actual. That is because philosophy seeks structural necessity. To understand a category is to understand not merely the actual instances falling under it, but the conditions any possible instance would have to satisfy. The actual is used as evidence or illustration, but the target is what could and could not be the case.

The discussion of uninstantiated properties makes this especially vivid. If one focused only on the actual, one might think one could understand properties by surveying their existing instances. But the possibility of uninstantiated properties—being a square circle, having a perfectly triangular shape, being a perfect husband, being a perfect soldier—shows that actual instances cannot exhaust the structure. The philosophical issue is what it is to be a property, and that question ranges over possible as well as actual instantiation. Similarly, in analyzing propositions, one asks not merely when this proposition is in fact true, but what must be the case in any possible world for it to be true.

That is why necessary truths and impossible combinations are philosophically central. A property may be necessarily instantiated, contingently instantiated, or uninstantiated; a proposition may be true or false depending on whether its constituent properties are jointly instantiated; some properties, like being three-sided if a triangle, are instantiated in every possible world where the relevant things exist; others, like being a square circle, are uninstantiable. These modal notions—possibility, necessity, impossibility—are not decorative additions. They are indispensable to delineating structure.

Philosophy therefore uses the actual as a clue to the necessary. It examines actual cases in order to discover what cannot be denied without incoherence and what distinctions would survive across possible situations. Its concern is not with what merely happens to be so, but with what must be so if our categories are to make sense at all.

Taken together, these points yield a sharply defined conception of the discipline. Philosophy is not empirical inquiry, not the compilation of facts, not merely the analysis of words, and not a rival natural science. It is the a priori explication of the categories through which all thought and inquiry proceed. It seeks the laws governing the laws, the preconditions of knowledge, the structure of propositions, truth, properties, and the other categories in terms of which we understand anything whatever. Its characteristic movement is from tacit competence to explicit structure, from the actual case to the possible and necessary conditions it reveals, and from apparent absurdity to clarified logical form.

title: The Meaning of Meaning
blurb: Three senses of “meaning,” why only one is linguistic, and why propositions—not intentions—anchor semantics.
body:
# The Meaning of Meaning

## The equivocity of “meaning”

There would be no language without **expressions**—words, phrases, sentences—and nothing meaningless is an expression. For that reason, the concept of language depends upon the concept of meaning. But the word “meaning” is itself ambiguous in a deep and philosophically consequential way. It has three distinct senses.

First, there is **evidential meaning**: one thing means another in the sense of being evidence for it. Smith’s hacking cough means that he has a violent lung infection. Smoke means fire. Here “means” does not concern language at all; it marks an evidential relation between states of affairs.

Second, there is **psychological meaning**: what a speaker means by an utterance. If, after hearing praise of Sally, one replies, “things aren’t always as they seem,” what one may mean is that Sally is devious. This is plainly psychological, because it consists in an intention to get something across.

Third, there is **linguistic meaning**: what a sentence says. The sentence “snow is white” says something about something; it attributes whiteness to snow. So it means that snow is white. Here “meaning” concerns the content literally expressed by the sentence itself.

These are not three shades of a single notion. They are three distinct relations. The first links one state of affairs to another as evidence. The second links a speaker to what he intends to communicate. The third links an expression to what it literally says.

That distinction matters because philosophy of language concerns language as such, not merely evidence in nature and not merely episodes of intending.

## Why only linguistic meaning belongs to the theory of language

Only the third sense bears directly on the nature of language. A language is constituted by expressions, and expressions are essentially meaningful. But what makes an expression part of a language is not that it serves as evidence for something, nor that someone once used it with a certain intention. It is that it has a determinate literal significance.

This is already enough to separate linguistic meaning from evidential meaning. Smoke would mean fire whether or not there were conventions, speakers, or languages. But that “snow” refers to snow rather than grass, and that “white” does not mean green, is at least partly a matter of convention. The sentence “snow is white” has its meaning because of the linguistic rules governing its parts. Its meaning is not a natural symptom, not an occurrence that simply results from a causal process in the way smoke results from fire.

Nor can linguistic meaning be reduced to psychological meaning. To say that a sentence means what speakers mean by it reverses the dependence. It treats the language as derivative from acts of communication when, in fact, communicative acts presuppose a language whose expressions already mean something.

Reduction fails in both directions:

1. **Linguistic meaning is not evidential meaning**, because the former is conventional, propositional, and judgment-embodying, whereas the latter is an evidential relation between states of affairs.
2. **Linguistic meaning is not psychological meaning**, because a sentence may have literal significance independently of anyone’s having used it to mean anything.

The theory of language therefore begins with linguistic meaning, not with evidence and not with intention.

## The priority of linguistic meaning over psychological meaning

Psychological meaning is not merely distinct from linguistic meaning; it is **parasitic** on it. To say that one means something by a sentence is to describe a psychological act whose possibility depends on the sentence already having a linguistic meaning.

Take the familiar case. In response to your saying that Sally is wonderful, I say, “things aren’t always as they seem.” Suppose what I mean is that Sally is devious. My psychological meaning is not identical with the linguistic meaning of the sentence uttered. The sentence literally means that things are not always as they seem. I exploit that preexisting literal meaning to convey something further. My communicative intention rides on the sentence’s prior meaning; it does not create it.

The dependence is easy to state step by step:

1. In uttering a sentence sincerely and literally, I rely on what I take that sentence already to mean.
2. If I intend to get across that snow is white by uttering “snow is white,” I must believe that “snow is white” means that snow is white.
3. If instead I believe that “snow is white” means that bananas are yellow, then, intending sincerity and literalness, I cannot use it to say that snow is white.
4. Therefore, speaker-meaning presupposes beliefs about sentence-meaning.
5. Hence psychological meaning depends upon linguistic meaning.

This remains true even when a speaker uses a sentence non-literally, ironically, or as a vehicle for some wholly different message. One might know perfectly well what “snow is white” actually means, yet use it to convey that the government is controlling our thoughts with alpha waves. Depending on the circumstances, that may indeed be what the utterance conveys. But even here the attempted communication depends upon the speaker’s grasp of the sentence’s actual meaning and of how that meaning bears on the message to be conveyed. Whatever one wishes to communicate, one must take it to stand in some relation to what the sentence itself means.

So, setting aside defective utterances, one cannot mean anything by a sentence unless one already knows what it means. The psychological phenomenon is secondary.

## Why sentence meaning cannot be identified with speaker-meaning

A decisive objection to the identification of linguistic meaning with psychological meaning is that many sentences have determinate meanings even though no one has ever uttered them. Consider:

> “the cube root of three is Sir Lawrence Olivier’s favorite irrational number between one and four”

That sentence almost certainly has never been uttered. Yet it has a determinate meaning. Its words are meaningful, their syntactic arrangement is determinate, and the sentence says something definite. Therefore, having a meaning cannot consist in there being actual occasions on which speakers mean something by uttering it.

This point is stronger than the mere observation that some meaningful sentences happen never to have been used. The deeper point is that when we say that “snow is white” means one thing and the cube-root sentence means another, the word “means” is used in the same sense in both cases. We are not equivocating. The relation a sentence bears to its literal meaning is uniform across uttered and unuttered sentences alike. So if, in the unuttered case, that relation cannot be identified with what speakers mean by uttering the sentence, then it cannot be so identified in the ordinary case either.

The conclusion is general: even when what a speaker means coincides with the literal meaning of the sentence used, that coincidence is not an identity. It is one thing for a sentence to have a proposition as its literal meaning; it is another for a speaker, on some occasion, to mean that proposition in uttering it.

## What a sentence means: propositions as the bearers of truth and falsity

If linguistic meaning is neither evidence nor intention, what is it? For a sentence that is true or false, its meaning is a **proposition**. A proposition is what is meant by an utterance of a sentence in the relevant semantic sense: what the sentence says. “Snow is white” means the proposition that snow is white. “That man is a scoundrel,” uttered while pointing at Smith, has as its meaning a proposition about Smith.

A proposition must be distinguished from the sentence expressing it. Sentences are linguistic items: inscriptions, sounds, types of expression. Propositions are what those expressions mean. The distinction is forced by several considerations already before us.

1. Different sentences can have the same meaning.
2. The same sentence type can be used by different speakers on different occasions.
3. A sentence can exist as meaningful even if never uttered.
4. Truth and falsity attach to what is said, not to the mere sequence of marks or sounds.

So the proposition is the primary bearer of truth-value. It is what is true or false. The sentence is meaningful by expressing that proposition.

The proposition is also not a psychological item. It is not an intention, not an idea in anyone’s mind, not an episode of consciousness. Sentences not yet uttered still express propositions. Thus propositions are **mind-independent abstract structures**: not spatiotemporal items, but entities capable of being the meanings of sentences and the bearers of truth.

## Evidential meaning as non-causal in the relevant sense

The evidential sense of “means” can now be characterized more carefully. To say that x means y in this sense is to say that x is evidence of y: x and y are causally interrelated in such a way that, given x, y may reasonably be inferred. But this relation is not simply causation, and that is why it differs so sharply from linguistic meaning.

It is neither necessary nor sufficient, for x to be evidence of y, that y cause x.

It is not necessary because:

- causes can be evidence of their own effects; Bill’s current drunkenness is evidence of poor performance on his upcoming economics exam;
- or x and y may share a common cause without either causing the other. Bill’s slurred speech is evidence that he will do poorly, not because the slurring causes the failure or the failure causes the slurring, but because both have a common causal ancestor: his drunkenness.

It is not sufficient because from the mere fact that y caused x on some occasion, it does not follow that x is evidence of y. Bill’s failing a test does not, by itself, count as evidence that he was drunk, because there are many reasonable alternative explanations for failure.

The evidential relation therefore requires more than causal connection. It requires the absence of any **reasonable alternative explanation**. Smith’s hacking cough is evidence of a violent lung infection only if it cannot reasonably be supposed that anything else produced the cough. So evidential meaning is best understood as a relation in which one state counts as evidence for another because no reasonable rival causal story remains.

That is why smoke means fire in a way profoundly unlike the way “snow is white” means that snow is white. Smoke does not embody a judgment. A sentence does. The former is an evidential sign; the latter is a semantically articulated vehicle of assertion.

## What propositions are: sets of properties

If propositions are abstract bearers of truth, what sort of abstract entities are they? The book’s answer is exact: propositions are **sets of properties**. Their truth consists in the **joint instantiatedness** of those properties.

Consider the proposition:

> Tommy is smoking.

Intuitively, this proposition has at least three constituents:

1. something individuative of Tommy,
2. the property of smoking,
3. something that synthesizes those two.

The first constituent can be represented by the property:

- **A**: being identical with Tommy.

The second is:

- **B**: smoking.

But A and B alone do not suffice. They could both be instantiated even in a world where Tommy is not smoking—for example, where Tommy exists and is playing golf while Larry is smoking. So a third property is needed:

- **C**: being identical with something that is smoking and is identical with Tommy.

Now let **S** be the set containing all and only A, B, and C. If C is instantiated, then A and B are instantiated. And the proposition “Tommy is smoking” is true if and only if C is instantiated, hence if and only if A, B, and C are jointly instantiated. This gives us the proposed identity:

- the proposition that Tommy is smoking = the set S;
- the truth of that proposition = the joint instantiatedness of S’s members.

This is not an arbitrary set-theoretic trick. True, infinitely many sets of properties will be such that their members are instantiated exactly when Tommy is smoking. But not all such sets mirror the proposition’s internal articulation. A set containing being identical with a smoking Tommy, being an even number, and being three-sided if a triangle would have the right truth-condition but the wrong constituency. It would fail to line up with what we know about the proposition’s parts.

By contrast, S aligns naturally with the proposition’s structure. A corresponds to what individuates Tommy, B corresponds to smoking, and C functions as the synthesizing constituent. In the relevant sense, C “combines” A and B because C is instantiated exactly when A and B are jointly instantiated.

Thus propositions are not amorphous contents. They are structured sets of properties.

## Truth as joint instantiatedness

Once propositions are identified with sets of properties, truth receives a correspondingly austere account. A proposition is true just in case the properties in the set with which it is identical are instantiated together. Truth is, roughly, **instantiatedness**; more exactly, it is the property of being a set of the relevant kind all of whose members are instantiated.

This account respects the proposition’s unity. One might ask: if C alone is instantiated exactly when Tommy is smoking, why not identify the proposition simply with C? The reply is that doing so obliterates the proposition’s articulated structure. The proposition “Tommy is smoking” is neatly parsed into something corresponding to Tommy, something corresponding to smoking, and something synthesizing them. C by itself does not obviously contain discrete parts matching those constituents.

The set S does preserve that articulation in its membership. So the truth of the proposition is not merely the obtaining of a single undifferentiated condition, but the joint instantiatedness of a structured set of properties whose members correspond to the proposition’s constituents.

This also helps explain why propositions are the right semantic values for sentences. A sentence does not merely correlate with a truth-condition in the abstract. It expresses a structured content whose parts are reflected in the semantic contributions of its parts.

## Compositionality and normativity in linguistic meaning

That last point brings us directly to the character of linguistic meaning itself. Linguistic meaning is **compositional** and **normative**.

By compositionality is meant that the meaning of a sentence is fixed by the meanings of its parts together with their mode of combination. “Snow is white” means that snow is white because “snow” does not refer to grass, “white” does not mean green, and the sentence’s structure attributes the latter property to the former referent. Likewise, the never-before-uttered sentence about the cube root of three and Sir Lawrence Olivier has a determinate meaning precisely because its constituent expressions already mean what they do and are combined in a determinate way.

By normativity is meant that semantic rules determine what expressions **literally say**, and thereby provide standards of correctness and incorrectness for use. When one knows the relevant rules, one knows that uttering “snow is white” would be making a correct statement if snow is white. One can misuse the sentence, mean something else by it, or falsely believe that it means bananas are yellow; but these are deviations from, not determinants of, its meaning.

The sentence’s literal meaning is therefore fixed regardless of individual intention. Intentions can exploit, flout, or presuppose semantic rules; they do not constitute them. That is why a speaker who sincerely and literally utters “snow is white” while believing it means bananas are yellow fails to say what he wanted to say. The norm governing literal correctness is independent of his private state.

## Why the Gricean reduction fails at the level of parts

The reduction of linguistic meaning to speaker-intention fails not only because there are meaningful unuttered sentences and because speaker-meaning presupposes sentence-meaning. It fails more fundamentally because it cannot account for the meanings of **subsentential expressions**.

A language is not made only of full sentences. It contains words, phrases, and logical particles. The sentence’s proposition is reached by composition out of the meanings of these smaller elements. Any theory identifying meaning with what speakers mean by uttering whole sentences therefore faces a problem: what is the meaning of terms whose role is not to be independently used to communicate a complete proposition?

Expressions such as “of” or “or” are the clearest cases. Their semantic contribution is indispensable, yet it is not plausible to analyze their meanings as what speakers mean by uttering them. A speaker may mean something by uttering a sentence containing “or,” but the word “or” itself contributes to literal content in virtue of a rule-governed role in composition. The same is true of “of.” Their meanings are not detachable speaker-intentions; they are structural contributions to what larger expressions say.

So any theory that attempts to reduce all linguistic meaning to acts of speaker-meaning misses the layered architecture of language. It may at best describe how speakers exploit already meaningful expressions to communicate. It cannot explain how the meanings of the expressions themselves, especially the subsentential ones, are fixed in the first place.

## Semantic rules are rules of literal saying, not reports of usage

The final lesson is that **semantic rules** are not psychological generalizations about what people happen to mean. They are rules defining what expressions literally say.

This distinction is essential. If semantic rules were merely reports of ordinary intentions—descriptions of what people in fact mean by uttering expressions—then the priority relation established earlier would collapse. But it does not collapse. What a person means is a function, among other things, of what he believes the sentence already means. Therefore the semantic rule must be prior to the psychological fact.

Semantic rules tell us, for example, that “snow” refers to snow and not grass, that “white” does not mean green, and that “snow is white” therefore does not mean that grass is green or that snow is green. These are not empirical summaries of what users are inclined to intend. They are constitutive of literal content.

That is why language can be used correctly or incorrectly, sincerely or insincerely, literally or non-literally. Such distinctions presuppose standards independent of what any particular speaker happens to have in mind. An utterance can convey that Sally is devious by means of the sentence “things aren’t always as they seem,” but the literal semantic rule governing that sentence remains what it is. One can exploit the rule precisely because the rule is stable and public.

So the theory of meaning culminates in a sharp hierarchy:

1. evidential meaning is an evidential relation among states of affairs;
2. psychological meaning is a matter of speaker intention;
3. linguistic meaning is the literal, rule-governed expression of propositions by expressions.

And among these three, only the third constitutes language itself. Sentences mean propositions; propositions are structured sets of properties; their truth is the joint instantiatedness of those properties; and the semantic rules of a language define what its expressions literally say, whether or not any speaker ever utters them, and regardless of what any speaker happens to intend.

title: Language and Thought
blurb: A rigorous defense of the priority of judgment over language, and of language as an aid to thought rather than its medium.
body:
# Language and Thought

## Language improves intelligence without being the medium of thought

It is obvious that knowledge of a language makes one more intelligent in certain important respects. A creature able to use a language can formulate, retain, compare, and communicate highly general claims—for example, that authoritarian governments tend to be less responsive to the needs of their constituents than democratic governments. It is therefore natural to suppose that the very capacity for **discursive thought**—thought that proceeds by grasping claims, consequences, and principles—depends upon language. The chapter’s central claim is that this natural supposition is false.

To deny that we think in language is to reject two distinct theses:

1. that speakers of English think in English, speakers of Spanish in Spanish, and so on; and
2. that all thinkers operate with an innate symbolic code, a **language of thought**.

The negative conclusion applies to both. Thought is not identical with tokens of English, Spanish, or any other natural language; nor is there reason to identify thought with sentence-like items in an innate code. The immediate reason is simple: we often have thoughts we cannot put into words, or can verbalize only with difficulty. If a thought were identical with a sentence occurrence, then failure to find the sentence would be failure to have the thought. But that is plainly not how our cognitive lives go. One may grasp a complex content and struggle to articulate it; the struggle itself shows that thinking is already underway prior to successful wording.

This point is stronger than it first appears. Some philosophers insist: if you cannot say it, you do not know it. The text rejects this outright. A person’s knowledge may be expressed in drawings, in movement, in discriminative behavior, or in other non-linguistic forms. If someone accurately paints two things differently because he knows their differences, that is not “pseudo-knowledge.” It is knowledge. Indeed, without such non-linguistic knowledge we could not know anything about language itself, since language learning and use require the ability to discriminate noises, marks, and perceptible patterns.

So there are really two claims to keep apart:

- language can greatly enhance intelligence; and
- thought is constituted by language.

The first is true. The second is false. The rest of the argument explains why the first does not entail the second.

## Thought is prior to language because language learning presupposes judgment

To say that **thought is prior to language** is not merely to say that infants happen to think before they speak. It is the deeper claim that linguistic competence presupposes a more fundamental cognitive power: the capacity to make **judgments**. A judgment, in the present framework, is the synthesizing of information into a truth-or-falsehood-bearing content. The objects of thought are always truths or falsehoods, never bare objects except derivatively. We think about rocks and people only by thinking truths or falsehoods concerning them.

Now consider what it is to learn a language. To learn English is to learn that certain sounds or inscriptions have certain meanings. But that is already to judge that this sound goes with that meaning, that this pattern of marks signifies this content, that this utterance was used in that circumstance to say such-and-such. No creature wholly lacking the ability to synthesize information could perform that pairing. Understanding even a simple sentence, such as “if snow is cold, then snow is not hot,” requires more than the sentence’s passing through consciousness. One must connect the sentence to the right content. Hearing an unfamiliar language may leave a mnemonic trace of the sounds, just as a song may echo in one’s mind, but without understanding. So the content-grasping act cannot consist merely in the occurrence of a sentence-image.

The order of explanation therefore runs from thought to language, not vice versa:

1. one first has the capacity to judge;
2. on that basis one can learn correlations between signs and contents;
3. on that basis one can understand and use a language.

If that order is correct, then language cannot be the fundamental medium of thought. A medium one must already understand by thinking cannot itself be what makes thought possible.

## Propositions are digital; perceptions are analogue

This priority claim is reinforced by a structural difference between what is thought and what is perceived. A **proposition**—what is believed when one thinks that Bob loves Mary, or that 1 + 1 = 2—is a truth-or-falsehood-bearing content. The text’s crucial point is that propositional thought is **digital**, whereas sense-perception is **analogue**.

A digital structure is one composed of discrete units. Sentences plainly have this character: they decompose into a finite number of distinct words. By contrast, a visual perception of a man wearing a leather jacket does not decompose into finitely many discrete, intrinsically significant units. It is seamless, continuous, and not articulated into word-like elements. That is what is meant here by analogue.

This matters because some of the most vivid candidates for “thinking in words” depend on conflating thought with sensory imagery. But perceptual presentation and propositional content have radically different structures. A perception delivers a visually organized array of **property-instances**—instances of shapes, colors, relations, motions, and so forth. Seeing Pat, for example, consists in being visually apprised that there are, at the present moment, instances of such-and-such properties, in such-and-such places, bearing such-and-such relations to one another. Perception is therefore descriptive, but descriptiveness here is not linguistic. It is the presentation of a structured existence-claim by way of sensory awareness.

The rock example makes the point exact. When you recognize the rock R—the rock Joey threw at your car—your visual perception itself does not say, “that is R.” What it tells you, considered in itself, is only that there is a rock having such-and-such characteristics over there. That content is consistent with R’s not existing and with your seeing a duplicate. Recognition adds something supplied by your standing knowledge; the perception alone gives only a descriptive existence-claim.

Hence two distinctions:

- perception is descriptive but non-linguistic;
- propositional thought concerns truth and falsity and is articulated differently from perception.

To understand thought, then, we must not model it either on verbal strings or on sensory images.

## Thoughts are not sentence-tokens because meaning outruns wording

If thoughts were literally identical with **sentence-tokens**, many ordinary facts would become unintelligible. A sentence-token is a particular occurrence of a sentence—an utterance, inscription, or mental replay of a sentence. The argument against identifying thoughts with such tokens has two parts.

First, distinct sentences can express the same proposition. “Bob loves Mary” and “Mary is loved by Bob” are different English sentences, but what you think in accepting either is the same. If thinking that Bob loves Mary consisted in entertaining the first sentence-token, then thinking that Mary is loved by Bob would have to be a distinct thought merely because a different sentence-token is involved. But that is wrong: the belief is identical.

Second, one sentence can be **ambiguous**, capable of expressing different contents. “Bob is dumb” may mean that Bob is unintelligent, or that he cannot speak. If your thought were identical with an occurrence of that sentence in your mind, then those two thoughts would collapse into one, because the same sentence occurs in both cases. But the thoughts are not identical. Therefore the thought cannot be the sentence-token.

The same lesson appears across languages. Monolingual Spanish speakers and monolingual English speakers can both believe that 1 + 1 = 2. Since they do not deploy the same sentences, the thought cannot be identical with any sentence of English, Spanish, or any other natural language. And once that point is understood, the temptation to posit an inner code as the true bearer of thought loses much of its force. For the key issue is not merely which language is involved; it is whether thought is fundamentally identical with meaningful symbols at all. The examples show that content and wording systematically come apart.

## Language aids thought by providing manipulable icons

Although thought is not linguistic, language can significantly enhance it. The chapter explains this by distinguishing the existence of a thought from the efficiency with which we can handle it. Language provides a manipulable system of **icons**—stable, repeatable signs, such as sounds or inscriptions, that we can use to retain, compare, and recombine contents. The point is not that signs create the contents. Rather, they furnish handles by which already graspable contents can be coordinated.

This helps explain the initial illusion that we think in words. Without language, streams of cognition may remain more **compartmentalized**. A creature may be able to make judgments but may lack an easy way to integrate them with one another, store them in stable form, or survey their inferential relations. Language supplies externally or internally manipulable markers that bring scattered cognitive achievements into common view.

The difference between perception and linguistic understanding sharpens this. A perception is self-interpreting in a way a sentence is not. To understand the sentence “there is a man wearing a leather jacket over there,” one must know the semantic rules that assign meaning to that sequence of words. But a visual perception of such a man need not be interpreted in that semantically rule-governed way. Sentences thus require a code already mastered; perceptions do not. Once a code has been mastered, however, it enables the subject to track contents by tracking sentence-types and their combinations. That is why language improves intelligence: not by constituting thought, but by making thought easier to marshal.

The result is a picture on which language is a cognitive technology. It is indispensable for certain practical and intellectual achievements, especially where coordination and communication are concerned. But a technology is not the activity it assists.

## Sentences decompose uniquely; images do not

The superiority of language as an aid to thought rests largely on its **discreteness**. A sentence has a unique decomposition into distinct significant parts. A visual image does not. This does not mean that perceptions are chaotic; on the contrary, they present highly organized structures of property-instances. But they lack any finite, word-like set of units each bearing determinate significance in the way words do.

A sentence such as “there is a man wearing a leather jacket over there” can be analyzed into a finite number of significant parts, and those parts can be reassembled into new sentences. This gives language a combinatorial power. By contrast, the visual perception of the man in the jacket is continuous. There is no finite catalogue of image-fragments that function as basic semantic units in the same way. That is why pictures, however rich, are not substitutes for sentence structure in the management of abstract reasoning.

This difference is not merely psychological; it bears on the nature of content. Perceiving Pat does not involve seeing Pat as an extra item over and above the organized property-instances. There is no featureless blank object plus visible features “piled on top.” The perception simply consists in being apprised of those interrelated instances and of an existence-claim they realize. Since the image is continuous, it cannot by itself play the role of a sentence in inferential operations that depend on discrete recombination.

Language, then, owes its power to the digitality of its meaningful parts. That power should not be confused with the genesis of the contents expressed through those parts.

## Language chiefly enhances intelligence by labeling abstract principles already graspable

The most important form of linguistic enhancement concerns **abstract principles**. We are strongly inclined to think that, absent language or some symbolic medium, a creature could not grasp propositions of great generality. But the text argues that this inclination is mistaken. Whatever can be grasped through language must be graspable independently of language. Language helps not by creating abstract content ex nihilo, but by labeling and stabilizing principles that the mind can already apprehend.

The reasoning is straightforward:

1. to understand a sentence expressing an abstract principle, one must pair the sentence with its meaning;
2. this pairing is itself a thought;
3. therefore the grasp of the abstract principle cannot consist in the sentence alone.

Suppose one understands the governmental principle mentioned at the outset. The words are useful because they allow one to formulate, revisit, and communicate the principle. But if grasping the principle just were grasping the words, then anyone capable of rehearsing the sentence would thereby understand it, which is false. The sentence can pass through consciousness uncomprehended. What matters is the prior capacity to apprehend the principle the sentence encodes.

This also explains why we often search for words. The words are sought because the thought is already there, though not yet conveniently packaged. Language gives us labels under which the thought can be manipulated, compared with others, and inserted into larger chains of reasoning. The enhancement of intelligence consists largely in this increase in manageability.

## Practical mastery precedes explicit statement

A further argument for the priority of thought over language comes from our ability to distinguish linguistic from non-linguistic behavior before we can formulate any theory of that distinction. We routinely identify noises, inscriptions, and gestures as linguistic or not. Yet our capacity to do so in practice far outstrips our ability to state necessary and sufficient conditions for being a linguistic sign.

This is an instance of a general phenomenon: one may possess a concept in use prior to possessing an articulated verbal analysis of it. The same point was already visible in the rejection of the “if you can’t say it, you don’t know it” doctrine. Our non-linguistic discriminations are not inferior pseudo-knowledge but the very basis on which linguistic knowledge depends. We could not learn that a sound means such-and-such unless we could first discriminate that sound from others, notice its recurrence, and register its use in varying circumstances.

So practical concept-possession outruns explicit verbal formulation. That matters here because the thesis that thought requires language often trades on the assumption that conceptual mastery must take a verbal form. The text denies this. Knowing how to pair signs with meanings presupposes a field of discriminations and judgments that is already in operation.

## Language-less creatures can think discursively

Once judgment is made primary, it becomes possible to say something that initially seems counterintuitive: **language-less creatures can have discursive thought**. The argument is not that every language-less creature in fact does, nor that such thought would be as sophisticated as ours. It is that nothing in the nature of discursive thought requires coding judgments in a language.

If a creature can make judgments—if it can synthesize information into contents that are true or false—then it already possesses the fundamental power involved in thought. Encoding those contents in a public or private code is an additional ability. Language is one way of doing that encoding, but it is not constitutive of the judgment itself.

The examples earlier already support this. A person can know differences that he cannot verbalize. Perception supplies descriptive information in non-linguistic form. Recognition of R depends on more than vision, but vision itself already delivers an existence-claim. The capacity to understand a sentence presupposes the capacity to grasp contents. So the space of judgment cannot be bounded by the space of language.

The reluctance to credit language-less creatures with discursive thought stems from overestimating the role of symbolic expression. Symbols enormously augment cognitive power, but they augment an underlying power rather than replacing it. A creature without language may lack our facility in integrating and communicating principles, yet still be able to think propositionally.

## Whatever language can convey can be grasped independently of language

The strongest conclusion is therefore this: whatever can be grasped through language can be grasped independently of it. This is not the claim that language adds nothing. It adds very much—precision, retention, communication, combinatorial manageability, and cognitive integration. But these are advantages of a tool, not marks of an ontological medium.

The claim follows from the cumulative argument:

1. understanding language requires thought;
2. thoughts can outstrip available words;
3. different sentences can express the same thought, and one sentence can express different thoughts;
4. perception and conception are fundamentally descriptive without being linguistic;
5. the objects of thought are truths and falsehoods, which language serves to communicate and coordinate.

Chapter 8 adds an important refinement by distinguishing **literal meaning** from **cognitive content**. What is literally meant by an expression does not always coincide with what a thinker has in mind. There is a systematic relation between them, but not identity. This blocks a persistent confusion. Facts about language—about what words literally mean—must not be mistaken for facts about thought itself. To think of an object is to think an existence-claim it uniquely satisfies; to perceive an object is to be sensibly apprised of such a claim. Language rides on top of this descriptive cognitive basis.

That is why communicated meaning has a **pre-semantic basis**. Before there can be semantics—before signs can mean—there must already be creatures capable of apprehending descriptive contents, differentiating perceptible forms, and making judgments. Language is then introduced as a system for exploiting those antecedent abilities.

The result is neither anti-language nor anti-intellectual. On the contrary, it explains both why language is so powerful and why it cannot be the essence of thinking. It is powerful because its digital structure gives us manipulable icons by which to integrate cognition. It is not the essence of thinking because all understanding of those icons presupposes the capacity to judge, and judgment is not itself a matter of running sentence-tokens through the mind.

The deepest point, then, is that thought is fundamentally about truth and falsity. We think by grasping propositions, by being apprised of existence-claims, by recognizing structured property-instances, by synthesizing information into judgments. Language is an instrument for expressing, storing, and coordinating these contents. Its importance is immense; its metaphysical role is secondary.

title: Do We Think in Words?
blurb: A rigorous argument that thought is not linguistic, though language and imagery powerfully scaffold reasoning.
body:
# Do We Think in Words?

## The initial temptation and the contrary datum

It is easy to see why one might think that discursive thought depends on language. A **discursive** thought is one that bears on reality in a structured, inferential, principle-governed way: not merely a sensation, but something whose consequences can be traced, compared, and judged. Consider the thought that authoritarian governments tend to be less responsive to the needs of their constituents than democratic governments. We are initially tempted to say that no creature lacking language could grasp such a thing. That temptation is not trivial. Knowledge of language plainly enhances intelligence in important respects.

But our untutored intuitions here are inconsistent with another datum that is at least as strong. We also know, directly and repeatedly, that we often have thoughts of considerable sophistication that we cannot yet put into words. Sometimes one sees exactly what one means, or exactly what follows from something, and only afterward struggles to articulate it. Indeed, articulating it may require prolonged prior thinking about which words to use. That order matters. If finding the words requires prior thought, then at least some thought cannot consist in the words.

The point is not merely that expression is sometimes difficult. It is that the difficulty of expression reveals a distinction between a thought and its linguistic vehicle. If the thought were identical with an English sentence-token occurring in the mind, then the experience of having the thought while searching for the sentence to express it would be impossible. One would already have the sentence. Yet one often has the content in hand and labors to find the formulation. So the first and most immediate reason for denying that we think in words is that sophisticated thought routinely outruns verbalization, and verbalization often depends upon antecedent non-linguistic cognition.

## Against the slogan that unsayable knowledge is no knowledge

Some philosophers deny this. The slogan is: if you cannot say it, you do not know it. The chapter explicitly associates this line with Wittgenstein, Blackburn, and McDowell. Their assumption is that what one believes is expressed only in the words one can utter. But that assumption is false, because beliefs can be manifested in forms other than speech.

A person’s knowledge of the difference between x and y may show itself:

- in that person’s drawings of x and y,
- in that person’s movements while in the vicinity of x and y,
- or in other non-linguistic forms of discrimination.

That matters because **knowledge** cannot be restricted to what is linguistically articulable without absurdity. A painter who accurately renders distinctions in what he sees does not thereby exhibit pseudo-knowledge. Nor does a person navigating among objects with finely tuned discriminatory behavior. The suggestion that such cases involve only pseudo-knowledge is, as the text says, obviously false.

The deeper error in the slogan is that it forgets what language itself presupposes. Our use of words depends on our ability to discriminate noises, ink-marks, and other perceptible differences. If all such non-verbal discrimination were downgraded to pseudo-knowledge, then our knowledge of language would rest upon pseudo-knowledge. But language cannot be epistemically more secure than the perceptual and practical capacities through which it is learned and deployed. So the anti-articulation thesis collapses under its own dependence on non-linguistic cognition. One can know without being able to say, and one must know in some non-linguistic ways if one is ever to say anything at all.

## Version #1: thinking in English, Spanish, Albanian, and the rest

Once the issue is sharpened, two very different theses must be distinguished. The first says that we think in the natural languages we learn: English speakers think in English, Spanish speakers in Spanish, and so on. A **natural language** is a language that arises organically through human interaction—English, Spanish, Arabic, Chinese. This is opposed to an artificial notation, such as those invented by programmers, mathematicians, or philosophers.

Version #1 fails for several connected reasons.

First, as already noted, we can have thoughts we cannot put into words, and we can think long and hard before finding words to express what we already grasp. That shows that at least some thought is prior to and independent of sentence-production.

Second, some information—visual information is the clearest case—seems inherently incapable of full expression in a natural language. A perception of a man wearing a leather jacket has a structure very unlike any sentence that describes it. A sentence is a **digital** structure: it decomposes into a finite number of discrete parts, words. A sense-perception is an **analogue** structure: it does not decompose into discrete parts in that way, but has a kind of seamlessness. The difference is not superficial. It shows that the representational format of at least some thought-related cognition differs fundamentally from the format of sentences.

Third, sentences require interpretation. To understand “there is a man wearing a leather jacket over there,” one must know the relevant **semantic rule**, the rule assigning meaning to that sentence. But a visual perception is, in the chapter’s phrase, “self-interpreting” in a way a sentence is not. One does not stand to one’s own visual awareness as a reader decoding a sentence. If thought simply consisted in the occurrence of natural-language items, then every thought would require this rule-governed semantic pairing. But much cognition does not.

Fourth, to learn a language one must already be able to think. Learning English is learning that certain sounds have certain meanings. That requires synthesizing information and making judgments, on the basis of experience, about which sounds mean what. A **judgment** is an act of taking something to be the case; and if language learning requires judgments, then thought cannot be constituted by language alone, since the capacity needed to acquire language would presuppose it.

These considerations already dislodge Version #1. But the decisive blow comes from meaning-relations among sentences.

## Paraphrase and ambiguity refute linguistic identity

Different sentences can have the same meaning, and a single sentence can have different meanings. Those two facts are fatal to the thesis that thinking is conducted in a natural language.

Take paraphrase. “Bob loves Mary” and “Mary is loved by Bob” are different English sentences. Yet what you think when you think the former is identical with what you think when you think the latter. If thoughts were identical with inner occurrences of English sentences, then these would have to be different thoughts, because the sentence-tokens are different. But they are not different thoughts. Therefore the thought is not identical with either sentence-token as such.

This point is direct and conclusive. **Paraphrase** is the expression of the same thought by different sentences. Its possibility shows that the sentence is not the thought. If the thought were the sentence, no two distinct sentences could ever express one and the same content. But they plainly do.

Now take ambiguity. “Bob is dumb” can mean that Bob is unintelligent, or that Bob cannot speak. If thinking that Bob is dumb were identical with an occurrence of the sentence “Bob is dumb” in one’s mind, then the thought with the first meaning and the thought with the second meaning would be numerically identical, since the same sentence-token would occur in both cases. But they are not identical thoughts. So the thought cannot be the sentence-token.

The same line extends beyond English. Monolingual Spanish speakers and monolingual English speakers both believe that 1 + 1 = 2. Yet they do not use the same sentences. Therefore the thought that 1 + 1 = 2 cannot be identical with an English sentence or with a Spanish sentence. More generally, speakers of different natural languages can share one and the same thought. That fact is unintelligible if thought just is inner speech in this or that public language.

So paraphrase, disambiguation, and cross-linguistic sameness all converge. Version #1 is false because meanings cut across sentence-types, while sentence-types differ within and across languages.

## Understanding a sentence already presupposes thought

There is an additional point, and it reaches deeper than the previous ones. Understanding a sentence is itself a cognitive achievement that cannot be reduced to the sentence’s mere occurrence in consciousness. One may hear a sentence in a language one does not understand; later the sounds may flash through one’s mind exactly as a familiar song does. But one still does not know what it means. So the occurrence of the auditory image is not understanding.

To understand “if snow is cold, then snow is not hot,” you must pair the sentence with the right meaning. That pairing is an act of thought. It is not identical with the sentence’s sounding inwardly in one’s head. Therefore, if having the thought that if snow is cold, then snow is not hot were identical with an inner occurrence of that sentence, then understanding and mere mental rehearsal would collapse into one another. They do not. Hence thought is not natural-language rehearsal.

This also clarifies why the inability to verbalize a thought refutes the linguistic theory so directly. If thinking were itself inner English or inner Spanish, then there could be no gap between having the thought and producing the sentence, except perhaps a motor gap. But the actual gap is semantic. One can have the meaning while still searching for the words. That would be impossible if the words constituted the meaning.

## Version #2: an innate code, or “language of thought”

A more sophisticated defender of linguistic thought may abandon public languages and retreat to an innate code. On this view, we do think in sentences, but not English or Spanish sentences. We think in a hard-wired symbolic system, a **language of thought**.

Some of the previous objections apply immediately. If images and perceptions have analogue structure, they are not obviously reducible to sentence-like digital items. And if the same thought can be expressed by different public sentences, that already suggests that the thought itself is not identical with any sentence as such. But the most serious objection to the innate-code theory is different: it is viciously circular.

Knowing a language involves understanding the expressions belonging to it. To understand expressions is to know the rules assigning meaning to them. This applies to any language whatever, including an innate one. But if all thought depends on that innate language, then one could know those rules only by already understanding the expressions, and one could understand the expressions only by already thinking in the code. The explanation runs in a circle: thought is explained by understanding the code, and understanding the code is explained by thought.

The circularity is not benign. It is explanatory failure. A code can mediate thought only if there is already a thinker able to take it as meaningful. But that is precisely what the theory was supposed to explain.

## Why “built to conform” does not rescue the innate-code view

Advocates of the innate-code picture respond by saying that, strictly speaking, we do not understand the sentences of the innate code. We are merely “built to conform” to them. The code is supposed to cause behavior appropriate to its meaning even though no one understands it. If the internal item meaning fire is hot occurs, it may dispose one to approach fire when cold and avoid it when hot, without any explicit interpretation.

But this move empties the notion of sentence of the very feature that made it explanatory. If a sentence is not understood by anyone, then from that creature’s point of view it is not functioning as a sentence. The chapter’s analogy is exact. Suppose one has a book and hurls it at one’s roommate as a weapon. The object is a book in one sense, but in that context it is not functioning as a book. For all intents and purposes, it is functioning as a projectile. Likewise, if internal “sentences” are never understood, then they are not functioning as sentences. They are merely neurological items causing behavior.

At that point, the claim that thought is identical with sentences becomes artificial and implausible. One has reintroduced symbolic language in name while removing the essential element of symbolism, namely meaningful use or understanding. The theory no longer explains thought through language; it merely redescribes causal mechanisms in linguistic vocabulary. That is not an account of thinking in words.

## Why it feels as though we think in words

Yet there remains a powerful phenomenological fact. It often does feel as though we think in words. When one reasons through a problem, one often hears an inner voice. When reading, one may mentally “switch voices”: after reading Frege for a time and then turning to Dave Barry, one may momentarily be startled by the apparent oddity of what “Frege” is now saying, until one notices that the text has changed and the inner voicing should change with it.

The correct conclusion is not that the voice is the thought. It is that **mental imagery** often accompanies thought and assists it. Mental images may be auditory, as in inner speech, or visual, as in mathematics. Many students of calculus and more advanced mathematics rely on visual surrogates. But these images are not constitutive of the ratiocinative activity itself. They are too feeble and schematic. One may use a five-sided figure to stand for a ten-sided figure simply because one cannot visualize the latter. The image need not depict the object exactly. It needs only to be sufficiently differentiated from other images so that it can serve as an icon for the relevant concept.

This matters. If the image can be inexact while the thought remains exact, then the image cannot be the thought. A creature might undergo the very same sequence of images without possessing the concepts those images represent in an actual reasoner’s cognition. No matter how conceptually impoverished a creature is, little follows about what images can occur in its consciousness. Therefore images, whether verbal or visual, are at best aids, not the essence of thought.

The chapter’s diagnosis is elegant: we mistake the accompanying icon for the ratiocinative process because consciousness is full of phenomenologically pregnant items—images, sensations, felt episodes—whereas thought itself is not phenomenologically pregnant in that way. The absence of a vivid phenomenal signature tempts one to identify thought with the images that accompany it. That temptation should be resisted.

## Against the assimilation of thought to overt or inner symbol-manipulation

Wittgenstein, according to the chapter, drew the wrong lesson from the fact that sensations and images are not thoughts. He concluded that thinking is not a private psychological act, but consists in overt behavior involving public symbols. The argument of this chapter rejects that as rank absurdity.

The right inference from the inadequacy of images is not that thought is non-mental. It is that not all psychological activity consists of sensations and images. One knows, for example, that one believes that 2 + 2 = 4, and one knows it relatively directly; but not by inspecting some sensation or image. Thought is psychological without being imagistic in the manner of tickles, itches, and pains.

Moreover, meaningful use of language presupposes thought. If I bark out sounds while having no idea what they mean, I am not really speaking. For noise-making to count as speech, it must be guided by knowledge of meaning. Thus the symbol-manipulation account reverses the order of dependence. Thought is not constituted by meaningful linguistic performance; rather, meaningful linguistic performance depends upon prior thought.

This is also why any code theory requires a standard of correct application that cannot itself be just more code. Thinking requires making judgments about whether a sound has this meaning rather than that one, whether a sentence is paired with the right content, whether a sign has been used correctly. But a judgment of correctness cannot simply be another uninterpreted sign. For then the problem would recur: that further sign would itself require correct application and interpretation. So the activity of taking a code to be correctly used must rest on non-linguistic thought.

## The proper role of the inner voice and other icons

The inner voice is therefore best understood as the mind’s use of linguistic icons to stabilize and direct otherwise difficult thought-processes. The chapter gives the computer-desktop analogy. On a computer, one manipulates icons to control patterns of electrical activity that the icons only schematically represent. Similarly, in reasoning, one manipulates verbal or visual imagery to manage patterns of ratiocinative activity that would otherwise be hard to control.

This explains both the utility of language and the falsity of the thesis that thought is language. Knowledge of language enhances cognitive capacity because linguistic and imagistic icons let us hold steady, sequence, compare, and revisit complex contents. In consciousness there are different streams of cognitive activity; imagery helps bring them into a manageable field. The inner voice, in particular, can stabilize attention during complex reasoning. It gives one something discrete and repeatable to work with. But that is a functional aid, not an identity claim. The icon is to the thought as the desktop symbol is to the electrical process: a handle, not the thing handled.

So when it feels as though one is thinking in words, what is typically happening is that linguistic imagery is serving as an instrument of attentional control and cognitive management. The words are not the thought any more than the polygon one visualizes in a mathematical proof is identical with the concept it helps one track.

## The regress against an innate language of thought

The final difficulty for the innate-code theory is that it does not merely circle; it threatens a regress. Suppose one says that an innate language of thought underlies all public-language thought. Then either that innate code is understood or it is not. If it is not understood, it is not functioning as language. If it is understood, then that understanding must consist either in grasping a further code or in non-linguistic cognition. If in a further code, the same question arises again: is that further code understood? If yes, by what? Another code? Then the regress begins. If no, then again it is not functioning as language. The only way to stop the regress is to admit a level of understanding not constituted by the interpretation of code at all.

That is exactly the chapter’s conclusion. Thought cannot be fundamentally linguistic, whether in English, Spanish, or an innate symbolism. Language is learned only by a thinker already capable of judgment. Sentences are understood only by being paired with meanings through thought. Paraphrase, ambiguity, and cross-linguistic sameness show that thoughts are not sentence-tokens. The familiar inner voice and the imagery that accompanies reasoning are genuine cognitive aids, but they are icons—schematic, manageable, phenomenologically vivid stand-ins by which we guide activities that are not themselves words.
