The result is not that language is cognitively unimportant. On the contrary, language enormously enhances intelligence. It lets us manage thoughts that we otherwise could not manage. But enhancement is not constitution. However much language enriches thought, whatever can be grasped through language must be graspable independently of language, because language itself can only be learned, interpreted, and used by a creature already able to think.

title: Perception and Conception
blurb: A rigorous account of perception and thought as fundamentally descriptive, and of meaning as thinner than cognition.
body:
# Perception and Conception

## Perception as the grasp of a uniquely satisfied existence-claim

The governing thesis is that **perception** is **purely descriptive**. To say that perception is descriptive is to say that what sense-perception gives us is not an object itself, as though the mind first seized a bare particular and only afterwards attached properties to it. What perception gives is the truth of an **existence-claim**: a claim that there exists something, here and now, of such-and-such a kind, with such-and-such characteristics, arranged in such-and-such ways. An object is perceived when it **uniquely satisfies** that existence-claim.

The book’s example of the rock named “R” makes the point with precision. You see a rock and immediately recognize it as the very rock Joey threw at your car. That recognition is psychologically immediate; but immediacy is not identity. We must distinguish:

1. what your eyes tell you, and
2. what, given your backlog of knowledge, you read into what your eyes tell you.

Your eyes do not tell you, “that’s R over there.” For all that is encoded in the visual message itself, you could be looking at a perfect duplicate. Indeed, the visual message is consistent with R’s no longer existing at all. What the eyes tell you is rather:

- there is a rock over there,
- having such-and-such characteristics.

Call that an existence-claim. R happens to satisfy it; and because of your antecedent knowledge, you identify the seen thing as R. But the perception itself carries no R-specific message. This is why perception is descriptive rather than object-involving in any stronger sense. The object perceived is the unique satisfier of what perception represents as instantiated.

This explains why the view does not collapse into skepticism about ordinary perception. We do see objects. But we see them by being perceptually apprised of truths of the form: there is exactly one thing here, now, with these relevant features. The object figures in perception only as that which makes the descriptive content true.

## Why one never perceives a bare object plus its properties

The second thesis deepens the first. You never perceive a bare object plus its properties. You perceive **organized property-instances** and **relation-instances**. A **property-instance** is an instance of a property had at a time and place; and the book stipulates that this terminology covers instances of relations as well.

Suppose you are looking at Pat. What does the visual episode contain? It contains instances of shape-related features, color-related features, motion-related features, and relations among them. You see not merely patches, lines, and movements, but these as organized: one thing to the right of another, something behind something else, a contour bounding a region, a movement continuous with a shape. The visual field is a coherent structure because the property-instances are represented as interrelated.

Now consider the tempting alternative: perhaps in seeing Pat one sees, in addition to these various instances, Pat himself as something over and above them. The book rejects this as absurd. If perception represented an object independently of the properties by which it is presented, the object would have to be represented as a **featureless blank**—a blank, undifferentiated lump to which properties were somehow added. But a featureless blank is precisely not something perceptually represented. The very idea is a non-starter. An object cannot be visually present apart from the very morphological, chromatic, and kinematic instances in which it is visually given.

So there is nothing to seeing Pat beyond seeing the relevant organized property-instances. Perception is not dual-layered, with a bare particular underneath and perceptual features above. It is a single descriptive representation of a structured field.

## Conception is descriptive for the same reason

What is true of perception is true also of **conception**, that is, thought or thinking-of. Conception, like perception, is fundamentally descriptive. To think of a thing is to grasp some existence-claim it uniquely satisfies. Russell, as the book notes, saw this.

This must be stated carefully. We obviously think about rocks, people, trees, and inscriptions. But things are objects of thought only in a derivative sense. Strictly speaking, the immediate objects of thought are always truths or falsehoods concerning things. To think of R is not to entertain R itself in some bare, objectual way. It is to think some proposition concerning the thing that satisfies a certain description: for example, that there is exactly one rock related to Joey’s attack on your car in such-and-such a way, or that the uniquely relevant rock has such-and-such features.

The argument mirrors the argument about perception:

1. A thing cannot be cognitively represented as a featureless blank any more than it can be perceptually represented that way.
2. Therefore thinking of an object cannot consist in mentally grasping a bare object independently of any descriptive content.
3. So thinking of an object consists in entertaining some truth-condition that only that object satisfies.

The object enters thought only as the satisfier of propositional content. There is, then, no gulf here between perception and conception. Both are descriptive through and through.

## Semantic rules are thin; their acquisition is not

Once thought and perception are understood in this way, the relation between thought and language can be correctly drawn. **Literal meaning** is what an expression or utterance means by the semantic rules of the language. **Cognitive content** is what a thinker is actually taking in or conveying, which can be richer than literal meaning. The book insists that these are systematically related but not always identical.

This matters because semantic rules are descriptively threadbare when compared with the perceptual and cognitive richness from which they are learned. The source gives the beginning of a simple case. You meet a person for the first time. He tells you his name: “Fred.” At that very moment you also see what he looks like, notice how he is behaving, and register a range of features—hair color, bodily movement, mannerisms. The semantic rule attached to the name is thin: this use of “Fred” concerns that man. But the route by which the name is learned is saturated with pre-semantic descriptive information.

The point is not merely developmental. It is structural. Names, common nouns, and other expressions function within a practice whose rules are comparatively spare; yet mastery of those rules is achieved only against a background of richly organized perceptual acquaintance with property-instances and relations. Before one can competently deploy an expression, one has already been presented with a mass of non-linguistic information. Semantic competence is therefore rooted in perception without being reducible to the whole of what perception delivers.

That is why one must not infer from richness of cognition to richness of literal meaning. Language rides atop a richer descriptive basis.

## Spare literal meaning and rich implicated content

The fifth thesis follows directly. An utterance can literally mean something spare while implicating something much richer absorbed from its pre-semantic context. The book’s distinction between literal meaning and cognitive content is designed precisely to block their conflation.

Suppose two speakers produce the same sentence. Even if they are in the same psychological state, it does not automatically follow that the utterances have the same meaning; Putnam’s Twin-Earth discussion shows this. But another, complementary point is also true: even when an utterance has a determinate literal meaning, what a speaker is cognitively bringing to it, and what hearers take from it, can be much richer.

Why? Because hearers do not process utterances in a vacuum. They bring to them perceptual information, stored knowledge, and contextual assumptions. In the “Fred” case, the introduction of the name occurs alongside a thick perceptual uptake of the speaker’s appearance and behavior. The literal semantic contribution made by the name is meager compared with the total cognitive package present in the encounter. The utterance is therefore semantically spare though cognitively rich.

This is exactly why the book urges care in moving from thought to language. Facts about what is mentally or perceptually available to the subject do not settle the semantic value of the expression; and facts about literal meaning do not exhaust what is cognitively conveyed in context.

## The structure of seeing: morphological, chromatic, kinematic organization

The sixth thesis returns to perception and states more concretely what its descriptive content is. Seeing an object involves seeing instances of its **morphological** properties, its **chromatic** properties, and its **kinematic** properties, all organized into a structure. Morphological properties are shape-related properties; chromatic properties are color-related properties; kinematic properties are motion-related properties.

This triad matters because it blocks any oversimplified picture on which perception reports only a list of detached features. When you see Pat, you do not receive:

- one isolated shape,
- one isolated color,
- one isolated movement.

You see an articulated whole. Certain contours bound certain colored regions; certain motions are motions of these regions; certain parts are to the right of others, behind others, above others. The relations among instances are as essential as the instances themselves. A coherent visual scene is constituted by represented relations no less than by represented properties.

The example of the last word of a sentence makes the same point from another angle. Your eyes tell you not merely that there is morphology of a certain kind and chromatic information of a certain kind; they tell you that in that location at that time there is exactly one such relevant inscriptional item. Perception is already structured toward individuation through organization. It is because the property-instances are arranged in a unique way at a place and time that an object is visually presented as one object.

Thus the descriptive content of perception is highly articulated without ceasing to be descriptive. It is not bare acquaintance with a thing; it is perceptual registration of a uniquely instantiated structure.

## Perception is always of propositions: truths or falsehoods

This leads naturally to the claim that perception is always of truths or falsehoods—of **propositions**. A proposition, in the present use, is something that can be true or false. The book states that the objects of thought are always truths or falsehoods, and the same pattern governs perception. What one sees is that such-and-such is the case: that there is a thing of such-and-such a kind over there, or that there are property-instances arranged thus.

This may sound strained only if one begins with the mistaken picture of perception as object-grasping prior to all predication. But once the “featureless blank” model is rejected, propositionality becomes unavoidable. Since what perception delivers is that there exists exactly one thing here and now with certain indexed properties and relations, perceptual content already has truth-conditions. It can be accurate or inaccurate. It says, in effect: there is such-and-such.

The rock case again illustrates the point. The visual system does not deliver R itself. It delivers something like:

- there is a rock over there with such-and-such characteristics.

That content is true if there is such a rock there, false if not. Perception is therefore not pre-propositional. It is not the mind’s passive receipt of a bare object, but its sensory apprehension of a proposition.

This is not a verbal thesis masquerading as psychology. The book stresses that the apprehending can be visual rather than verbal. One need not silently articulate a sentence in order perceptually to grasp an existence-claim. The claim is about the structure of the content, not about inner speech.

## Why sensory messages do not report identity

The eighth thesis is one of the chapter’s sharpest. Every sensory message is consistent with the non-existence of the object one takes oneself to perceive. Therefore the senses report property-instantiation, not identity.

Take any sensory modality. The information it delivers can in principle be duplicated. Given only what your eyes tell you, you might be seeing a duplicate of R. Given only what your ears tell you, the source might be numerically different though qualitatively alike. So for any particular external object O, the sensory message is consistent with O’s not existing. This generalizes the point made about the rock: no sensory message, taken by itself, says of any particular object that it itself is present.

From this the conclusion follows:

1. If a sensory message reported identity with a specific object, it would not be consistent with that object’s non-existence.
2. But every sensory message is consistent with that object’s non-existence.
3. Therefore sensory messages do not report identity with specific objects.

What they report are instances of properties and relations at times and places. Identity is supplied, if at all, by the subject’s collateral knowledge. That is why recognition, however immediate, is never to be confused with the bare perceptual deliverance. The senses tell us that some thing of a certain sort is there; they do not tell us that it is this very individual rather than a duplicate.

## Thought about things as derivative of propositional thought

The ninth thesis simply states in the cognitive case what the previous points have established in the perceptual case: to think about a thing is derivative of propositional thought. Really to think about a thing is to think that some truth holds concerning it.

The formulation “about a thing” is ordinary and harmless, provided one remembers the derivative status of the object. Strictly, one thinks that the rock Joey threw had such-and-such characteristics, that Pat is standing before one, that the word on the page has a certain morphology, that Fred is behaving nervously. In each case the content thought is propositional. The thing enters as that concerning which the proposition is true or false.

This claim also helps explain why conception must be descriptive. If all thought is fundamentally of truths and falsehoods, then any seeming object-directedness must be analyzed through the truth-condition entertained. To think of Pat is to think some proposition only Pat satisfies under the circumstances. To think of water, likewise, is not merely to entertain a private image or conception; what the word means and what proposition the utterance expresses outruns the merely psychological state, as Putnam shows.

Smith in the seventeenth century can think and say true things about water without knowing that water is H2O. Yet his utterance means what it does because “water” refers to the substance that is in fact H2O. Twin-Smith, who is psychologically indistinguishable and produces the same noises, expresses a different proposition because on Twin-Earth “water” refers to XYZ. This confirms two connected points:

- thought about things is propositionally articulated;
- what words mean is not exhausted by the speaker’s inward cognitive state.

## The standing confusion: perception versus identification

The final thesis gathers the rest. We constantly confuse what the eyes tell us with what prior knowledge reads into that deliverance. This confusion is natural because identification is often instantaneous. But philosophical clarity requires a strict separation.

When you see your fiancée at your wedding, or when you see R again after many years, recognition may occur without any conscious inference. It may be obvious. Still, the eyes do not report: that is my fiancée; that is R. What they report is a richly organized set of morphological, chromatic, kinematic, and relational instances, amounting to an existence-claim uniquely satisfied by some object there and then. Your history, memory, and background knowledge transform that perceptual content into identification.

The same confusion recurs in language. Because learning a name or using a word occurs amid rich pre-semantic perception and thought, one is tempted to pack all that richness into literal meaning. But the book’s distinction between cognitive content and literal meaning forbids that. Semantic rules are thinner than the cognitive lives in which they operate. Putnam’s Earth/Twin-Earth case then shows that even the literal meaning of an utterance is not determined solely by what is in the head. Smith and Twin-Smith are molecule-for-molecule alike and utter the same sounds with the same sentiments, yet one utterance concerns H2O and the other XYZ.

The central lesson is therefore double. First, both perception and conception are descriptive: they consist in the apprehension of propositions, especially existence-claims uniquely satisfied by objects. Second, language must not be confused either with the totality of cognition or with the whole richness of perception from which its use is learned. We perceive organized property-instantiations; we think truths or falsehoods concerning things; and only against that background do we identify, name, and mean.

Once these distinctions are held firmly in place, the tempting myth of direct presentation—the myth that we first grasp bare objects and only later say or think things about them—falls away. What remains is a more exact picture: the senses deliver structured descriptive content; thought inherits that descriptive form; and language, though tethered to thought, has semantic contours that are often leaner than cognition and partly fixed by the world itself.

# Names, Reference, and Literal vs. Implied Meaning

## Mill on names: denotation without connotation

The first point is Mill’s thesis that **proper names** denote without connoting. To **denote** is to pick out an object; to **connote** is to present that object as falling under some descriptive condition. On this view, a name such as “Larry” contributes one thing to literal meaning: its bearer. It does not literally mean *the man with such-and-such features*, *the person I met yesterday*, or *the one who uniquely satisfies some associated description*. That is why names are **rigid designators**, whereas descriptions are not.

The contrast with a **definite description** is immediate. “The author of *Hamlet*” presents whoever fits a condition: being the unique author of *Hamlet*. “Larry” does not work that way. If the semantic rule for “Larry” were descriptive, then understanding the name would require associating it with some condition, and the name would shift with shifts in which object satisfies that condition. But a genuine name does not shift in that way. It picks out one individual, and in every possible world in which that individual exists, the name still picks out that same individual.

That is the force of calling names rigid. A **possible world** here is simply a way things could have been. To say that “Larry” is rigid is to say: once the bearer is fixed, the name continues to designate that very object across counterfactual situations. By contrast, a description such as “the author of *Hamlet*” is governed by satisfaction-conditions. In one world Shakespeare uniquely authored *Hamlet*; in another, someone else did; in another, no one did. So the description’s semantic contribution varies with what satisfies it. That is non-rigidity.

This Millian thesis is not a superficial point about style of speech. It is a thesis about logical and semantic structure. The denoting role of names differs fundamentally from the descriptive role of descriptions, and much philosophical confusion begins when one mistakes the latter for the former.

## Russell’s decisive break: definite descriptions are not singular terms

Russell’s Theory of Descriptions sharpens that difference by denying that definite descriptions are **singular terms** at all. A singular term is an expression whose semantic role is to stand for an individual. Russell’s claim is that “the phi” does not do that. Although a sentence like “The inventor of Velcro is intelligent” has the same grammatical shape as “Bob is intelligent,” its **logical form** is quite different from its **grammatical form**.

Russell’s analysis proceeds by examining truth-conditions. “The inventor of Velcro is intelligent” is true only if:

1. at least one person invented Velcro,
2. at most one person invented Velcro, and
3. whoever did so is intelligent.

So the sentence says: **something uniquely invented Velcro, and any such thing is intelligent**.

This shows that “the inventor of Velcro” is not functioning as a referring expression whose contribution is some object. The sentence does not work by first supplying an individual and then predicating intelligence of that individual. Rather, it works by quantifying: it says there exists exactly one thing with a certain property, and that thing has another property. Russell’s canonical insight is that “the phi is psi” does not have the semantic structure name-plus-predicate. It has quantified structure.

That is why definite descriptions are contextually defined. Their meaning is given not by assigning them a referent, but by specifying what whole sentences containing them mean. The description contributes to a pattern of existential and uniqueness claims. Hence Russell’s two defining claims:

1. definite descriptions do not refer to anything;
2. sentences containing them, in virtue of that fact, attribute properties to properties rather than to individuals.

“The inventor of Velcro is seven-feet tall” is thus about the property of uniquely inventing Velcro and the property of being a seven-feet-tall inventor of Velcro. It is not semantically a simple statement about Bob, even if Bob actually invented Velcro.

## Literal meaning and what exceeds it

Once that distinction is clear, the third thesis follows: a name’s **literal meaning** is exhausted by its referent. Whatever richer material accompanies the use of the name belongs not to semantics proper but to **implicature**, that is, to what is conveyed or suggested without being literally encoded.

The source text insists on a crucial separation between thought and language. **Cognitive content** is what one thinks; **literal meaning** is what the words semantically say. These need not coincide. Human thought is fundamentally descriptive: to think of an object is to think some existence-claim it uniquely satisfies. Perception too is descriptive. Your eyes tell you, not “that is R” or “that is Pat,” but that there exists, here and now, an organized structure of property-instances of such-and-such kinds. Recognition goes beyond bare perception; it combines present sensory information with stored knowledge.

Exactly the same distinction matters for names. A speaker may use “Larry” while relying on a mass of descriptive material: that Larry has no mustache, that he is this person rather than that one, that he is the one encountered in such circumstances. But none of that descriptive material is the name’s literal meaning. It belongs instead to the pre-semantic basis on which communication succeeds. The communicated message often carries more than the sentence literally says, because hearers naturally import the descriptive basis used in identifying the referent. But that importation is not itself semantics.

The result is austere but powerful: if “Larry” is a name, then semantically its role is just to denote Larry. Not Larry-as-the-man-with-no-mustache, not Larry-as-the-one-we-both-know, not Larry-under-any-description at all. Those enrichments may be psychologically indispensable in thought and conversation, but they are not part of the literal meaning.

## Why competent speakers distinguish falsity from contradiction

That distinction explains the fourth point. Competent speakers can separate literal meaning from implicature. Thus “Larry doesn’t have a mustache” is merely false, not self-contradictory, even if the descriptive information by which a speaker fixed the referent of “Larry” included that Larry lacks a mustache.

If the meaning of “Larry” included the description *the man without a mustache*, then “Larry doesn’t have a mustache” would come out analytic, while “Larry has a mustache” would be contradictory. But competent speakers do not treat these utterances that way. They understand perfectly well that one can discover, perhaps to one’s surprise, that Larry in fact has a mustache. That discovery would show that some associated belief was mistaken; it would not show that one had failed to understand the name.

This is exactly parallel to the perceptual point in the source text. When you see Pat, what perception itself gives you is an existence-claim involving property-instances. You may immediately recognize Pat, but that recognition incorporates stored information not contained in the raw perceptual content. Likewise, when you use a name, you may immediately connect it with descriptive information. But that information is not part of the semantic rule for the name. Otherwise ordinary empirical corrections would collapse into conceptual impossibilities.

A contradiction arises when a sentence’s truth-conditions cannot possibly be met by virtue of its meaning alone, as with a “square circle.” Mere falsity occurs when the world fails to match a meaningful claim. “Larry doesn’t have a mustache” can be false because Larry has a mustache; but it is not self-contradictory, because the name itself does not encode mustachelessness.

## Reference-fixing is not meaning-giving

This leads directly to the fifth thesis: **reference-fixing** is not **meaning-giving**. To fix the reference of a name is to settle which individual the name picks out. To give its meaning, in the semantic sense, is to state the rule by which the expression contributes to literal truth-conditions. Those are not the same act.

A description may be used to introduce or secure a name’s bearer. One may effectively say: let “Larry” name the man standing there, or the person with such-and-such features, or the one we met yesterday. But once the reference is fixed, the description falls away from the semantic content of subsequent uses. It may explain how users latched onto the bearer; it does not become what the name means.

The source text’s discussion of perception makes this entirely intelligible. You can recognize R as the rock Joey threw at your car, but the sensory content itself does not contain an R-specific message. Similarly, you can come to use “Fred” after meeting someone and registering his brown hair and nervous hand-wringing. Those descriptive features constitute the pre-semantic basis on which you identify him. But the literal meaning of “Fred” is not a conjunction of those observed features. If it were, then any error in those observations would alter the name’s meaning, which is absurd.

So there is no inference from “a description fixed the bearer” to “the name means that description.” Reference-fixing belongs to the psychology and epistemology of identification; meaning belongs to semantics. The book’s entire distinction between thought and language is designed to prevent exactly this conflation.

## Rigidity: names track one object across worlds

Now the sixth point can be put with precision. Names are rigid because they pick out the same object in every possible world in which that object exists. Once “Larry” denotes Larry, then in considering a world where Larry shaved, or grew a beard, or changed careers, or never had a mustache, we are still talking about Larry. The counterfactual variation concerns Larry’s properties, not the name’s referent.

This is the natural result of Mill’s doctrine. If a name denoted by connoting a descriptive profile, then changing the world could change which object, if any, satisfies the profile; that would make the name non-rigid. But if the name’s literal meaning is exhausted by the bearer itself, then the semantic role remains constant across worlds. The same object is designated throughout.

Notice how this differs from the descriptive structure of thought. Since conception is descriptive, a thinker may use different existence-claims to think about the same person. But the semantics of the name need not mirror that structure. The temptation to transfer the descriptive architecture of cognition into the semantics of names is precisely the temptation the book rejects. Rigid designation is the sign that the transfer has not occurred.

## Why descriptions are non-rigid

By contrast, descriptions like “the author of *Hamlet*” are non-rigid. Their contribution depends on which, if any, object satisfies the descriptive condition in the world under consideration. In one possible world Shakespeare authored *Hamlet*; in another Bacon did; in another the work was collaboratively written and so had no unique author; in another *Hamlet* was never written. The description therefore shifts or fails across worlds.

This follows from Russell’s theory of their logical form. Since “the phi is psi” quantifies, its truth depends on whether the property phi is uniquely instantiated and whether the unique phi is also psi. Since those facts vary from world to world, the semantic behavior of the description varies with them. There is no individual x such that, for all worlds semantically like ours, “the phi has psi” is true iff x has psi. The source text makes this point with “the inventor of Velcro”: even if Bob is actually the inventor, a world in which Bob exists but did not invent Velcro is a world in which the sentence may have a different truth-value without any change in semantics. That is enough to show that the description’s meaning is not exhausted by Bob.

Descriptions, then, are satisfactional rather than referential in the relevant sense. They are governed by unique instantiation, not by rigid objecthood.

## The Frege-Russell mistake about names

The eighth point is subtler. Frege and Russell were right that our concepts of people are descriptive. They were wrong to infer that the names for those people must therefore be descriptive too.

The source text gives the core reason. Perception and conception are fundamentally descriptive because objects cannot be represented as “featureless blanks.” To think of Pat is to think some existence-claim uniquely satisfied by Pat; to see Pat is to be apprised of a structured array of property-instances uniquely associated with him here and now. Russell saw this about thought. But from the truth that cognition is descriptive it does not follow that language must encode that same descriptiveness in the semantics of names.

That inference conflates two levels:

1. the **pre-semantic** level, where speakers identify, recognize, and think about objects by means of descriptive information;
2. the **semantic** level, where expressions contribute to literal truth-conditions.

Frege and Russell noticed, correctly, that we know and think of people under descriptions. But then they allowed that fact about cognition to govern their account of names. The book’s correction is to separate cognitive content from literal meaning. One may need descriptive resources in order to use “Socrates” or “Hesperus,” but it does not follow that the name itself literally means a description.

This is why competent speakers can be ignorant or mistaken about the bearer’s properties while still understanding the name. The descriptive material is part of how they find the person, not what the name semantically says.

## “Hesperus is Phosphorus” and the source of informativeness

The ninth thesis applies this distinction to a famous identity statement: “Hesperus is Phosphorus.” If names had only their referents as literal meaning, then the sentence, semantically considered, says of one object that it is identical with itself. Why, then, is it informative?

The answer is not that the sentence has hidden descriptive meanings encoded in the names. Rather, the informativeness arises because the **pre-semantic information** used to fix the names is smuggled into the communicated message. Speakers and hearers commonly attach to “Hesperus” one route of identification and to “Phosphorus” another. The sentence is therefore heard against a background of distinct descriptive dossiers. When one learns that Hesperus is Phosphorus, what one gains is not a new semantic rule for either name, but the discovery that the two pre-semantic routes converge on a single object.

This fits exactly with the book’s larger doctrine. Cognitive content often outstrips literal meaning. Communication rides on a systematic relation between the two, but not an identity relation. “Hesperus is Phosphorus” is informative because hearers do not process it as the bare logical form *a = a*. They import the descriptive basis by which each name was independently fixed or cognitively grasped. The semantic core is thin; the communicated content is thick.

That is not an accident or a defect. It is the normal structure of meaningful discourse involving names. Semantics supplies reference; cognition and conversation supply descriptive enrichment. Confusion enters only when the enrichment is mistaken for the literal meaning.

## Why “Socrates died of hemlock” is not a tautology

The final point follows almost mechanically. “Socrates died of hemlock” is not a tautology. A **tautology** is true purely in virtue of meaning or logical form. But one can know the semantic rule for “Socrates” without knowing Socrates’ biography. To understand the name is just to know whom it names; it is not to know that he was a philosopher, that he taught Plato, or that he died of hemlock.

If the name “Socrates” literally meant some descriptive content including death by hemlock, then the sentence would be analytically guaranteed. But it plainly is not. It reports a substantive historical fact. A person could fully grasp the language, competently use the name, and still be ignorant of that fact. Learning it would enlarge the person’s knowledge of Socrates, not the person’s understanding of the word “Socrates.”

The same pattern underlies the earlier case of Larry’s mustache. One may associate a name with descriptive information, even biographical information, and still find that information corrected by experience. Those corrections are empirical, not semantic. Literal meaning remains stable while one’s descriptive beliefs change.

The general lesson is now in view. Names and descriptions differ at the level of semantics. Descriptions quantify and are non-rigid; names denote and are rigid. Our thought about objects is indeed descriptive, and our use of names depends heavily on descriptive, pre-semantic materials. But that fact about cognition does not convert names into disguised descriptions. Once literal meaning is sharply distinguished from what is implied, suggested, presupposed in thought, or imported by hearers, the central phenomena fall into place:

- why definite descriptions are not singular terms,
- why names can be rigid,
- why identity statements involving names can be informative,
- why ordinary predications about named individuals are empirical rather than analytic,
- and why speakers rightly distinguish contradiction from mere falsity.

Mill supplies the essential insight that names denote without connoting. Russell supplies the machinery for seeing that descriptions do not refer but quantify. The book’s own contribution is to place both insights within a broader account of the relation between thought and language: conception is descriptive, but literal meaning need not be. Once that distinction is respected, names can do exactly what names do—pick out their bearers, and no more—while the richness of ordinary communication is explained by the descriptive basis that speakers and hearers bring to the act of reference.

title: Necessity, Possibility, and the Analytic–Synthetic Distinction

body:
# Necessity, Possibility, and the Analytic–Synthetic Distinction

## Modality belongs to propositions, not to things

A **modal statement** says what **must** be the case or what **could** be the case. Thus, “Triangles must have three sides,” “It’s possible to make money without selling out,” and “There’s no way anyone could have survived that fall” are modal because they ascribe necessity or possibility. The first point to get clear is where these modal properties are located. They are not properties of objects. They are properties of **propositions**.

The basic equivalences are straightforward:

1. For any proposition *P*, it is **necessary** that *P* iff it is **not possible** that not-*P*.
2. It is **possible** that *P* iff it is **not necessary** that not-*P*.

So if it is necessarily the case that Jim is in the barn, then it is not possible that Jim is not in the barn. And if it is possibly the case that Jim is in the barn, then it is not necessary that Jim is not in the barn. These are relations among propositions: Jim-is-in-the-barn, Jim-is-not-in-the-barn.

This matters because ordinary language tempts us into a false ontology. We say “square circles cannot possibly exist,” and the surface grammar invites us to think we are talking about a peculiar sort of object, an **impossible object**. But that is exactly wrong. What “square circles cannot possibly exist” really says is that the proposition “there are square circles” cannot possibly be true. It does **not** say that there exists some object that is both a square circle and unable to exist. That would be self-defeating nonsense.

Likewise, “happiness is a possibility for Jim, even though he’s still miserable” does not posit some object—Jim’s as-yet nonexistent happiness—which hovers in a limbo of mere possibility. It says only that the proposition “Jim is happy” could be true. There are, then, no impossible objects and no merely possible but non-actual objects. There are only propositions that are impossible, propositions that are possible, propositions that are true, and propositions that are false.

The same point appears in the treatment of existence and non-existence. “Fred Flintstone doesn’t exist” cannot mean that there is some object, Fred Flintstone, that has the property of non-existence. Nothing doesn’t exist. There exists no *x* such that *x* doesn’t exist. Rather, what exists is a statement, encoded in the cartoon or story, roughly to the effect that there exists a boorish man with a pet dinosaur named Dino, a wife named Wilma, and so forth. That statement exists, but it is false. Nothing answers to it. Non-existence, like impossibility, is not a property of objects but of propositions and existential claims.

This is the first indispensable clarification. If one misses it, one begins to populate reality with impossible things, fictional entities, and merely possible individuals. But once the grammar is cleaned up, all that is needed is a sober semantics of propositions.

## Necessity has no degrees

A second confusion follows quickly from the first. It is natural to say that some truths are “more necessary” than others. “Squares have four sides” seems necessary in the strongest sense. “Metal expands when heated” seems necessary in some weaker sense. “After surgery, people are unusually prone to get infections” may seem weaker still. The temptation is to posit **degrees of necessity**.

That view is false. There are only two degrees of necessity: having it completely and lacking it completely.

Why, then, do some statements seem more necessary than others? Because what varies is not necessity itself but the **conditions required for truth**.

The argument is simple:

1. A proposition is necessary if it cannot be false.
2. If a proposition can be false, then it is not necessary at all.
3. What differs among propositions is the range of circumstances under which they hold.
4. Therefore, apparent “degrees” of necessity are really differences in how much assistance a proposition needs from the rest of the world in order to be true.

“Squares have four sides” is maximally necessary because it holds unconditionally. No matter how mass-energy is distributed in the universe, it is true. Nothing special has to happen for it to come out true. By contrast, “metal expands when heated” requires a great many conditions concerning the physical constitution of things. And “after surgery, people are unusually prone to get infections” requires still more specific biological and medical conditions.

So when we say the first is “more necessary” than the second, we are not really assigning a greater amount of necessity to it. We are saying that fewer conditions need to obtain for it to be true. The proposition receives less help from contingent reality. In that sense, “two is bigger than one” needs almost no help, while “people who wear hats are bad drivers” would need a great deal.

Necessity itself is not scalar. A proposition either holds in all possible circumstances or it does not. Once one sees that modality belongs to propositions, this follows naturally. What varies is the proposition’s dependence on further truths, not its modal status.

## There is no necessary a posteriori

This prepares us for the chapter’s most pointed controversy: the rejection of the **necessary a posteriori**, that is, the denial that there are truths that are both necessary and knowable only through empirical investigation. Kripke’s celebrated example is “Hesperus is Phosphorous.” The author’s claim is uncompromising: there is no necessary a posteriori, and Kripke’s argument depends on a confusion between a name’s threadbare semantic rule and the rich pre-semantic information through which we attach the name.

The Kripkean reasoning runs as follows. The ancients used one term for the last celestial body to disappear from the morning sky and another for the first celestial body to appear in the evening sky. Both turned out to be Venus. That discovery was empirical and non-trivial. Yet, if “Hesperus” and “Phosphorous” are rigid designators—names that refer to the same object in every semantically identical world—then “Hesperus is Phosphorous” is true exactly if Venus is identical with Venus, and identity with itself is necessary. Hence, a non-analytic necessary truth.

The reply is that this argument contains a massive non-sequitur. To expose it, the chapter constructs a story.

Suppose I meet a man face to face, and he tells me his name is “Hesperus.” What I thereby learn, semantically, is only this:

- “Hesperus” is *x*’s name.

Call this the threadbare semantic rule. It is exceedingly thin. It merely assigns a label to an object. It says nothing about height, mustache, location, or date. Yet the information through which I learn that rule is rich and descriptive: there is some individual standing before me in my office in Richmond, Virginia, at 3:00 P.M. on March 13, 2009, with such-and-such characteristics, and he is telling me his name is “Hesperus.” That descriptive material is not part of the meaning of the name. It is **pre-semantic**. It helps me latch the name onto the right object.

The next evening I receive a threatening phone call from someone using a voice-modulation device, who says his name is “Phosphorous.” Again, semantically I learn only:

- “Phosphorous” is *y*’s name.

But again the information through which I learn it is much richer: there is some individual calling at around 7:00 P.M. on March 14, disguising his voice, making threats, and announcing that “Phosphorous” is his name. That too is descriptive and pre-semantic. It is not part of the semantic rule.

Now notice what happens in communication. If the police tell me “Phosphorous is a professor of political science,” the literal content is simply that *y* is a professor of political science. But what is conveyed to me, given the pre-semantic background, is far richer: the threatening caller is a professor of political science. Likewise, if someone says “Hesperus is an avid tennis player,” what I take away is that the man I met in my office—the tall, mustached man who said his name was Hesperus—is an avid tennis player. The conveyed content is enriched by prior descriptive information that is not itself part of the semantics of the name.

Kripke’s mistake is to treat this rich, non-semantic, discovery-enabling information as though it were somehow built into the proposition itself. The ancient astronomers indeed made an empirical discovery, but the discovery was not that a bare identity statement with rigid names expresses a special sort of necessary truth knowable only a posteriori. Rather, empirical investigation was needed to determine that the two thin naming-rules latched onto the same object. The empirically gained material belongs to the pre-semantic stage of assignment, not to the semantics of the names once assigned.

So the truth at issue is not a necessary empirical proposition. The necessity belongs only to the trivial identity of the object with itself. The empirical labor belongs to learning that both names attach to that one object. Kripke’s argument slides illicitly from one to the other. It confuses what is semantically contained in the proposition with the descriptive route by which a speaker comes to know which object the names denote.

## Analytic truth as structural truth

Once that confusion is removed, necessity falls back where it belongs: on **analytic truth**. An **analytic truth** is best understood as a high-resolution **structural truth**. It is true in virtue of its structure together with the substructure of its constituents.

This must be stated carefully. It is not enough to say vaguely that analytic truths are “true by meaning,” if that slogan suggests something occult. The better thought is this: some propositions are such that, once one grasps the internal articulation of the proposition and the internally articulated content of its terms, denial collapses into incoherence.

“Triangles have three sides” is an obvious case. The proposition is not made true by how mass-energy happens to be distributed. Its truth is secured by the structure of the concept triangle and the role of three-sidedness within that structure. Similarly, “squares have four sides” holds unconditionally. No contingent assistance is needed.

This account also explains why the chapter insists there is no necessary a posteriori. If necessity is grounded in structure and constituent-substructure, then a necessary truth is one whose falsity is excluded by what the proposition itself is. Empirical inquiry may be required to determine whether some contingent proposition is true, but when truth is necessary, the necessity comes from the proposition’s own articulated content, not from the world’s supplying some hidden essence discovered by experiment.

Analyticity, then, is not a verbal triviality. It is structural necessity at a high level of resolution.

## Why Quine’s denial of analyticity defeats itself

The analytic–synthetic distinction is often challenged by denying that there is any principled boundary between truths true by meaning and truths true by fact. But the denial is self-defeating. If there were no analytic truths, then the very notion of confirmation would collapse, and nothing would confirm anything.

Why? Because confirmation requires that evidence count in favor of a claim by standing in some intelligible relation to it. But the relation between evidence and hypothesis itself presupposes conceptual articulation. If no statement’s content is fixed in a way that makes some inferences or incompatibilities hold independently of further factual discovery, then no evidential connection can even be identified as a connection rather than a mere causal accompaniment.

Put negatively: to deny analyticity is to deny that any negation can be ruled out as conceptually incoherent. But then no statement has determinate content sharp enough for observation to bear on it as confirmation rather than as just one more event in the stream. If all statements face experience only as an undifferentiated corporate body, then the notion that this observation supports that statement loses any clear sense. One does not save empiricism by abolishing analyticity; one abolishes confirmation.

That is why the attack on analyticity turns on itself. It presents itself as an epistemological austerity, but its consequence is epistemic bankruptcy.

## Analyticity and incoherence

We can now state the criterion directly. A statement is **analytic** when its negation is **incoherent** or **internally inconsistent**. This is the operational heart of the distinction.

The phrase “internally inconsistent” must not be treated loosely. It does not mean merely surprising, deeply entrenched, or hard to imagine false. It means that the denial falls apart by virtue of the structure of what is said. “Squares do not have four sides” is not false because the world happens not to cooperate. It is false because the negation destroys the very content of square. Likewise, “there are square circles” is not an exotic metaphysical possibility blocked by the universe; it is an incoherent proposition.

This criterion explains the first thesis as well. When we say that square circles cannot exist, what we really say is that the existential proposition “there are square circles” is internally inconsistent. The impossibility is a property of the proposition. There is no object lurking there with the strange feature of being impossible.

Analyticity is therefore identified by the collapse of its negation into nonsense or contradiction. The modal status and the semantic status align: what is analytic is necessary because its denial is incoherent.

## Formal truth as one species of the analytic

Among analytic truths, some are **formal truths**. A formal truth is true under all interpretations. Its truth depends on logical form alone. But it is a mistake to identify analyticity with formality. Formal truth is only a special case of analytic truth.

The distinction is easy to mark. A statement may be true solely because of its logical structure, independently of what non-logical terms mean; that is formal truth. But many analytic truths depend not merely on logical form but on the meanings, or internal substructures, of non-logical terms. “Triangles have three sides” is not true under all interpretations of its non-logical vocabulary. Its truth depends on what “triangle” and “three sides” mean. It is analytic, but not merely formal.

This is why the earlier characterization of analytic truth as high-resolution structural truth is useful. Some structures are purely logical; others include the constituent-content of terms. The formal case is the limiting case where logical structure by itself suffices.

Thus:

1. Every formal truth is analytic.
2. Not every analytic truth is formal.

The difference matters because otherwise one might suppose that only the truths of logic qualify as necessary in virtue of structure. But the book’s point is broader: there are also informal analytic truths grounded in conceptually articulated meaning.

## Against naturalized epistemology

The denial of analyticity often travels together with **naturalized epistemology**, the proposal that epistemology should simply become part of science. But that position is incoherent for a precise reason. Science cannot scientifically prove that observation is a source of knowledge.

Any scientific inquiry already presupposes that observation yields knowledge. Scientific testing, measurement, and confirmation all rely on observational input as evidence. To ask science itself to establish that observation is epistemically authoritative is therefore to ask a practice to validate the very condition of its possibility by using that condition. The procedure is circular.

The incoherence is parallel to the earlier self-defeat. Once the conceptual distinction between clarification and discovery is blurred, epistemology is swallowed by empirical inquiry. But empirical inquiry cannot, from within its own methods, justify those methods’ epistemic credentials. It can describe how observers form beliefs; it cannot, by those same observational procedures, prove that observation is genuinely a source of knowledge.

So naturalized epistemology does not replace traditional epistemology. It presupposes what it cannot establish. And the suppressed presupposition depends on precisely the sort of conceptual distinction the rejection of analyticity would dissolve.

## Informal analytic truths depend on meaning, not form alone

This is why examples such as “triangles have three sides” are so important. They are **informal analytic truths**. Their truth turns on the meanings of their terms, not on logical form alone.

Suppose one tried to assimilate all necessity to formal logic. Then one could account for identity statements like *x* = *x*, but not for the necessity of geometrical or conceptual truths. Yet “triangles have three sides” is no less unconditional than “squares have four sides.” It does not become true only under favorable physical circumstances. It is true because the constituent concept triangle includes three-sidedness in its very structure.

The negation—“some triangle lacks three sides”—is not a surprising empirical possibility awaiting disconfirmation. It is conceptually incoherent. That is exactly what makes the truth analytic.

This also shows why the chapter’s critique of Kripke matters. If one mistakes empirical procedures for parts of meaning, one will begin to imagine that necessity attaches to discoveries made by observation. But in reality the observation helps us identify objects, attach labels, or discover contingent features. Analytic necessity rests elsewhere: in the articulated content of propositions whose negations are internally inconsistent.

## Why the analytic–synthetic distinction must be preserved

Everything culminates here. The **analytic–synthetic distinction** must be kept because without it one cannot mark the difference between **clarifying a concept** and **discovering a fact**.

To clarify a concept is to expose the structure and substructure already contained in a proposition or term. When one explains that triangles have three sides, or that squares have four sides, one is not adding a worldly discovery to the concept. One is articulating what was already there. The work is conceptual, structural, semantic.

To discover a fact is different. It is to determine, by empirical means, how the world is. Learning that metal expands when heated, or that after surgery people are unusually prone to get infections, requires the world’s cooperation in a way analytic truth does not. Such truths need more help from surrounding conditions. They are not less necessary; they are simply not necessary at all. Their truth is contingent on how things happen to be.

And the Hesperus–Phosphorous case, properly understood, does not undermine this distinction. It illustrates it. The empirical inquiry belongs to discovering that two names attach to one object. The necessity belongs only to the identity of that object with itself and to the threadbare semantics once the names are fixed. Confusing the descriptive, pre-semantic route of discovery with the proposition’s literal semantic content generates the illusion of a necessary a posteriori.

Once one rejects that illusion, the map is clean:

- modality belongs to propositions, not to objects;
- necessity is all-or-nothing, though propositions differ in how many conditions they require for truth;
- analytic truth is structural truth whose negation is incoherent;
- formal truth is one species of such analyticity, not its whole extent;
- and the distinction between analytic clarification and synthetic discovery is indispensable both to logic and to epistemology.

Without that distinction, not only do necessity and possibility become confused; confirmation, observation, and scientific knowledge themselves lose their footing.
