body:
# A Priori vs. A Posteriori Knowledge

## The analytic/synthetic division and the epistemic division

The chapter’s central contention is that the distinction between **a priori** and **a posteriori** knowledge is not an independent distinction floating free of the distinction between **analytic** and **synthetic** truth. The two lines coincide. To say that a truth is **a priori** is to say that it is knowable independently of sense-perception; to say that it is **a posteriori** is to say that it is knowable only through sense-perception. To say that a truth is **analytic** is to say that it is true in virtue of the meanings or contents of the concepts involved; to say that it is **synthetic** is to say that its truth outruns conceptual content and depends on how things stand in the world. The book’s position is that these are not two cross-cutting distinctions. They are one and the same division seen under two descriptions.

That claim has to be earned. It is not enough merely to announce that analytic truths are a priori and synthetic truths are a posteriori. One must explain what sort of object each kind of knowledge concerns, how such knowledge is acquired, why empirical knowledge presupposes non-empirical knowledge, and why celebrated counterexamples—most notably Kripke’s alleged cases of the necessary a posteriori—fail.

## 1. Analytic knowledge as conceptual knowledge

**Analytic knowledge** is acquired by analyzing the object of belief. The analysis here is **conceptual analysis**: one attends to what is contained in the concept and thereby sees what must be true of anything falling under it. If one knows that circles are figures of uniform curvature, that knowledge is obtained not by surveying circular things in space and time, but by understanding what it is to be a circle. The mind inspects the concept, not the world.

That is why analytic knowledge is often called **conceptual knowledge**. Its paradigm cases are truths like “triangles must have three sides” and, more generally, truths whose denial would be incoherent because the predicate is already contained in the subject-concept. The source text formulates this modal point by saying that statements such as “Squares have four sides” hold unconditionally. No distribution of mass-energy could make them false, because they are not hostage to any empirical arrangement of particulars.

This way of knowing is possible because thought and language necessarily involve **universals**—properties, characteristics, natures, or ways of being. Sense-perception gives us only particulars: this page, that light-ray, this person, that event. But to think that Bob and Ted are both human, or that Hitler and Stalin had much in common, is already to traffic in universals. The chapter insists that every sentence and every thought demands at least one universal. Analytic knowledge is knowledge of relations among such universals: for example, that being a square entails having four sides, or that being a circle entails uniform curvature.

The crucial point is methodological. In analytic knowledge, one does not discover by observation that circles happen, so far, to exhibit uniform curvature. One sees that if something lacked uniform curvature, it would not be a circle. The object of scrutiny is the concept itself.

## 2. Synthetic knowledge as non-conceptual knowledge

By contrast, **synthetic knowledge** includes a non-conceptual component. No analysis of concepts by itself settles it. Whether Rumsfeld was born in the United States is the kind of fact one cannot extract from the concept of Rumsfeld or from the concept of being born in the United States. One must look to the world. The proposition is about a particular individual in a particular historical circumstance.

The source text repeatedly emphasizes the **particularist nature of sense-perception**. Perception discloses particular objects with particular property-instances. That is exactly the kind of material from which synthetic knowledge is drawn. If the truth depends on where a certain person was born, whether a certain celestial body appears first in the evening sky, whether someone survived a fall, or whether metal expands when heated, then conceptual analysis is insufficient. In each case, the concepts may be perfectly clear while the truth remains unsettled until the world is consulted.

This gives synthetic knowledge its distinctive character. It is not merely that such truths are harder to know. It is that their truth is not fixed by the concepts involved. Even complete command of the meanings leaves open multiple ways the world might be. Thus the synthetic has a non-conceptual element built into it from the start.

## 3. Spatiotemporal facts versus timeless relations among properties

This difference in method tracks a difference in subject matter. **Synthetic/a posteriori knowledge** concerns **spatiotemporal facts**: what is the case in space and time, with respect to particulars and their arrangements. **Analytic/a priori knowledge** concerns **timeless relations among properties** or universals.

The chapter’s anti-empiricist argument is indispensable here. Universals are not in space-time. They cannot be perceived, because perception requires causal interaction, and causal relations hold only among spatiotemporal entities. Yet universals are presupposed by all explanation and all thought. If Max stole the money because he is greedy and amoral and believed it strategically advantageous, the explanation invokes universals such as greed, amorality, money, and theft. These are not themselves visible items; rather, they are the structures in terms of which particulars are understood.

A priori knowledge therefore concerns this non-spatiotemporal order: how properties are related, what follows from what, what is included in what. Such truths are timeless not in the sense of being old, but in the sense of not depending on temporal occurrences. It is no part of the world’s history that triangles have three sides. The truth does not wait on events.

By contrast, a posteriori truths are precisely those tied to worldly arrangements. That Hesperus is the first celestial body to appear in the evening sky and that Phosphorus is the last celestial body to disappear from the morning sky are matters about the behavior of a celestial body under observational conditions. Such facts occupy space-time. So too does anyone’s birthplace.

## 4. No necessary a posteriori and no synthetic a priori

From this, the book draws a strong conclusion: there is **no necessary a posteriori** and **no synthetic a priori**. The a priori/a posteriori distinction tracks the analytic/synthetic distinction exactly.

Why deny the mixed categories? Because necessity belongs to truths that hold independently of the empirical distribution of particulars. The source text says necessity does not come in degrees: something either is necessary or is not. Necessary truths are those that hold unconditionally; contingent truths are those whose truth depends on conditions. But the truths whose content is fixed by spatiotemporal facts are precisely the ones whose truth depends on how the world happens to be. Those are synthetic and empirical. Conversely, truths knowable independently of sense-perception are precisely truths secured by conceptual content or by relations among universals; those are analytic and necessary.

So the proposed hybrid categories collapse. A **necessary a posteriori** truth would have to be both fixed by empirical reality and yet independent of all empirical contingency. A **synthetic a priori** truth would have to outrun conceptual content and yet be knowable without appeal to experience. The chapter treats both combinations as incoherent once the underlying categories are properly understood.

This is not a verbal stipulation. It follows from the nature of the objects known. The synthetic concerns particulars in space-time; the analytic concerns non-spatiotemporal relations among properties. The first cannot yield necessity; the second cannot require observation.

## 5. Non-empirical knowledge as a prerequisite for empirical knowledge

The argument does not stop with the claim that some knowledge is non-empirical. It goes further: **non-empirical knowledge is itself a prerequisite for empirical knowledge**.

Empiricism says that all knowledge derives from sense-perception. The chapter rejects this on the ground that perception by itself gives only particulars, never universals; but without universals there can be no thought, no language, no explanation, and therefore no knowledge worthy of the name. To know empirically that Bob and Ted are both human already presupposes grasp of the universal humanity. To describe a perceived item as wet, red, circular, metallic, or alive is already to classify it under universals that are not themselves given in sense-perception.

The step-by-step structure is straightforward:

1. Sense-perception discloses only particulars and property-instances.
2. Knowledge, thought, and language require universals or properties.
3. Universals are non-spatiotemporal and cannot be sense-perceived.
4. Therefore, our grasp of universals cannot come from sense-perception.
5. Therefore, some non-empirical knowledge is presupposed by every empirical judgment.

This is why empiricism in its strict form is indefensible. Even the empiricist, in reporting what is seen, must already possess concepts whose content is not itself read off from sensory contact. The chapter’s examples—“Hitler and Stalin had a lot in common,” “Smith has what it takes to be a great pianist,” “Smith is different from Jones”—all reveal that ordinary, obvious truths depend on quantification over properties. Empirical knowledge is parasitic on prior conceptual resources.

## 6. A priori knowledge as built into the structure of mind

The book’s rationalism should not be misunderstood as claiming that the mind first stares directly at Platonic objects in some mystical way. The more modest and defensible point is that **a priori knowledge is available merely in virtue of how the mind is structured**. It is like software bundled with a new computer: not derived from what the machine later receives as input, but already part of what makes reception and processing possible at all.

That comparison captures the asymmetry between empirical input and conceptual capacity. A new computer can receive data only because it already has the operating structure required to handle data. Likewise, a mind can form empirical judgments only because it already has access to certain conceptual relations and logical capacities. The chapter’s argument about universals presses exactly this point. We do not first accumulate sensations and then somehow infer the very possibility of classification. Rather, classification is already built into our manner of cognition.

This is why a priori knowledge is non-trivial. Rationalists, the chapter says, hold that reason is the vehicle through which some knowledge is acquired, and that such knowledge is important. If universals are indispensable to explanation and if their existence cannot be observationally grounded, then reason’s contribution is not ornamental. It is foundational.

## 7. Why “Hesperus is Phosphorus” is not necessary a posteriori

The most famous challenge comes from Kripke’s claim that “Hesperus is Phosphorus” is a necessary truth known only a posteriori. The chapter rejects this. Its core reply is that the literal identity at issue is just the analytic truth **x = x**.

The ancients used one expression for the last celestial body to disappear from the morning sky and another for the first celestial body to appear in the evening sky. Eventually they discovered that one and the same celestial body fit both descriptions. That discovery was empirical, but what they discovered empirically was not a necessary identity between two names as such. The empirical discovery concerned a contingent astronomical fact: that the thing answering one description also answered the other.

The chapter insists on distinguishing the sentence from the proposition discovered. If “Hesperus” and “Phosphorus” are directly referring names of the same object, then the literal semantic content of “Hesperus is Phosphorus” is simply that Venus is Venus, that is, x = x. And that is analytic and a priori. No empirical investigation is needed to know that anything is self-identical.

What required empirical investigation was not the literal identity proposition, but the fact that the thing called by one name was also the thing fitting the other associated description. That is not necessity discovered by observation; it is contingent astronomical information conveyed by the use of those names in a community that had attached different descriptive associations to them.

## 8. Literal meaning versus contingent connotation

The illusion of the **necessary a posteriori** arises from conflating a sentence’s **literal meaning** with its contingent **connotations**. This is the decisive diagnosis.

A name may carry descriptive associations in use. “Hesperus” may suggest the first evening star; “Phosphorus” may suggest the last morning star. Those connotations are historically and empirically loaded. One can learn through observation that the bearer of one associated description is also the bearer of the other. But the literal semantic contribution of each name, on the direct-reference view adopted here, is just the object itself, not the associated description.

Once this distinction is observed, the puzzle disappears:

1. The sentence “Hesperus is Phosphorus” literally expresses a self-identity, since both names designate Venus.
2. Self-identity is analytic and knowable a priori.
3. The informative, empirical content comes from the contingent descriptive connotations attached to the names in ordinary use.
4. Therefore, what is a posteriori is not the necessary identity itself, but the contingent descriptive information communicated alongside it.

The same pattern explains why identity statements can seem substantial. They often function pragmatically as vehicles for telling us that one thing satisfying one description also satisfies another. But that communicated information should not be mistaken for the sentence’s literal content.

## 9. Rigid designators and semantic rules

This account also explains **rigid designators**. A rigid designator is an expression that picks out the same object in every possible world in which that object exists. The chapter’s explanation is austere: names do this because their **semantic rules** do not depend on the object’s properties.

If a name referred by means of a descriptive property—say, by meaning “the LMS” or “the FES”—then a change in the object’s properties across possible worlds could change the referent or leave the expression empty. But proper names, on this account, do not work that way. Their reference is direct. The rule is not “whoever uniquely satisfies such-and-such properties,” but simply: this object.

That is why “Hesperus” and “Phosphorus,” if they are genuine names, each designate Venus in every possible world relevant to the semantics of those names. The name does not wait on Venus’s continuing to be the first evening star or the last morning star. Those are contingent features or associated descriptions. The referential rule is indifferent to them.

So rigid designation does not support the necessary a posteriori. It supports the claim that once reference is fixed directly, an identity of names has an analytic literal content. The necessity comes from self-identity; the empirical element comes from contingent descriptive associations used in fixing or communicating reference.

## 10. Direct reference and the fate of identity statements

The final consequence is precise. Since names refer directly, an identity between two names is either:

1. an **analytic triviality**, if taken literally, because both names contribute the same object and the sentence says only that the object is identical with itself; or
2. a vehicle for communicating a **contingent description**, namely that the object associated by one route of acquaintance or description is also the object associated by another route.

There is no third option in which an identity of names is both literally non-trivial and necessary while also known only by experience. If the statement is about the object directly, it is x = x. If it informs us, that informative content derives from contingent descriptive material in the background.

This mirrors earlier points about existence and modality. Just as “square circles cannot possibly exist” is really a claim about a proposition’s impossibility rather than about some impossible object, so too the force of identity claims must be located at the level of proposition and semantics, not in a mysterious realm of necessary empirical discoveries. “The present King of France” is not a name of a strange non-existent object; it is part of a false existence-claim. Likewise, “Hesperus is Phosphorus,” insofar as it seems substantial, borrows its substance from descriptive contingencies, not from a special class of necessary empirical truths.

The larger philosophical moral is that epistemology, semantics, and metaphysics lock together. Because thought requires universals, empiricism fails in its strict form. Because universals are non-spatiotemporal, some knowledge must be rational rather than sensory. Because analytic truths concern timeless relations among properties, they are knowable a priori. Because synthetic truths concern spatiotemporal particulars, they are knowable only a posteriori. And because names refer directly, Kripkean examples do not break this alignment. The line between a priori and a posteriori knowledge is the line between analytic and synthetic truth itself.

title: Knowledge by Acquaintance, Self-Knowledge, and the Intuitive vs. Discursive
blurb: On why acquaintance mostly reduces to propositional knowledge, with self-knowledge as the central partial exception.
lectureTitle: 2.4 Knowledge by Acquaintance, Self-Knowledge, and the Intuitive vs. Discursive
body:
# Knowledge by Acquaintance, Self-Knowledge, and the Intuitive vs. Discursive

## The ambiguity of knowing, and why it matters

The ordinary word “know” is ambiguous. Sometimes it marks **awareness of objects**: “I know Smith.” Sometimes it marks **awareness of truths**: “I know that snow is white.” The book’s central claim is that this ambiguity is not merely verbal. It tracks a distinction that matters epistemologically. Yet the distinction does not remain intact once we ask what, exactly, a subject is aware of in purported cases of acquaintance. The pressure of analysis pushes us toward the thesis that what appears to be knowledge of objects is, in most cases, reducible to **knowledge of truths**, that is, to justified true belief with propositional content.

The initial reason is simple. Knowledge, in the philosophical sense, is primarily **justified true belief**. A subject knows only if:
1. the content is true,
2. the subject believes it,
3. the belief is justified.

Now object-awareness does not itself fit this triad unless it can be reconstrued as involving belief with truth-conditions. “Knowing Smith,” if it is to be epistemically assessable, must amount to some set of truths one is in a position to believe truly and with justification: that this man is Smith, that he has such-and-such features, that one has met him before, that one can identify him again, and so on. This is why languages sometimes distinguish the two notions and sometimes do not. The collapse of one into the other is not a mere logical faux pas; it has, as the chapter says, a “solid epistemological basis.”

## Acquaintance largely collapses into knowledge of truths

The first thesis, then, is that awareness of objects largely collapses into knowledge of truths, so that acquaintance is mostly descriptive and propositional. Why should this be so?

Because when one claims to know an object, what one can actually justify is always some proposition about it. Perceptual justification, **perceptual evidence**, is evidence delivered through the senses: sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell, bodily sensation, the sense of motion, the sense of resistance. But perceptual evidence does not hand us a bare object detached from judgment. It justifies beliefs: that there is a computer in front of me, that the stove is hot, that one cup is heavier than another. Even the most ordinary perceptual case has propositional form.

To put the point more sharply: an object can only figure in knowledge by entering a proposition. Chapter 3 gives the metaphysical background. A **proposition** is what is meant by an utterance of a sentence, and propositions are sets of properties. “Tommy is smoking” is not a bare relation to Tommy; it is a structured proposition involving at least:
- something individuative of Tommy,
- the property of smoking,
- and a synthesizing property, the property of being identical with something that is smoking and is identical with Tommy.

Knowledge therefore attaches, strictly speaking, to a proposition whose truth consists in the joint instantiation of the relevant properties. If one says “I know Tommy,” the epistemically respectable content must be analyzable in that same style: truths involving something individuative of Tommy and properties he instantiates. Acquaintance, once made answerable to justification and truth, becomes descriptive.

This is why the apparent immediacy of object-awareness is misleading. What the subject can know is never merely Tommy, but that this is Tommy, or that Tommy is smoking, or that Tommy is before me. Every such case has propositional articulation.

## The likely exception: direct awareness of one’s own conscious states

There is, however, a likely exception, and it is of great importance: direct awareness of one’s own conscious states, especially paradigmatic cases such as intense pain. Here appearance and reality seem to merge.

The contrast is with ordinary perception. In perception, one can seem to see a computer and yet there be no computer. One can seem to hear something and be mistaken. The sensory message, taken by itself, does not guarantee the existence of the external object. But in introspection, at least in certain cases, the situation is different. **Introspective evidence** is direct awareness of one’s own mental contents. I may be aware that I am thinking about the theory of knowledge, or about this chapter, or about tonight’s dinner. In the case of severe pain, the distinction between how things appear and how they are seems to collapse: if it introspectively appears that I am in intense pain, then I am in intense pain. There is no further gap to be bridged between seeming and being.

That is why this case is the best candidate for genuine non-descriptive acquaintance. The subject is not inferring from sensory signs to an external cause. Nor is the subject identifying an object under independent criteria. The state is just present to consciousness. Here the object known and the truth known threaten to become inseparable, because the truth “I am in pain” is grounded in the conscious state itself, not in evidence that points beyond it.

Still, even here the knowledge takes propositional form when stated. What makes the case exceptional is not that it escapes truth altogether, but that the proposition is justified by a kind of awareness in which the reality itself is manifest.

## Self-knowledge: partly direct, largely theoretical

From this follows the next thesis: some self-knowledge is more direct than external knowledge, but much self-knowledge is theoretical and indirect.

The direct portion consists in introspective awareness of current conscious contents. I can know directly that I am having thoughts, and even what I am now thinking about, without seeing or touching those thoughts and without drawing an inference. This is a genuine epistemic advantage over knowledge of the external world, which standardly combines perception with **rational inference**. External knowledge often requires moving from sensory presentation to a judgment about what exists.

But it would be a grave mistake to generalize this directness to the whole of the mind. Much of what we say about ourselves is not introspectively given. To know why I acted as I did, what enduring belief I hold, what dispositional tendency I have, what repressed hostility or unacknowledged motive operates in me—these are not all simply read off from consciousness. They are, rather, inferred from behavior, memory, patterns of thought, and other evidence. They are theoretical.

The structure is the same as elsewhere in epistemology. A belief may be justified by:
- perceptual evidence,
- introspective evidence,
- rational inference.

Self-knowledge often uses the second source, but not exclusively. A subject can be mistaken about his own motives for the same reason a subject can be mistaken about the external world: the relevant facts are not wholly present in immediate awareness.

## Unconscious mentality and psychoanalysis

This leads directly to the fourth thesis. Beliefs like “1+1=2” are not constituents of consciousness, so much of the mind is unconscious. In that respect, a core claim of psychoanalysis is vindicated.

The point is not that every mental state is unconscious; plainly some are conscious. The point is that mentality outruns consciousness. If I believe that 1+1=2, that belief is ordinarily not something continuously present within the stream of consciousness. It is not a conscious item in the way a pain or an occurrent thought about dinner may be. Yet it is undeniably part of my mind. The mind therefore cannot be identified with what is currently conscious.

Once that is admitted, the possibility of unconscious belief, motive, and tendency is no longer exotic. It is simply an extension of a familiar fact: we possess knowledge that is not occurrently before consciousness. This supports the idea that self-knowledge often requires interpretation. If a great deal of the mind is unconscious, then introspection can never be the whole story. One must sometimes infer to one’s own mental states, much as one infers to external facts.

The significance for epistemology is considerable. It undermines the fantasy that the mind is transparent to itself. Some self-knowledge is privileged, but the privilege is partial and local, not absolute.

## Intuitive and discursive knowledge, and Moore’s paradox of analysis

We can now understand the distinction between the **intuitive** and the **discursive**. Suppose Timmy and Jones both know that a figure is a circle. Timmy simply sees that it is a circle. Jones also knows it is a circle, but Jones additionally knows the grounds of that judgment and knows the fact under two descriptions. This dissolves Moore’s paradox of analysis.

An item of knowledge is **intuitive** when the subject has the belief without currently grasping or articulating its justification. An item of knowledge is **discursive** when the subject proceeds by articulated grounds, by inference, by explicit awareness of why the proposition is true or justified, or by possession of the proposition under multiple descriptions that reveal its structure.

Thus Timmy and Jones may converge on the same true belief—“it is a circle”—yet differ epistemically. Timmy’s cognition is immediate. Jones’s is reflective and analytically informed. Jones knows not merely that it is a circle, but why that classification is warranted. He can connect the belief to further truths.

This is where Moore’s paradox of analysis loses its sting. The paradox arises when one suspects that an analysis cannot be informative if the analysandum and the analysans concern the same fact. But the Timmy/Jones contrast shows the mistake. The same fact can be known under one description intuitively and under another discursively. There is no contradiction in saying that Jones has learned something, even if the proposition known is, in one sense, the same. What has changed is the structure of justification and the subject’s cognitive access to the grounds.

The book’s metaphysics of propositions helps here as well. A proposition has articulated constituents. To know the proposition discursively is to know more about that articulation—to understand not only that the relevant property-instance is present, but how the proposition is structured, what grounds support it, what descriptions co-refer or co-classify. The gain is not a new object, but a new mode of epistemic possession.

## Discursive thought as remedial

From this we reach a striking thesis: discursive thought is remedial; thought is most efficient precisely insofar as it remains intuitive.

This is not anti-rationalism. It is an account of cognitive economy. The book insists that **procedural knowledge** is genuine knowledge and, indeed, that as knowledge deepens it becomes increasingly proceduralized. What the virtuoso knows procedurally, the incompetent neophyte knows only discursively. Discursive cognition is the mark of knowledge not yet fully integrated.

The same is true here. Intuitive cognition is efficient because the justificatory links have already been built into the system. The subject need not rehearse them. Discursive reasoning is required when those links are missing, weak, or in need of repair. One reasons step by step because one cannot yet simply see. It is therefore remedial—not in the sense of inferior as such, but in the sense of compensating for incomplete integration.

This point is easy to mishandle. Discursive reasoning is often necessary, and without it one cannot acquire or vindicate many beliefs. But the aim of successful thought is not endless discursiveness. It is mastery so well integrated that what was once laborious becomes direct. That is why proceduralized knowledge is not non-knowledge. It is superior integration.

So the intuitive/discursive distinction is not a contrast between primitive blindness and genuine intellect. Rather, intuitive thought often marks the culmination of discursive labor, the point at which justification remains in force though no longer consciously traversed.

## Knowing a person as knowing many truths

With that distinction in hand, we can return to acquaintance in a more concrete form. To “know” a person is usually a derivative way of saying one knows many specific truths about that person.

When someone says “I know Smith,” what is ordinarily meant is not mysterious contact with Smith as a bare individual. It is that one can recognize him, identify him, describe his history, anticipate some of his behavior, distinguish him from Brown, and so forth. The knowledge is a body of truths: that Smith looks thus, speaks thus, has done such-and-such, stands in these relations, instantiates those properties. Even recognition is a propositional achievement: that this person is Smith.

The reduction is not merely semantic. It is epistemological. Justification can attach only to beliefs with truth-conditions. One cannot justify bare awareness of Smith except by citing truths one is in a position to know. The phrase “I know Smith” is therefore derivative shorthand for a dense network of justified true beliefs.

This is why object-knowledge and truth-knowledge are not utterly separate domains. The former is parasitic on the latter.

## Even acquaintance-talk reduces to descriptive recognition of property-instances

The reduction goes further. Even acquaintance-talk reduces to descriptive recognition of **property-instances** rather than contact with bare objects.

Chapter 3 is decisive here. A proposition concerning an individual does not contain the individual as a sheer, unstructured thing; rather, it contains something **individuative** of the individual, a property such as being identical with Tommy. To think of Tommy in a proposition is already to bring him in under a property. Likewise, to judge that Tommy is smoking is to grasp a proposition structured by properties whose joint instantiation makes it true.

So if one says that one is acquainted with Tommy, what one is actually in a position to recognize are instantiations of properties: being identical with Tommy, smoking, being before me, being the same person as the one previously encountered, and the synthesizing property that combines these. The metaphysical lesson and the epistemological lesson coincide. There is no need to posit a primitive, relationless cognitive touch upon a bare object. The content is always articulated.

This also explains why acquaintance can be more or less rich. One may know only a few truths about Smith or many. One may identify him under one description or several. But nowhere is there an epistemically intelligible residue of mere contact severed from predication.

## Sensory messages and existential propositions

The ninth thesis gives the deepest reason for all this. Because every sensory message is consistent with non-existence, the object of thought is always a propositional existence-claim, not the thing itself.

Perceptual experience does not, by itself, entail that the corresponding external object exists. Seeing-as-of-a-computer is consistent with there being no computer. Hearing-as-of-a-sound is consistent with there being no source of that kind. The sensory message underdetermines existence. Therefore what one is justified in believing is not the object itself, but a proposition: that there is a computer in front of me; that the stove is hot; that one cup is heavier than another.

This is why the intentional object of ordinary cognition is propositional. Even when the mind seems to reach directly outward, the content of the belief is existential and descriptive. One does not simply have the object. One believes that something of a certain sort exists or is present. Since the sensory basis is always compatible with non-existence, the epistemic act necessarily takes the form of a claim that such-and-such exists.

That is precisely where the self-knowledge exception differs. In intense pain, the appearance is not consistent with the non-existence of the state. Hence the seeming/reality gap closes. But in perception of external objects, the gap remains, and with it the propositional form of cognition.

## Intuition as belief with currently unknown justification

The final thesis now falls into place. An **intuition** is a belief whose justification is currently unknown to the holder, even though that justification may exist and be valid.

This definition preserves what is right in the contrast between intuitive and discursive knowledge without mystifying intuition. Intuition is not justification-free. Nor is it magical access to truth. It is a case in which the believer has not presently traced or articulated the justificatory route. The route may nonetheless be there. It may consist in perceptual evidence, introspective evidence, inferential integration, or proceduralized competence.

That is exactly how Timmy and Jones differ. Timmy’s belief that it is a circle is intuitive because he does not possess, at least not occurrently, the articulated grounds Jones possesses. Jones’s belief is discursive because he does. Yet Timmy’s belief may still be knowledge if it is true, believed, and justified. The justification need not be transparent to him at the moment.

This conception of intuition also fits the earlier claims about procedural knowledge. When knowledge becomes integrated, one often ceases to carry its grounds consciously before the mind. The justification is not absent; it has become unavailable in current awareness because cognition has become more efficient. Intuition, then, is frequently the phenomenology of well-integrated justification.

The overall picture is therefore tightly unified. Knowledge, strictly speaking, is knowledge of truths. Acquaintance with objects is mostly reducible to propositional, descriptive knowledge. The principal exception lies in direct awareness of certain conscious states, where appearance and reality coincide. Even there, however, what is known is expressible propositionally. Self-knowledge is partly privileged but largely inferential, because much of the mind is unconscious. The intuitive/discursive distinction concerns not whether there is justification, but whether the subject presently knows or articulates it. Discursive thought is the labor required when integration is incomplete; intuitive thought is cognition at its most efficient. And once sensory evidence is recognized as always consistent with non-existence, it becomes clear why the object of thought is not a bare thing but an existence-claim, a proposition structured by property-instances and justified true belief.

title: Skepticism and the Foundations of Knowledge
blurb: A rigorous reconstruction of skepticism, induction, and Descartes’ foundational project through Hume, MC, and direct knowledge.

body:
# Skepticism and the Foundations of Knowledge

## Skepticism as doubt about categories of claim

A **skeptic** is a doubter, not a disbeliever. That distinction matters at once. If I am skeptical of Smith’s assertion that he is an astronaut, I do not thereby believe that Smith is not an astronaut. I suspend acceptance; I question whether there is adequate reason to affirm what he says. Disbelief is a different attitude: it is the positive acceptance of the negation. The book insists on this difference because philosophical skepticism is often caricatured as the thesis that whole domains of discourse are false. Its real form is subtler and more powerful. It is the thesis that we lack sufficient reason to accept claims of a certain kind.

This is why philosophical skepticisms are not ordinarily directed at isolated propositions but at entire classes of truths. One may be skeptical about the external world, meaning that one doubts that sense-perception provides any good reason to believe that one’s experiences represent reality rather than hallucination. One may be skeptical about **inductive inference**, meaning that one doubts whether any **non-deductive inference** can ever yield knowledge. One may be skeptical about **unconscious ideation**, doubting that we have beliefs, feelings, or emotions of which we are unaware. One may be skeptical about **platonic entities**, doubting the existence of non-spatiotemporal entities. One may be skeptical about theoretical entities such as electrons. Earlier philosophy also focused heavily on **universals**, properties or characteristics, and whether they exist independently of thought. In every case, the skeptic targets a category: all truths affirming, or presupposing, entities or methods of a given sort.

The importance of this opening distinction is methodological. Since skepticism is doubt rather than denial, refuting it does not require proving that the skeptical negation is false. It requires showing that there is a logically adequate basis for belief. That is why skepticism presses epistemology toward its central concern: not what is true, but what can be established.

## Hume’s problem of induction and the circle of the Uniformity Principle

The deepest skeptical challenge in this terrain concerns induction. Some knowledge is **direct**: it is not figured out from prior beliefs. If one is experiencing a searing pain, one knows that without inference. Other knowledge is **indirect**: one arrives at it by reasoning from premises to a conclusion. An **inference** has premises, the beliefs or assumptions from which one reasons, and a conclusion, the belief reached thereby. A **deductive inference** is one in which, if the premises are true and the reasoning is non-faulty, it is impossible for the conclusion to be false. If x is a square, then x has four sides. An **inductive inference** is one in which, even given true premises and non-faulty reasoning, the conclusion might still be false. The case of drinking tap water illustrates this: from the fact that I have never become sick from tap water in thirty-five years, it does not follow with logical necessity that I will not become sick from the glass before me.

Hume’s challenge begins from this obvious fact. Consider an enumerative induction: the sun has always risen in the past; therefore, it will rise tomorrow. The argument is not deductive. The sun might explode. So the question becomes: what warrants the move from observed cases to unobserved ones, from past instances to future instances?

The tempting answer is the **Uniformity Principle**, or **UP**: nature is uniform; the past resembles the future; the known resembles the unknown. If nature is uniform, then from the fact that pinewood has floated, metal has expanded when heated, and water has quenched thirst, we may infer that these regularities will continue.

Hume’s point is that this answer collapses into a circle.

1. We do not directly know that UP holds universally, across all times and places.
2. At most, we know only that regularities have held in the fragment of nature we have observed.
3. Any claim extending beyond what has been directly observed must be inferential.
4. That inference cannot be deductive. From the fact that all ravens thus far known to me have been black, it does not deductively follow that ravens not yet known to me are black.
5. So the inference to UP itself must be inductive.
6. But if inductive reasoning is warranted only on condition that UP is already granted, then one cannot use induction to justify UP.
7. Therefore the purported justification of induction by appeal to UP is viciously circular.

The force of the argument is not that induction often fails. Its force is principled. If the very principle needed to license inductive projection can itself be known only by induction, then there is no non-circular justification of induction. That is the skeptical threat.

## The real operative principle: minimization of causal anomalies

The book’s response does not attempt to rescue induction by a more sophisticated formulation of UP. It claims that Hume has identified the wrong principle entirely. The operative principle behind rational non-deductive inference is not that nature is uniform, but that good explanations **minimize causal anomalies**. Call this principle **MC**.

A **causal anomaly** here is an unexplained causal connection, a causal link that a theory must simply take for granted and leave unexplained. If one theory describes the world in such a way that more causal connections are left brute, while another theory explains more of those connections through fewer assumptions, then, other things being equal, the latter is the better theory. MC says precisely this: prefer the theory that leaves fewer unexplained connections.

This shifts the whole epistemological picture. The issue is not whether we are entitled to assume in advance that nature must be uniform. The issue is whether explanatory practice itself commits us to preferring theories that reduce the amount of unexplained causation. A theory is not superior because it predicts more by arbitrary stipulation. It is superior because it explains more while taking less as primitive. The movement from what is observed to what is unobserved is therefore not basically a leap licensed by a global thesis about nature’s sameness. It is an explanatory inference: we accept the account that best systematizes what we observe with the fewest unexplained causal links.

The importance of this replacement will become clearer once we see why MC differs in logical status from UP.

## MC as analytically true, and the breaking of Hume’s circle

The decisive claim is that MC is **analytically true**. To call a principle analytically true is to say that its truth is contained in the concepts involved; it is inherent in the meaning or nature of the matter, not a substantive empirical discovery requiring observational confirmation. The book’s claim is that MC is built into the very concept of an explanation. To count as a better explanation is, in part, to leave fewer causal anomalies.

That matters because a principle that is analytically true does not require inductive validation. Hume’s circle arises only if the principle required to justify induction is itself a contingent, world-directed principle whose scope must be established by inference from observed cases. That is exactly what UP is supposed to be. We observe regularities here and now, then attempt to generalize to all nature. But MC does not purport to describe an empirical regularity spanning all times and places. It articulates a standard internal to explanation as such.

The structure of the reply is therefore:

1. Hume assumes that non-deductive inference requires a substantive empirical bridge principle, UP.
2. Such a principle would indeed need inferential support extending beyond direct observation.
3. If that support were itself inductive, the justification would be circular.
4. But the real principle governing rational non-deductive inference is MC, not UP.
5. MC is analytically true, because minimizing unexplained causal connections is constitutive of explanatory superiority.
6. Therefore MC needs no inductive justification.
7. Hence the circle is broken.

This does not beg the question. To beg the question would be to assume the legitimacy of induction in order to prove the legitimacy of induction. But the appeal to MC does not assume that observed regularities will continue merely because they have continued. It identifies a non-empirical constraint on what counts as a good explanation. Since the standard is conceptual rather than inductively established, the Humean complaint about circularity loses its target.

## Why enumerative induction is secondary, not primary

This reply becomes stronger once one notices a second error in Hume’s setup. Hume treats **induction by enumeration** as the primary form of non-deductive inference: one counts observed instances and projects the pattern. But the book denies that this is epistemologically basic. Enumerative induction is less important than, and subordinate to, **inference to the best explanation**.

That claim reverses the standard order of dependence. On Hume’s picture, explanatory reasoning would have to rest on prior confidence in enumerative induction, since explanations are confirmed by observed regularities. On the book’s picture, the opposite is true. Enumerative induction works only because the projection from observed to unobserved cases is already embedded in an explanatory framework.

Why does the repeated rising of the sun support the claim that it will rise tomorrow? Not because repetition by itself has some mysterious rational force. Mere repetition is inert unless construed under an explanatory description. The same holds for black ravens, floating pinewood, expanding metal, and thirst-quenching water. These do not support future-directed expectations by bare counting. They do so because the best explanation of the pattern makes future continuation more reasonable than competing accounts, and because rival accounts would multiply unexplained causal anomalies.

So enumeration is parasitic. It contributes evidence only within a background practice of explanatory comparison. Once that is seen, Hume’s formulation looks doubly distorted: he mistakes both the governing principle and the primary inferential form. The genuine engine of ampliative reasoning is not counting but explanatory preference under MC.

## Skepticism about the external world

The second great skepticism concerns the external world. Here the skeptical thesis is not that there is no external world, but that we have no good reason to believe that our perceptions represent it accurately. The challenge is starkly Cartesian: I believe that I am now typing on a keyboard. But how do I know this? The obvious answer is that I can see it. Yet that simply reintroduces the question. How do I know that I am not hallucinating or dreaming? Given only that I seem to see a keyboard, it does not follow that there really is one.

The skeptical possibility is a **vast, consistent hallucination** or dream. One’s visual experience as of a table and computer, one’s tactile experience as of resistance in the keys, and one’s memory of similar episodes might all occur even if no external objects correspond to them. Skepticism about the external world is therefore the doubt that perception represents reality rather than merely presenting experience.

This issue creates the pressure toward theories of epistemic structure. A **foundationalist** holds that all knowledge coincides with or rests upon certain self-evident principles, like a building on a foundation. A **coherentist** denies that there are foundational items of knowledge and holds that knowledge emerges when various data support one another in the right ways, allowing reasonable inference. Descartes seeks indubitable foundations. Coherentism, though not his initial strategy, enters because our perceptual lives exhibit extensive mutual support: visual experiences of keyboards are regularly connected with tactile experiences as of touching keyboards; our sensory experiences jointly form a coherent and consistent picture. But regardless of which structure one ultimately accepts, the skeptical problem is the same: what entitles us to move from appearances to reality?

## MC as a logical requirement of explanation, not a mere rule of thumb

At this point MC reappears, now with broader significance. It is not a convenient heuristic, not an empirical rule of thumb that usually works. It is a requirement of the logic of explanation. To explain is to reduce arbitrariness in the pattern of causal dependence one posits. A theory that requires more unexplained explainers is worse for that very reason.

The phrase “fewer unexplained explainers” captures what is at stake. A theory can always be saved by adding further brute causes, hidden interventions, or unexplained coincidences. But such additions degrade explanatory value. If one account of my perceptual life says that there is a stable external world producing my experiences in regular and predictable ways, and a rival says that all of the same order is generated by a massive hallucination, the crucial question is not simply which is conceivable. It is which account leaves fewer unexplained causal connections. A hallucination theory that must take as brute the entire organized match between visual, tactile, and other experiences across time will, other things being equal, suffer from more causal anomalies than the external-world theory.

Thus MC is not merely useful in science. It is integral to the very possibility of preferring one explanation over another. Without it, explanatory comparison would collapse, because any pattern could be accommodated by multiplying unexplained causal links at will. The skeptical scenario would then be irrefutable not because it is better supported, but because explanation itself would have no standards. MC blocks that collapse by fixing the logic of explanatory assessment.

## Direct and indirect knowledge

This connects with the distinction between **direct knowledge** and **indirect knowledge**. Direct knowledge is known without inference. The book’s example is pain: somebody who is experiencing a searing pain knows it and did not have to figure it out. Descartes makes a related point about mind. I can doubt that there is an external world, because I might be dreaming; but I cannot coherently doubt that my mind exists while I am doubting, since doubting is itself a mental activity. Doubt about the existence of mental processes is self-undermining.

By contrast, knowledge of the external world is not direct. For reasons stated in the chapter, no knowledge about the external world is direct, and only some knowledge of ourselves is direct. So if we know anything about tables, keyboards, hands, or the sun’s future rising, that knowledge must be **indirect**. It must be arrived at through inference, deductive or non-deductive.

That is why skepticism about induction and skepticism about the external world converge. If non-deductive inference could not yield knowledge, then almost everything we take ourselves to know about the world would be lost. External-world knowledge cannot simply be read off experience. It has to be figured out from experience, and therefore must be justified by some inferential route. The central issue is whether such inference is legitimate. The book’s answer is yes: indirect knowledge is possible because explanatory reasoning under MC is rationally compelling.

## Incoherent demands and pseudo-tasks

A useful clarification enters here. Some purported epistemic or metaphysical demands are not merely difficult; they are incoherent. An incoherent demand is like the demand for a **square circle**. This does not describe a very hard-to-find object. It fails to describe any possible state of affairs at all, because the predicates are incompatible. Such cases mark **pseudo-tasks**: apparent assignments that do not genuinely specify something that could be done or obtained.

This distinction matters in skepticism because one can formulate demands for justification that only seem rigorous. If a skeptic demands that we produce a kind of establishment whose requirements are internally inconsistent, the failure to satisfy that demand would reveal no limitation in our powers and no defect in knowledge. It would show only that the demand failed to express a coherent possibility.

The point is not to dismiss skepticism cheaply. Hume’s challenge is not a square circle. Descartes’ dream problem is not a pseudo-task. But the distinction disciplines epistemology. One must ask whether a proposed standard of certainty, demonstration, or vindication is genuinely intelligible. If not, then inability to meet it no more counts against knowledge than inability to draw a square circle counts against geometric skill. Philosophical rigor requires not merely raising demands but ensuring that they formulate possible tasks.

## Descartes and the axiomatization of knowledge

Descartes’ enduring importance lies precisely in the rigor of his demand. He believed that nothing ought to be accepted unless there is a logical, rather than faith-based, reason for doing so. Nothing should be taken on faith, not even God’s existence or the legitimacy of scripture. He thus inaugurated analytic epistemology by insisting that beliefs be rigorously established.

Because Descartes was also a great mathematician and the inventor of analytic geometry, his epistemology is shaped by Euclid. Euclid tried to derive all of geometry from a small number of self-evident axioms, truths that neither required nor admitted of justification. Descartes hoped that all human knowledge could be similarly **axiomatized**: derived from a few indubitable first principles. This is the foundationalist ambition in its pure form.

Why does this ambition arise? Because the skeptical problem of the external world is not merely local. If I can doubt whether I have two hands, whether I am typing on a keyboard, whether I am awake rather than dreaming, then what is needed is not a piecemeal reassurance but a structure of justification showing how our representations connect to reality. Descartes seeks self-evident truths from which that connection can be established. The pressure of his method is therefore exactly as the book states: to show that our sense-perceptions are not “just one big hallucination or dream.”

He fails in both grand projects. He fails to refute skepticism conclusively, and he fails to derive all knowledge from a few self-evident principles. Yet the shape of modern epistemology is set by his effort. Foundationalism and coherentism take form against the Cartesian demand. The distinction between what is directly known and what must be inferred becomes central. And the requirement that belief rest on logical reason rather than faith becomes the defining tenet of modern philosophy.

The result is not that we must accept Descartes’ particular conclusions. It is that the problem of knowledge becomes explicit: how, starting from what is indubitable or from what coheres, can we justify the claim that our experiences represent an external world? The book’s own answer joins a Cartesian seriousness about justification with a post-Humean correction about non-deductive inference. Knowledge of the world is not axiomatized in Euclidean fashion from self-evident premises alone. But neither is it undermined by Hume’s circle. It is sustained by explanatory reasoning whose governing norm, MC, is built into explanation itself.

That is why skepticism remains philosophically fruitful rather than merely destructive. By forcing us to distinguish doubt from disbelief, direct from indirect knowledge, deduction from induction, and empirical principles from analytic constraints, it reveals what any adequate theory of knowledge must contain. Descartes supplies the demand for rigorous establishment. Hume sharpens the problem by exposing the circularity in appeals to UP. The resolution proposed here is that the rationality of our non-deductive inferences rests not on a questionable hypothesis that nature is uniform, but on the analytically true requirement that good explanations minimize causal anomalies. Under that requirement, our move from appearances to reality is not blind habit. It is reasoned inference.

title: Empiricism vs. Rationalism
blurb: Why strict empiricism fails, and why a Platonic ontology of properties requires rationalism.
body:
# Empiricism vs. Rationalism

## The collapse of strict empiricism

**Empiricism** is the doctrine that all knowledge is derived from **sense-perception**—from sight, hearing, touch, and the like. **Rationalism** is the doctrine that some knowledge is acquired entirely through the use of reason. The opposition, in the present context, is not between those who accept the senses and those who reject them. Rationalists plainly grant that we know much through perception. The issue is whether perception exhausts the sources of knowledge.

The strict empiricist thesis is indefensible, and the reason is not obscure. Sense-perception gives us only what is particular: this object, that color-instance, this sound, that surface. But our thought and knowledge are not confined to bare particulars. We know, explain, and describe in terms that outrun any particular perceptual encounter. We do not merely register that this thing is thus and that thing is thus; we understand things as falling under kinds, natures, essences, or **universals**.

The argument is straightforward:

1. Sense-perception discloses only particular objects and particular property-instances.
2. Knowledge, explanation, and thought require us to grasp what different particulars have in common.
3. What different particulars have in common are universals or properties.
4. Universals are not themselves perceptible.
5. Therefore, at least some knowledge has a non-perceptual basis.

That conclusion is exactly what strict empiricism denies. So strict empiricism fails. The failure is not at the margins but at the center, because the indispensable structures of thought are not themselves objects of sense.

One might try to evade this by saying that perhaps all that is required is an especially cautious inference from perceptual data. But the chapter’s point is stronger: where universals are concerned, there can be no observational basis at all. The issue is not that the inference is too bold. It is that the sort of thing to be known is of such a kind that no sensory route to it is logically possible.

## Universals and the limits of what can be seen

A **universal** is a property, a nature, a “way of being” exemplified by particulars. The book insists that these are **non-spatiotemporal**: they do not exist in space and time. Because causal relations hold only among spatiotemporal entities, universals are also **causally impotent**. And because one cannot perceive an object without being causally affected by it, universals are **unperceivable**.

This yields a decisive anti-empiricist line of reasoning:

1. To perceive something, one must be causally affected by it.
2. Only spatiotemporal things enter into causal relations.
3. Universals are not spatiotemporal.
4. Therefore universals cannot be perceived.
5. Nor can there be sensory evidence of them, since evidence requires a suitable causal interconnection.
6. Therefore no observational basis for their existence is even logically available.

Yet universals are indispensable. We cannot understand the world except in terms of them. To understand something is to know how, in virtue of having such and such characteristics, it is subject to such and such principles or laws. The book’s example is explanatory:

- Why did Max steal the money?
- Because Max is greedy and amoral and believed it to be to his strategic advantage to steal the money.

This is not a mere list of observed particulars. It explains by subsuming Max under universals: greed, amorality, money, theft, strategic advantage. The explanation works only because those universals are taken to be real determinants of intelligibility. The very idea of an explanation that did not presuppose universals is said to be incoherent. That is exactly right. Explanation is not a heap of observations; it is an account of why a thing, having a certain nature or falling under certain properties, behaves as it does.

So empiricism faces a dilemma. If it denies universals, it cannot make sense of thought, language, or explanation. If it admits universals, it admits objects that cannot be sensed and thus abandons its own principle. The sensible conclusion is not to reject universals but to reject strict empiricism.

## Thought is not exhausted by imagery

The empiricist tradition often tempts one toward the idea that thought is fundamentally imagistic: to think is, at bottom, to entertain some sort of mental picture. The chapter’s discussion of universals already undermines that temptation, but the point can be sharpened. Not all thoughts are pictorial. Some cannot be captured in an image at all.

The relevant cases are thoughts involving logical form: **conditionals**, **negations**, **disjunctions**, and relations of dependence such as “in virtue of,” “for that very reason,” or “ipso facto.” A conditional is a thought of the form *if p, then q*. A negation is a thought of the form *not-p*. A disjunction is a thought of the form *p or q*. These are not kinds of pictures.

An image may perhaps accompany such thoughts, but it cannot constitute them. No image is intrinsically conditional. No image is intrinsically negative. No image is intrinsically disjunctive. If one tries to imagine a negation, one merely imagines something positive and then mentally appends a non-imagistic act of denial. If one tries to imagine a disjunction, one either imagines one disjunct, or the other, or both in succession; but “or” is not itself visible. Likewise for dependence-relations.

The text’s treatment of statements involving “for that very reason” makes the point with special clarity. Consider:

- everything that is square is a rectangle;
- everything that is square is for that very reason a rectangle.

The second does not merely record a co-occurrence. It says that a thing’s being square is responsible for its being rectangular. That “for that very reason” relation is not pictorial. It is a relation among properties grasped by understanding. Similarly, if exactly two square things happened to be green, then “everything that is square is green” would be true, but “squareness is a form of greenness” would be false. The image of two green squares does not reveal the difference. What reveals it is rational grasp of property-relations.

So the attempt to reduce thought to imagery fails because the logical and explanatory structure of thought outruns anything visible or imaginable.

## Why images cannot yield truth

Even where imagery has a role, it cannot account for our grasp of truth and falsity. Images are defective in three different ways.

First, they are **too specific**. Any image of a triangle will be some particular triangle—perhaps equilateral, perhaps scalene, perhaps slanted this way, perhaps large or small. But the thought of triangularity is not tied to these accidental specifics. If one tried to identify the universal with the image, one would illicitly build contingent features into what is meant to be general.

Second, images are **too general**. An image may leave indeterminate what a proposition requires to be fixed. A vague picture may fit countless different descriptions. It does not by itself determine exactly what is being asserted.

Third, images are not **self-referentially true or false**. A belief is true or false; an image, as such, is neither. A mental picture of a square and a circle side by side is not true or false. Truth and falsity belong to what is asserted, denied, judged, or meant—to propositionally articulated thought, not to bare imagery.

That last point is decisive. Grasping truth requires more than possessing sensory or quasi-sensory content. It requires apprehending a content as the case or not the case. Since images themselves are not truth-apt, our understanding of truth cannot be sense-based in the strict empiricist way.

This is why the effort to derive all thought from images is hopeless. The very act of taking something as true already presupposes capacities that outstrip sensation. The senses present particulars. Reason grasps structure, universality, and truth.

## Berkeley’s partial insight and his disastrous conclusion

George Berkeley is especially instructive because he sees one of empiricism’s central problems with unusual sharpness. Locke had held that universals are “the workmanship of the understanding”: we create them so as to make sense of the world. Berkeley objects, in effect, that no **general idea** can be an image. On that point he is right. An image is always this way rather than that, and thus cannot be the very thing common to indefinitely many particulars.

But Berkeley does not take the correct lesson. Instead of concluding that at least some cognition is non-sensory, he remains faithful to empiricist scruples and moves toward the doctrine that objects are identical with our perceptions of them. That is, he slides into **idealism**. The result is not a repair of empiricism but its collapse into an “outrageous doctrine.”

Berkeley therefore unwittingly refutes empiricism at one of its roots. Once one sees that no general idea is an image, one must choose. Either one embraces a rationalist account of our grasp of universals, or one dissolves the external world into perceptions. Berkeley chose the latter. The text clearly takes that to be a reductio of the empiricist impulse.

The correct conclusion is the opposite: if universals are indispensable and not imagistic, and if generality cannot be reduced to sensations or images, then cognition of properties must be rational in character. A **Platonism about properties** thus requires a rationalist epistemology. That is not an optional supplement. It is forced by the ontology.

## Why Platonism forces rationalism

**Platonism** is the doctrine that spatiotemporal things are instances of non-spatiotemporal properties. The text treats this as the theory of universals. If every spatiotemporal thing is an instance of at least one property, and if properties are not themselves in space-time, then reality contains entities that cannot be encountered by the senses.

Now combine that metaphysical claim with the earlier epistemological one. If the world is intelligible only through universals, and if universals are non-spatiotemporal and causally inert, then any knowledge of them must be acquired by reason. Hence: a Platonic metaphysics requires a rationalist epistemology.

This is why the chapter says that those who believe in non-spatiotemporal entities are necessarily rationalists. “Give or take a few nuances,” empiricism is the view that you do not know it if you do not see it. But one never sees properties themselves. One sees only their instances. Therefore anyone who believes that properties are real and non-spatiotemporal has already abandoned strict empiricism, whether or not he acknowledges it.

The relation here is not accidental. Epistemology is being driven by ontology. If one’s ontology includes only spatiotemporal particulars, empiricism is tempting. But if one’s ontology includes non-spatiotemporal properties, then reason must be admitted as a source of knowledge.

## Predication commits us to shared properties

The case for properties is not merely that explanation needs them. Common predication itself commits us to them. Consider:

1. Sally and Fred are both intelligent.

From this it follows that:

2. There exists some property P such that Fred is an instance of P and Sally is an instance of P.

That inference is valid. It reveals that ordinary predication is already ontologically loaded. When we say of two distinct things that both are intelligent, we commit ourselves to a shared entity, a property they both instantiate. This shared entity cannot be identical with either instance. Einstein’s intelligence and Keynes’s intelligence are in space-time because Einstein and Keynes were in space-time. But intelligence itself is not in space-time.

The same point appears in more complex cases. Sentences such as the following straightforwardly presuppose properties:

- Hitler and Stalin had a lot in common.
- Smith has what it takes to be a great pianist, but he doesn’t have what it takes to be a great composer.
- Even though Smith is different from Jones, that has nothing to do with the fact that they don’t like each other.

Their meanings quantify over properties. Without such quantification, obvious truths become inexpressible. So anti-Platonism is not merely metaphysically thin; it is semantically impoverished. It cannot account for what we plainly say and think.

## Why reduction to aggregates or instances fails

The anti-Platonist often grants property-instances while denying properties per se. Perhaps, one is told, a property is just some aggregate of its instances, or just a fact about all the things that fall under a predicate. But this reduction fails for more than one reason.

The first is the problem of **uninstantiated properties**. Consider the property of having a perfectly triangular shape. Nothing has it. Must we say the property therefore does not exist? The text rightly calls this absurd. To say that triangularity does not exist because it has no instances is already to refer to that very property.

The second failure is that co-extensive properties—properties with exactly the same instances—can nonetheless be distinct. The chapter gives a striking story. Max is the world’s greatest harpsichord player. He is also the only red-haired person who ever has, or ever will, set foot in house X. Then the property of being a red-haired person who sets foot in X is co-extensive with the property of being the world’s greatest harpsichord player. If properties were aggregates of instances, there would be no difference between them, since the relevant aggregate is exactly the same. But plainly the properties are distinct.

The source also makes the point with uninstantiated properties: the property of being a perfect husband is distinct from the property of being a perfect soldier, even though neither is instantiated. Again, reduction to instance-aggregates collapses distinctions we are rationally compelled to preserve.

The same lesson is captured by the contrast between:

- squareness is a form of rectangularity;
- everything square is green.

Even if all squares happened to be green, greenness would not thereby become what squareness is “for that very reason.” Co-extension is not identity. Property identity and property inclusion are grounded in the natures of properties, not in the census of instances.

So anti-Platonist reductions fail because they cannot distinguish what must be distinguished.

## Higher-order properties and the independence of the property realm

The reality of properties becomes still clearer once we notice that properties themselves have properties. A property of a property is a **higher-order property**. The example given is decisive: the property of being a square circle has the property of **being uninstantiated**.

Now if higher-order properties are real, their instances are themselves properties, and those instances are not in space-time. This shows that the realm of properties does not depend on there being spatiotemporal members exemplifying first-order properties. Indeed, the property of being a square circle is not instantiated by anything in space-time, yet it has the higher-order property of being uninstantiated. The property realm therefore contains structure independently of the existence of ordinary objects exemplifying it.

This matters for empiricism because it cuts off the thought that properties are somehow abstractions from encountered particulars. Some are not abstracted from anything encountered, because they are not instantiated at all. Yet we can truly say of them that they are uninstantiated, distinct, or related in certain ways. A realm whose members can bear higher-order properties independently of spatiotemporal instantiation is not a byproduct of sensation.

The point generalizes. Everything that exists is either a property or is in space-time. Propositions and sets, the text says, turn out also to be properties. The underlying metaphysical picture is thus property-based, not sensation-based.

## Against conceptualism: properties before minds

A final anti-empiricist temptation is **conceptualism**, the view that properties are ideas in minds, or exist only because they are conceived. This too is false. If properties such as resemblances or ways of being depended on minds, then before there were minds there would have been no such properties. But that is absurd. The resemblance among rocks, for example, existed before there were any minds to conceive it. Their similarity was not created by acts of thought.

Locke’s suggestion that universals are the workmanship of the understanding therefore cannot be right. We do not manufacture universals in order to organize a sensory manifold. Rather, we recognize universals that are there to be recognized. The understanding does not create the property; it apprehends it.

This is not to say that words or classifications are never human products. Of course they are. But the property to which a true predication answers is not made true by our conceiving it. Sally and Fred do not become intelligent because we group them together under a term. They fall under the same property independently of our doing so.

Once conceptualism is rejected, the anti-Platonist options are exhausted. Properties are not aggregates of instances, not mere words, not ideas in minds. They are non-spatiotemporal realities instantiated by spatiotemporal things and related to one another in ways graspable only by reason.

## The upshot: rationalism as demanded by common sense properly understood

The irony is that strict empiricism presents itself as sober and commonsensical, while Platonism can seem extravagant. But the argument of these chapters reverses that appearance. Common sense tells us that different things really can have something in common; that explanations cite genuine characteristics; that some predicates mark non-fortuitous connections and others do not; that a thing can be rectangular in virtue of being square; that distinct properties do not collapse merely because they happen to share their instances; that some properties are uninstantiated; and that the world’s structure did not wait upon the arrival of minds.

All of that points toward a Platonic ontology of properties. And once that ontology is accepted, rationalism follows. We know many things by sense-perception, but not all. We do not perceive universals themselves, nor can there be observational evidence for them. Yet they are indispensable to thought, language, predication, logic, and explanation. Therefore at least some knowledge is non-perceptual. The intellect does not merely shuffle images furnished by the senses. It apprehends properties, higher-order properties, and relations among them. Strict empiricism is thus not merely incomplete but untenable. Rationalism is required, not as a speculative excess, but as the epistemological condition of understanding the world at all.

title: The Mind–Body Problem: Dualism vs. Materialism
blurb: A defense of materialism through causation, identity, intentionality, and the failure of behaviorism and functionalism.
lectureTitle: 3.1 The Mind–Body Problem: Dualism vs. Materialism
body:
# The Mind–Body Problem: Dualism vs. Materialism

## Materialism as the default position

The fundamental options are stated starkly in the assigned text. **Mental** entities are those that involve thought or feeling: beliefs, intentions, regrets, experiences. **Physical** entities are those that are spatiotemporal and do not involve thought or feeling: rocks, trees, explosions, neural events, bodily motions. **Materialism** is the thesis that mental entities are identical with certain physical entities, “presumably neural events or structures.” **Dualism** denies this and holds that the mental is non-physical.

The most powerful initial reason for materialism comes from causation. The mental plainly affects the physical. An intention can lead to an arm’s rising; a regret can lead to a letter being written; a decision can lead to someone’s leaving a room. But if something affects the physical world, then it belongs to the physical world. That is the force of the argument associated here with Fodor: if the physical world is governed by physical law, then anything that enters into the causal order of physical events must itself be something physical. Otherwise we would have physical effects with non-physical inputs, and the physical world would not be causally self-contained.

The text gives us the needed background. The physical world is treated as deterministic: given the state of the system at one time and the laws governing it, later states are fixed. That means physical events do not occur lawlessly. If my hand rises, there is some physical story to be told about muscles, nerves, and brain states. A mental event that genuinely makes a difference to whether my hand rises must therefore be located within that physical story, not outside it. Materialism secures exactly this: the decision to raise the hand just is a neural event or structure within the causal nexus.

The point is not that mental causation violates physical law. On the contrary, if materialism is correct, it does not violate physical law at all. The causal efficacy of the mental is simply the causal efficacy of the physical event with which the mental event is numerically identical. We must be careful here about **numerical identity**. The chapter on identity distinguishes numerical identity from mere resemblance. If water is H2O, that is not the claim that water resembles H2O very closely; it is the claim that they are one thing. Likewise, if a mental event is a neural event, we do not have two events standing side by side, one mental and one physical, mysteriously synchronized. We have one event under two descriptions.
