That identity model has an immediate advantage over dualism. It preserves both the reality of mental causation and the integrity of physical law. The dualist must either explain how a non-physical cause enters a deterministic physical system without disrupting its law-governed character, or else retreat from interaction. The materialist need do neither.

## Why epiphenomenalism is untenable

A common attempt to preserve dualism while protecting physical law is **epiphenomenalism**, the view that the physical affects the mental but the mental does not affect the physical. Neural events produce experiences, but experiences do no work. This view is false.

The reason is that causation here is bidirectional. The source text insists that decisions are products of a person’s prior mental condition: choices are rooted in values, desires, beliefs, and previous intentions. Those are mental items affecting later mental events. But those same choices also issue in bodily motions and overt actions. If prior physical states affect mental states, and those mental states in turn shape later conduct, then the mental is not a mere shadow cast by the physical. It is part of the causal sequence.

The argument can be set out simply:

1. The physical affects the mental; for example, brain conditions and bodily conditions plainly shape what one thinks and feels.
2. Choices and actions are rooted in beliefs, desires, values, and previous intentions.
3. Bodily behavior depends on those choices and intentions.
4. Therefore mental states affect the physical.

The compatibilist discussion in the text actually strengthens this point. Freedom, on that view, requires that choices be “adequately rooted in who you are as a person.” A choice disconnected from one’s values, desires, beliefs, and previous intentions is not freer but less free; it resembles a compulsion or seizure. But if values, desires, beliefs, and intentions are the very things in which the difference between free action and mere compulsive happening consists, then they are explanatorily and causally serious. Epiphenomenalism deprives them of that seriousness. It leaves us saying that what matters most to action makes no difference to action, which is incoherent.

If one tried to preserve epiphenomenalism by saying that the physical alone does all the work and the mental merely accompanies it, one would collapse the explanation of action into a description from which agency has been evacuated. The book’s entire treatment of personality-rooted choice resists that move. The architecture of the person is explanatory because it is causally efficacious.

## The dualist’s strongest cards

Still, dualism is not foolish. Its strongest cards are real. The mental seems to possess at least two properties that the physical, as such, seems to lack: **intentionality** and **phenomenology**.

**Intentionality** is the property of being about something. A belief that it is raining is about rain. An intention to leave the room is about leaving the room. A regret about yesterday is directed toward the past. Physical things, by contrast, seem merely to be what they are. A rock is not about anything. A tree does not mean anything. Mere matter, the dualist says, may push and pull, but it does not represent.

**Phenomenology** is the felt, experiential character of mental life: what pain feels like, what regret is like from the inside, what it is like to see or think or hope. The dualist’s point is not merely that the physical vocabulary of mass, motion, extension, and neural configuration does not mention these features. It is that such features seem categorically different.

A second strong dualist intuition concerns hidden structure. A physical object can have unseen parts. Water can turn out to be H2O; light can turn out to be electromagnetic radiation; the man in the photograph can turn out to be the professor before us. Identity discoveries are possible because the thing identified may have a nature not obvious from appearance. But an appearance itself, the dualist says, cannot have hidden parts. The feel of pain is simply present to consciousness. The appearance is exhausted by how it appears. If that is right, then the strategy of saying “this experience is really a neural state” looks unlike “water is H2O.” Water could have hidden microstructure; a pain, as appearance, seems not to.

These are the best reasons to resist materialism. They explain why the problem is difficult and why a crude reduction will not do.

## The explanatory gap without dualist conclusion

There is therefore a real **explanatory gap**: a gap between a physical description of neural events and an understanding of intentionality and phenomenology. One can know much about the brain and still feel that one has not yet been told why a given neural event is a thought about Paris or what it is like to feel regret. The gap is not imaginary.

But it does not establish dualism. Here the chapter on identity provides the crucial logical point. Identity does not require translatability. Two expressions can pick out one thing even if they differ in sense, use, or descriptive content. “Clark Kent is Superman,” “water is H2O,” and “light is electromagnetic radiation” are informative identity statements precisely because the terms on either side are not synonymous. If they were merely interchangeable in meaning, the identity discovery would be trivial.

This is the proper answer to Davidson’s temptation to infer from irreducibility of description to distinctness of entity. Failure of translation is not failure of identity. That one vocabulary cannot be neatly rendered into another does not show that it denotes another thing. We must keep separate:

- a difference in language,
- a difference in mode of presentation,
- and a difference in object.

The chapter’s treatment of the ambiguity of “is” helps here. Sometimes “is” predicates a property: “Smith is tall.” Sometimes it expresses identity: “Smith is the guy who washes my windows.” The mind–body thesis at issue is an identity claim, not a predication claim. To say that pain is a neural event is not to say that pain has the property neural-event-ishness in addition to being something else; it is to say that one and the same occurrence can be picked out in experiential language and in neurophysical language.

So the explanatory gap shows that the two modes of access are different. It does not show that there are two substances. Identity statements are often cognitively significant exactly because the identities they state are not transparent.

## Why behaviorism and functionalism fail

Two major attempts to avoid dualism without embracing straightforward mind-brain identity are behaviorism and functionalism. On the view taught here, both fail, though for different reasons.

**Behaviorism** identifies mental states with behavior or with dispositions to behave. But the text’s treatment of choice already gives the objection. Responses depend on prior mental states. A bodily movement is not intelligible as an action merely by pairing stimulus with response. The same outward behavior can issue from different beliefs, intentions, or regrets; and different outward behavior can issue from what is, in one respect, the same belief, depending on what other mental states are present.

That is why beliefs and intentions cannot be mere dispositions to behave. If someone leaves a room, whether that bodily motion is fleeing, searching, obeying, helping, or abandoning depends on prior mental states. The behaviorist leaves out the very internal architecture in terms of which action is explained. The source text insists that a free choice must express a person’s values, desires, beliefs, and previous intentions. Behaviorism cannot make proper sense of this dependence because it tries to reconstruct the mental from overt behavior while ignoring the prior mental condition that gives behavior its significance.

**Functionalism** seems more sophisticated. It defines mental states by their causal role: what tends to cause them and what they tend to cause. Yet on the present view it too fails, because it strips the mental of genuine causal powers by relocating all efficacy to an abstract role-description. A functional state, described only by its place in a network of inputs, outputs, and transitions, is too thin. It captures a pattern while detaching that pattern from the concrete, enduring structure in which actual mentality consists. The result is that the mind becomes an organizational schema rather than a causally efficacious reality.

The problem is not that causal role is irrelevant. It is that role cannot substitute for bearer. A personality structure, rooted in neural organization, actually explains why one choice rather than another occurs. A merely functional characterization does not by itself provide the entity whose states are doing the causing. The favored account therefore rejects both the behaviorist externalization of mind and the functionalist abstraction of mind.

## The identity theory: mind as neural event or structure

The positive view is direct. Mental states are identical with neural events or structures. This makes the mental a subset of the physical world, not a rival realm.

The chapter on identity supplies the conceptual resources. An informative identity statement tells us that two seemingly different items are one. Water is H2O; Superman is Clark Kent; the square of 4 is 16. In the same form, the claim here is that a pain, a belief, or an intention is a neural event or neural structure. The difference between the mental and the neural is not numerical difference but descriptive difference.

This permits one to preserve all of the following together:

1. Mental events are real.
2. Mental events are causally efficacious.
3. Physical law is not violated.
4. Human beings are wholly within the natural world.

The key is to avoid thinking of identity as obliterating one side of the equation. To identify water with H2O is not to deny that there is water; it is to tell us what water is. Likewise, to identify a belief with a neural pattern is not to deny that there are beliefs. It is to place beliefs in the ontology of the world.

## Intentionality and the dualist’s challenge

The hardest remaining issue is intentionality. A belief is about something; an intention is directed at something; a regret concerns something. The dualist insists that no purely physical arrangement could possess this property. Matter, arranged however intricately, would still be mere matter. Aboutness would be missing.

That challenge must be taken seriously because intentionality is not peripheral; it is constitutive of much of mental life. Yet the challenge overreaches when it assumes that “purely physical” means “devoid of structure capable of mediation.” The materialist need not say that a bare atom is about anything. The claim is that certain neural organizations are the physical realizers of representational states. The relevant comparison is not between belief and rock, but between belief and the enduring neural architecture that stores, links, and deploys information in the life of a person.

This point harmonizes with the text’s emphasis on personality-rooted choice. Choices express beliefs, desires, values, and previous intentions because the person possesses a stable structure in which such states are connected. Intentionality therefore should not be sought in isolated physical bits considered abstractly, but in the organized neural patterns that mediate mentation across time.

## Closing the gap by shifting from stream to structure

The explanatory gap narrows once we stop identifying the mind with the passing stream of thoughts and instead identify it with the enduring structure that mediates mentation. A thought flashes and is gone. If we take the mind to be nothing more than such passing occurrences, then of course the relation between a transient experiential item and a neural process can seem mysterious. But the source text repeatedly directs us toward a person’s prior condition, enduring personality, values, desires, beliefs, and previous intentions. What explains current mentation is not a disembodied stream but a structured subject.

That enduring subject should be understood materially: as stable neural architecture. The architecture persists through changing experiences much as the same person persists through dramatic changes over time. The chapter on personal identity is relevant here. A middle-aged professor may differ radically from the young party animal he once was, yet the problem is not solved by multiplying persons. Identity across change requires an underlying persisting individual. Analogously, identity of mind through changing thoughts points us toward a persisting neural structure rather than toward an immaterial soul.

Once that move is made, phenomenology and intentionality become properties of states and processes within an enduring physical system. The system has hidden structure in the legitimate sense required for identity explanations. An appearance as such may not have hidden parts, but the subject whose appearance it is certainly can. And if the appearance is an event in that subject, then discovering its neural identity need not amount to discovering hidden parts of the appearance considered in abstraction; it amounts to discovering what event in the persisting subject that appearance is.

## Materialism without eliminating the mental

A final confusion must be removed. A materialist, on this view, still counts as a **mentalist**. That is, one still treats beliefs, intentions, regrets, experiences, and personality as real and explanatory. Materialism does not force us into the vocabulary of rocks and explosions alone. It says rather that when mental events are correctly identified, they turn out to be neural patterns.

This is especially important for the self. The self is not a momentary thought, nor a mere sequence of behaviors, nor an abstract functional profile detached from any bearer. It is grounded in stable personality architecture: the enduring structure in virtue of which choices express values, desires, beliefs, and previous intentions. The compatibilist argument about freedom depends on this. Freedom requires that action come from who you are. On the present account, “who you are” is not something over and above your neural organization; it is that organization insofar as it constitutes your personality.

So materialism does not deny the mind. It locates it. It says that the mental world is part of the physical world, and indeed a highly organized part. That is why mental causation is real, why epiphenomenalism is untenable, why identity need not wait upon translation, and why the failures of behaviorism and functionalism matter.

## The decisive objection to behaviorism restated

Behaviorism deserves one final rejection because it repeatedly returns in crude and subtle forms. Beliefs and intentions are not mere dispositions to behave. The book’s own examples of free and unfree choice show why. Smith’s bizarre decision to become a pilot “out of the blue,” or the student’s sudden choice to abandon an A-average and become a drug dealer, are not criticized merely because of the behaviors that follow. They are criticized because the choices are not rooted in prior mental states. What matters is antecedent personality.

Hence behavior depends on prior mentality in at least three ways:

1. A response is shaped by existing beliefs, desires, and intentions.
2. The same behavior can express different states depending on that antecedent condition.
3. The difference between free action and compulsion lies in the relation of present choice to prior personality.

A theory that reduces the mental to behavioral disposition leaves out the explanatory ground of action. The correct direction of analysis runs the other way: behavior is to be explained by mental states, and those mental states are to be identified with neural patterns in an enduring physical subject.

That is the materialist resolution of the mind–body problem taught here. Dualism sees something real—the peculiarity of intentionality, phenomenology, and first-person appearance—but mistakes explanatory distinctness for ontological distinctness. The better conclusion is that the mind is real, causally potent, and indispensable, precisely because it is not outside the physical order but a structured part of it.

title: Free Will, Determinism, and the Libet Experiment
blurb: A compatibilist account of freedom: why randomness undermines agency and determinism supplies its conditions.
lectureTitle: 3.2 Free Will, Determinism, and the Libet Experiment
body:
# Free Will, Determinism, and the Libet Experiment

## Randomness is not freedom

The first temptation in the free will debate is to suppose that if determinism is threatening, then its opposite must be liberating. That temptation is the central mistake. **Indeterminism** is the doctrine that determinism is false: at some point, how the world is does not completely fix how it will later be. This is, as the text emphasizes, a very moderate doctrine. It requires only one renegade event. But even if one grants such renegade events, it does not follow that freedom has thereby appeared.

Why not? Because a free choice must be *your* choice in more than the thin sense that it occurs in your mind. It must be rooted in your beliefs, desires, values, intentions, and settled personality. If a “choice” is not determined by anything at all, then it is not determined by those things either. And then the event ceases to look like an exercise of agency and begins to look like an interruption of agency.

That is exactly why the book’s examples are so effective. Smith is walking along and suddenly decides to become a pilot. Nothing in his prior personality supports this. He never liked flying, already has a career he enjoys, would find the change inconvenient, and knows all of this. Yet the decision simply occurs. The natural description is not: here, at last, is pure freedom. The natural description is: something has gone wrong. The event seems compulsive, rootless, as though it overcame him. If such episodes were frequent, we would not praise Smith for radical autonomy; we would say that his psychological integrity was disintegrating.

The same point is sharpened by the more dramatic case of the A-student who, in the middle of a test, suddenly throws down the pen, bolts from the room, and becomes a drug dealer. If the choice is genuinely undetermined—caused by nothing, fixed by neither the state of the universe nor the state of the agent’s personality—then it resembles not a considered judgment but a fit. The text’s language is exact: such a “choice” is more like a seizure. It is as though the person were taken over. So indeterminism does not merely fail to help freedom; it positively harms it. Freedom requires psychic integration. Randomness is psychic disintegration.

## Why determinism is needed for agency at all

This yields the second and deeper point. **Determinism** is not merely compatible with freedom; in an important sense it is a prerequisite for it. A deterministic structure is what allows a choice to be connected to the agent at all. If your action is to express your character, your values, your standing concerns, your prior intentions, then there must be a lawful, dependable connection between those inner states and the resulting action.

To see the force of this, contrast willing with effective control. A person may want to perform some action and yet be unable to translate that wanting into bodily movement. The condition is not freedom but impairment. The text’s general point is that if the mechanism linking what you want to what you do were indeterministic in the relevant way, you would be willing but unable. You would not thereby acquire a larger field of freedom; you would lose command. That is why the comparison to disorders of control is apt. One is not freer when one’s limbs or actions fail to respond in a stable way to one’s intentions. One is less free.

So the dialectic is not: determinism threatens freedom, indeterminism saves it. Rather:

1. If actions are detached from the person’s settled motivational structure, they are not free but compulsive or seizure-like.
2. If actions are connected to that structure, they arise through a regular, law-governed nexus.
3. That nexus is precisely the sort of thing determinism supplies.

The consequence is striking. The very features that make an action attributable to the agent—its being intelligibly produced by the agent’s beliefs, desires, and intentions—are deterministic features. Randomness does not create authorship; it disrupts authorship.

## The basic compatibilist insight: freedom as doing what you choose

This brings us to **compatibilism**, the view that free will can exist in a deterministic world. The crude or straightforward version, associated in the text with Locke- and Moore-style thinking, begins from a simple distinction between wanting and being prevented. On this view, you are free to the extent that you can do what you want; unfree to the extent that you cannot.

G.E. Moore formulates the point in counterfactual terms: an act is performed freely if the agent would have done something else had he chosen to do something else. The important idea is not metaphysical openness in the sense that the past might have been different while remaining exactly as it was. The important idea is practical control: if you had chosen otherwise, your behavior would have been otherwise. A free act, then, is one caused by your choice.

This is the enduring core of compatibilism. It explains the ordinary contrast between coercion and freedom. If I want to leave the room and can leave, then in that respect I am free. If I want to leave but am locked in, then in that respect I am unfree. The difference is not whether my wanting has causes. Of course it does. The difference is whether my action issues from that wanting or is blocked by something else.

Frankfurt-style cases complicate but do not overthrow this core. Their function is to show that freedom is not exhausted by abstract alternative possibilities. It is not enough merely to say that one could not have done otherwise in some remote sense and therefore was unfree. What matters is whether the action flowed from the agent’s own motivational structure. The Moorean insight remains: freedom centrally concerns the relation between choice and action.

## Frankfurt’s deeper refinement: second-order desire

Yet straightforward compatibilism is not sufficient. A person can do exactly what he wants and still seem unfree. This is Frankfurt’s deeper point. We need a distinction between **first-order desires** and **second-order desires**.

A first-order desire is a desire to do or have some ordinary thing: to drink, to leave, to speak, to take a drug. A second-order desire is a desire about a desire: a desire to have, or not to have, some first-order desire. The problem with the crude account is that it treats any successful satisfaction of a first-order desire as freedom. But that misses cases in which the agent repudiates the desire on which he acts.

Suppose someone acts on a desire that he does not want to have. He may say, in full sincerity: “Yes, I wanted the drug, but I hated that I wanted it.” If the action issues from that first-order desire alone, we do not have a satisfactory picture of freedom, even though the behavior did originate in the agent and even though no external force prevented him from doing what he wanted in the first-order sense. What is lacking is identification. The person’s higher-order standpoint repudiates the motive that moved him.

Frankfurt’s refinement therefore adds an internal hierarchy. Freedom requires not merely acting on desire, but acting from a first-order desire that is endorsed at the level of second-order desire. The agent must not be estranged from the motive.

## Ego-syntonic and ego-dystonic desires

This can be put in the vocabulary of **ego-syntonic** and **ego-dystonic** states. A desire is ego-syntonic when it is experienced as consonant with the self, fitting with the person’s self-conception and endorsed motivational outlook. A desire is ego-dystonic when it is alien to the self, felt as intrusive, disowned, or rejected.

The significance of the distinction is that it explains why freedom is a matter of identification rather than mere internal causation. Not every motive arising within one’s psychology counts equally as one’s own in the sense relevant to freedom. Some motives feel like intrusions, compulsions, or pathologies. The Smith case already prepared this point: a rootless decision that “just comes out of the blue” is not free because it manifests a lack of psychological integrity. Ego-dystonic desires are the everyday form of that same phenomenon. The person may be the causal site of the desire without being, in the relevant normative sense, its author.

Freedom therefore requires more than inward origin. It requires that the operative desire be one with which the agent identifies. That is why the text insists on choices being “adequately rooted in who you are as a person.” Rootedness means not merely causal ancestry, but integration with the self.

## Determinism and the flow from the distant past

At this point the classic pressure of determinism returns with full force. Determinism says that the state of the world at any given time fixes the state of the world at all later times. If the physical world is deterministic, and if materialism is true so that mental events are just part of the physical world, then whatever experience or decision you have now was made inevitable by the state of the universe long ago. Given the world a million years ago, your present choice had to occur exactly as it does.

This is why incompatibilism seems so compelling. You have no control over the distant past. If the distant past, together with the laws governing the world, completely fixed your present choice, then something over which you have no control seems completely responsible for what you now do. The choice appears to flow from outside you—from history, from the state of the universe, from antecedent conditions extending back beyond any reach of agency.

But the compatibilist reply is not to deny the flow from the past. It is to redescribe what matters in that flow. Of course your present character, beliefs, and desires have histories. Of course they were shaped by earlier conditions. But if freedom required absolute independence from all causation, then no action could ever be free, for an uncaused action would be a mere eruption. The relevant question is not whether your action has causes reaching into the past; every intelligible action does. The relevant question is whether, in the present, the action flows through the right kind of causal pathway—through your own deliberation, choice, and endorsed desires.

## The right causes, not absence of causes

This gives the central compatibilist formula: freedom is not the absence of causes but the presence of the right causes. The contrast is not between caused action and uncaused action. It is between action caused by your own choice and desire, and action blocked, bypassed, or driven by motives you do not own.

The book’s discussion of perception helps illuminate the general methodological point here. There, predictability and determinism are carefully distinguished. One must not confuse superficially associated notions. Likewise in the free will debate, one must not confuse freedom with causelessness. Causelessness would deprive action of intelligibility; it would make it impossible to see why the act belonged to the agent rather than to chance. The causes relevant to freedom are precisely those that connect action to the person: beliefs, intentions, values, and choices.

A person is therefore free when:

1. he forms a choice or acts from a desire,
2. the resulting action occurs because of that choice or desire,
3. the desire or choice is integrated with his person rather than alien to it.

This is why determinism can coexist with freedom. Determinism guarantees a stable nexus between reasons, motives, and behavior. Freedom consists in occupying that nexus in the right way.

## Internal origin is not enough

Still, one further complication must be faced. An action may originate within the agent and yet be unfree. This is the importance of the ego-dystonic case. If freedom were merely internal causation, then every action caused by some inner state would be free. But that is false.

Consider again the compulsive model suggested by the text. Suppose the operative desire arises in the agent and issues directly in action. No external jailer restrains him; no outside force moves his limbs. Yet he experiences the motive as alien, as something he repudiates, as a desire he wishes not to have. Then the act, though internally caused, is not free. It is an instance of the self being moved by a part of itself with which it does not identify.

This is why the simple contrast between internal and external compulsion is inadequate. The structure of the self matters. There can be a division within the person such that the lower-order desire prevails against the person’s higher-order standpoint. In such a case, the action originates “within” and still fails to express the agent as a unified person. Psychological integrity, not mere interiority, is the criterion.

## The positive account: aligned first- and second-order desire

We can now state the positive compatibilist conception with precision. A free agent acts on first-order desires that he also wants to have. The relevant second-order desire endorses the first-order desire as one that should move him.

This account solves the earlier puzzles. It preserves the Moorean insight that action must be caused by the agent’s own choice. It incorporates Frankfurt’s improvement by insisting that not every desire counts equally as the agent’s own. And it explains why indeterminism undermines rather than grounds freedom: if a choice is cut loose from the person’s motivational hierarchy, it ceases to be an exercise of self-government.

The structure is hierarchical but unified:

- **First-order level**: the desire to perform some action.
- **Second-order level**: the desire that this first-order desire be effective, or the desire not to have it.
- **Freedom**: action flowing from a first-order desire that is endorsed by the corresponding second-order standpoint.

Where the levels align, the person governs himself. Where they conflict and the repudiated desire wins, the person is unfree in the relevant respect. The operative ideal is not metaphysical spontaneity but coherent self-rule.

## Unpredictability does not show indeterminism

A final confusion remains: the inference from unpredictability to indeterminism. Human behavior is often difficult to predict. But the text insists that **predictability** and determinism are not the same thing. An indeterministic system is indeed unpredictable, except by luck. But a deterministic system may also be unpredictable, and for reasons of logic.

The book’s treatment of perception establishes the first reason. Any creature learns about the external world through causal processes—light, disturbances, information-bearing media. Those processes take time and alter what they reveal. What one perceives at a time is always, to some degree, dated information. Attempts to remove the gap by further observation only introduce further disturbance. This is not a contingent human limitation but a logical condition on sense-perception as such. Knowledge of a system’s exact present state is therefore limited in principle.

That matters because prediction requires information about present states. If one cannot have perfectly exact and perfectly current information about the relevant system, then there are principled limits on prediction even where the underlying process is deterministic. Thus the opacity and practical unpredictability of human action do not support indeterminism. A deterministic system can be beyond a creature’s predictive powers.

So one must not reason: “I cannot predict what someone will choose; therefore the choice is undetermined.” The inference fails. Determinism concerns what fixes what; predictability concerns what a knower can know in advance. Those are different matters. The world of medium-sized objects in which we operate is, for most intents and purposes, deterministic even though our predictive reach is sharply bounded.

## The resulting conception of freedom

The cumulative view is now clear. Determinism says that each present choice flows from the distant past. That is no threat to freedom unless one mistakenly defines freedom as exemption from causation. Once freedom is correctly understood, the picture changes. Random, rootless events are not exercises of agency but its breakdown. Freedom requires reliable causal connections between the person’s standing character and the action performed. A free act is one caused by the agent’s choice; more deeply, it is one caused by a first-order desire with which the agent identifies at the second order. Ego-syntonic motives can ground free action; ego-dystonic motives, even when internal, cannot. And the unpredictability of behavior provides no refuge for indeterminism, since deterministic processes may be unpredictable in principle.

The compatibilist conclusion is therefore not a concession to mechanism, but the only view that preserves the idea of a person acting as a person. An action is free when it is not rootless, not compulsive, not alien, but issued by the agent’s own integrated motivational structure. Determinism is not the enemy of that condition. It is what makes the condition possible.

title: Personal Identity
blurb: A rigorous account of personal identity as causal-structural succession, against bodily and four-dimensional alternatives.
body:
# Personal Identity

## Identity, strictly speaking

The topic becomes tractable only once we remove two confusions. First, the verb **“to be”** is ambiguous. Sometimes it is **predicative**: “Smith is tall” attributes a property to Smith. Sometimes it expresses **identity**: “he is George,” “that’s the eraser I was looking for,” “Superman is Clark Kent.” Second, “identity” itself is ambiguous between **numerical identity** and **qualitative identity**. Numerical identity is strict sameness: not two things exactly alike, but one thing. Qualitative identity is resemblance, even exact resemblance short of strict samenness.

This distinction matters immediately, because change over time would be impossible if identity required sameness of all properties. The sandwich at 11:00 A.M. on the counter is cool; the sandwich at 1:00 P.M. in Smith’s hands is warm and yucky. Those differ qualitatively. Yet the statement that they are the same sandwich is perfectly intelligible and, in the case described, true. So personal identity, like objectual identity generally, cannot consist in the possession at different times of all the same properties. It must instead consist in a relation that permits qualitative difference across time while preserving numerical identity.

The book’s fundamental claim is that **statements of personal identity share the logical structure of object identity**. Once we understand what makes the 11:00 sandwich identical with the 1:00 sandwich, we have the formal model for understanding what makes the young roustabout identical with the middle-aged professor. In each case, one and the same thing is present in temporally distinct installments.

## The two logical forms of identity and their application to persons

The chapter distinguishes two basic logical forms of identity statements.

1. **Diachronic identity**: x and y are different installments in one **causal sequence**.
2. **Synchronic identity**: some one thing uniquely instantiates two uniquely identifying properties at a time.

A **causal sequence** is a continuous series of events each connected to the next by causal dependence and spatial-temporal adjacency, or by chains of such adjacency. Since ordinary objects are ultimately swarms of events—movements and exchanges of mass-energy—an ordinary object persists by being constituted by temporally ordered, causally connected events. That is why the cool sandwich and the warm sandwich can be numerically one thing despite qualitative alteration: they are parts of one causal sequence.

The synchronic pattern appears in cases like “the world’s most valuable diamond is identical with the only diamond in the Hawthorn Museum” and “Superman is Clark Kent.” These do not connect temporal stages by causation. They say, rather, that one thing uniquely has two different sets of identifying properties.

The first thesis, then, is that **personal identity statements share this same logical structure**. When one says, “I am the guy in the photo,” one may be speaking diachronically: the current person and the photographed person are installments in one causal history. When one says, “Clark Kent is Superman,” and if the subject were a person rather than a comic-book figure, one would be saying that one being uniquely instantiates two identifying property-clusters. There is no special, sui generis logical form reserved for persons. The identity of persons is a case of identity full stop. That is why objectual identity is more fundamental: the conceptual machinery is forged there first.

## You are your mind

The next thesis is the chapter’s most important substantive commitment: **you are your mind**. The reason is simple. Statements about personal identity concern bodies only indirectly. Bodies, as such, are objects. If I say, “this is the hand that signed the paper,” I am making an objectual identity statement about a bodily part. But a person is not merely a body considered as an object. The personal standpoint enters where mindedness enters: thought, awareness, memory, intention, sensation. The bearer of those is what you are.

This does not force dualism. A **materialist**—one who holds that everything that exists is material or physical—may still count as a **mentalist** in the relevant sense if mental events are identical with patterns of neural activity. If pains, perceptions, acts of remembering, and episodes of deliberation just are certain neural occurrences, then to say that you are your mind is not to deny physicalism. It is to locate your identity not in your body considered as a mere chunk of matter, but in the organized system whose activity constitutes mindedness. A physicalist may therefore say: the mind is physical, but the person is identical with that minded structure rather than with the body taken simply as a biological object.

This point matters because otherwise bodily continuity would be made decisive in a way the phenomena do not support. The persistence of a hand, a liver, or a torso is not yet the persistence of the subject. Bodies are objects; persons are subjects. A theory of personal identity that begins and ends with the body misses the very difference between objectual and personal identity that made the topic philosophically interesting in the first place.

## The strongest physicalist challenge: coma and the apparent return from nonexistence

Still, a powerful challenge arises. A person can survive a **thought-free coma**. During such a period there is, let us suppose, no occurrent thinking at all. If you are your mind, and if your mind is just your actual episodes of thinking, then during the coma you do not exist. But if you cease to exist, nothing can later come back into existence and be strictly identical with what has gone out of existence. Numerical identity cannot be interrupted and then restarted. So the strongest challenge to the view that you are your mind is this: the comatose person survives, yet consciousness has disappeared. Does this not show that the person is really the body, not the mind?

The force of the objection depends on a hidden premise:

1. If you are your mind, then you are identical with your actual thoughts.
2. In a thought-free coma, there are no actual thoughts.
3. Therefore, in a thought-free coma, you do not exist.
4. What does not exist cannot later resume existence as numerically the same thing.
5. So, if coma survival is possible, you are not your mind.

The reply therefore has to reject the first premise. The mistake is to identify the mind with the stream of currently occurring thoughts rather than with that which generates, organizes, and sustains them.

## The mind as persisting structure rather than occurrent thought

The better formulation is this: **you are your mind, but your mind is a structure that generates thoughts rather than the thoughts themselves**. A structure can persist through periods in which it is not producing its characteristic outputs. The relevant analogy is supplied by the chapter’s treatment of objects generally. An object is not identical with a single micro-event among the swarms of mass-energy that compose it at an instant. It is a structured causal sequence. Likewise, a mind is not identical with this or that fleeting thought, any more than the sandwich is identical with one vibrating atom or one instantary event among its constituents.

Once mind is understood structurally, coma no longer implies temporary nonexistence. The thought-free interval is a gap in mental activity, not a destruction of the mind. The organized basis that explains and predicts the resumption of thought remains. It is that organized basis—under materialism, a neural structure and activity-pattern of the right kind—that constitutes the person. Thus:

1. A person is identical with the mind.
2. A mind is a persisting structure with the capacity to generate conscious episodes.
3. Temporary inactivity of that structure is not annihilation.
4. Therefore a person can persist through a gap in consciousness.

This preserves both sides of what seemed incompatible: the centrality of the mental and the possibility of surviving thoughtless intervals.

## Structural continuity, not duplication

From here the account becomes stricter. **Structure-preserving continuity is the essence of diachronic identity**. Mere reproduction of structure elsewhere is not enough. If a machine records every feature of you, destroys your body, and assembles elsewhere a being exactly like you atom-for-atom, that being would at most be a **duplicate**, not you. The same holds for atom-by-atom reassembly after total destruction. Why? Because diachronic identity is not founded on the possession of a blueprint or even on exact reconstruction. It is founded on **continuous causal succession**.

The sandwich at 1:00 is the sandwich at 11:00 because the later sandwich resulted from the earlier by a continuous sequence of causally connected events. If instead the original were destroyed at 11:30 and, at 1:00, a molecule-for-molecule duplicate were assembled elsewhere, we would not have one sandwich persisting; we would have one sandwich replaced by another exactly similar sandwich. Similarity, however exact, is not succession.

This is why teleportation and atom-reassembly fail as models of survival. They preserve pattern but sever continuity. The resulting being may inherit every memory, every trait, every disposition, every neural pattern. But inheritance is not identity. Numerical identity requires that the later person be the successor of the earlier in one continuous causal sequence. Where that sequence is cut and only pattern is reinstantiated, persistence has not been secured.

## Numerical identity and qualitative identity

This allows us to sharpen the sixth thesis: **numerical identity is distinct from qualitative identity; only the former is required for persistence**. The clone example makes the point with complete clarity. If you are cloned, you and your clone may be qualitatively identical—very similar, even exactly alike in all ordinary respects. Yet there are plainly two of you, not one. So exact similarity does not suffice for strict identity.

At the same time, within a single moment, genuine perfect qualitative identity would collapse into numerical identity by the **Identity of Indiscernibles**: if there were literally no difference whatever between x and y, each would have all the properties of the other, including the property of being identical with x, and therefore y would be x. The philosophical payoff is that what matters in persistence across time is not the retention of every property—impossible, since change is constant—but the preservation of one thing through change.

Hence the old professor and the youthful party animal can be numerically one despite radical qualitative difference. Taste in music, bodily agility, tolerance for nightlife, arthritic condition, even outlook and habits may all change. If persistence demanded qualitative sameness, no one would survive ordinary life. The entire problem of diachronic identity arises only because numerical identity can coexist with profound qualitative unlikeness. Personal identity therefore cannot be read off from resemblance to one’s past self.

## Causal succession, explanatory connectedness, and degrees

The account can now be stated positively. **Diachronic identity consists in causal succession with robust explanatory and predictive connectedness**. The later self must stand to the earlier self as successor in a continuous causal sequence. But not every causal linkage is equally strong. Some later stages explain and predict earlier ones more robustly than others. Memory, character, dispositions, capacities, bodily and neural organization, and the persistence of the thought-generating structure all contribute to the degree of connectedness.

That is why the chapter’s account admits that diachronic identity **comes in degrees**. This does not mean that numerical identity itself is vague in the sense that one thing can be half identical with another at a moment. It means that the relation of causal-structural connectedness that underwrites our identity judgments can be stronger or weaker. The middle-aged professor is unquestionably the successor of the younger man, but much has dropped away: tastes, habits, physical capacities, interests. The explanatory and predictive continuity remains robust enough for identity, yet it is less intimate than the continuity between one’s present self and oneself five minutes ago.

This graded element also explains why some bizarre cases tempt hesitation. Where continuity is attenuated, identity judgments become less secure because the explanatory nexus becomes thinner. But the framework remains the same: seek the strongest continuous causal sequence, not mere likeness.

## Interruption without destruction: the ice-man case

The **ice-man** type case brings the previous points together. Suppose a sentient creature’s mental activity is interrupted altogether, but its underlying structure remains intact. Frozen, inactive, unthinking—yet not structurally destroyed. When revived, thought resumes. The right judgment is that the creature survives. Why? Not because there was consciousness throughout; there was not. Not because all its properties remained unchanged; they need not have. It survives because the **structure stayed intact**, and the later conscious life is the continuation of the earlier via a preserved causal basis.

This case is the animate analogue of the sandwich and of every ordinary object. Objects are swarms of events organized in continuous sequences. A temporary arrest in manifest activity does not by itself destroy the object if the relevant organization remains and later activity issues from it. Likewise for persons. The sentient creature before freezing and after thawing is one creature because the latter is produced by the former through preserved structure, not by independent duplication.

The ice-man case therefore answers the coma objection without abandoning the mentalist thesis. Survival through unconsciousness is possible because what persists is the mind as structure, not consciousness as uninterrupted occurrence.

## Against the space-time worm

This account also excludes a rival picture: personal identity is **not** the identity of a four-dimensional **space-time worm**. On that view, a persisting thing is really a total spread of temporal parts, and change is merely the possession of different properties by different temporal segments. The chapter rejects this because it denies genuine change and mishandles fission.

Why does it deny genuine change? Because if the whole worm simply has all its temporal parts timelessly, then the young roustabout and the elderly professor are merely different parts of one extended object. The subject does not really become different; rather, one temporal slice has one set of properties and another has another. But our original problem concerned how one thing can survive through change, not how an aggregate of temporal slices can contain incompatibilities. The worm view dissolves the phenomenon instead of explaining it.

Why does it mishandle fission? Because if personal persistence were just inclusion within a larger four-dimensional entity, branching cases would tempt the absurd result that one earlier person is literally identical with two later persons. But strict identity is one-one, not one-many. The causal-successor view avoids this by requiring a continuous succession relation of the right explanatory sort. Where one line branches into two equally good continuers, we do not get one numerically identical person becoming two numerically identical persons. We get, at best, two successors or duplicates standing in derivative relations to the original. Identity is not multiplied by fission.

## Successorship, not total property-sharing

The final thesis gives the most concise formula for the chapter’s position: **to be identical with your past self is to be its successor in a continuous causal sequence, not to share all properties at once**. This follows from everything already established.

The demand for total property-sharing confuses numerical with qualitative identity and collapses diachronic identity into impossibility. The present professor lacks countless properties the youthful reveler had: athletic capacity, musical taste, patterns of conduct, bodily condition. Yet he stands to that earlier person in the right successor relation. His current mental and bodily organization resulted from the earlier person through continuous causally connected events. The present stage is explained by the earlier one and permits predictions from it. That is why the identity claim is true.

So the full view can be summarized in a connected sequence:

1. Identity statements have two principal logical forms: co-instantiation of unique properties and membership in one causal sequence.
2. Personal identity is not a sui generis mystery but a species of this general phenomenon.
3. Since a person is a subject, not merely a body as object, the bearer of personal identity is the mind.
4. Even the physicalist can accept this, if mental events are neural patterns.
5. The mind is a persisting, thought-generating structure, not the mere series of occurrent thoughts.
6. Therefore unconscious gaps do not entail nonexistence.
7. Persistence requires continuous causal-structural succession, not mere replication of form.
8. Thus exact duplicates produced by teleportation or reassembly are not numerically identical with the original.
9. Identity through time tolerates, indeed presupposes, qualitative change.
10. What makes the later self the earlier self is successorship within one continuous causal history.

Once these distinctions are kept clear, the initially baffling fact of personal persistence becomes no more mysterious in form than the persistence of the sandwich, the diamond, or the shirt—though it remains more interesting because, in the personal case, what persists is not merely an object but a mind.

title: Causation
blurb: A rigorous account of causation as event-based, INUS-structured, irreducible to regularity, counterfactuals, or mere sequence.
body:
# Causation

## Events, conditions, and the spatiotemporal domain

The first point is a logical one about the category to which causes belong. **Causes** are not objects; they are **events**. An event is a change in conditions. Thus the rock is not the cause of the window’s breaking. What causes the breaking is some event involving the rock: the rock’s striking the window at a certain time, with a certain trajectory and force. Ordinary speech often obscures this. We say that Carter caused a recession or Hitler caused World War II. But such claims are elliptical. What is meant is that certain events involving Carter, or certain events involving Hitler, were causally responsible.

This matters because causal explanation is always explanation of one occurrence by another occurrence. If we fail to keep that straight, we confuse a thing’s being involved in a causal process with the thing itself being a cause. The distinction is parallel to another one: between something’s being a cause and its having **causal properties**. The rock is not a cause, but its having a certain mass can be a partial cause. By contrast, its being such that it either is or is not identical with the number 7 does no causal work. Some properties are causally sterile; some are causally loaded.

A complication arises from **conditions**. A condition seems not to be an event, because a condition appears to be a persisting state, as when the water has a temperature of 101°. Yet conditions plainly function as causes: the water’s having that temperature softens the spaghetti. The resolution is that conditions are not eventless. A condition consists in a pattern of ongoing events. The water’s remaining at 101° for five minutes consists in molecular changes remaining within certain limits; the molecules continue to move, but the manner of their change does not itself change beyond those bounds. A condition is therefore a pattern of constant change, and an event is a change in the manner of change. So when a condition causes something, what does the causal work is still an event-structure. Conditions are causes only because they consist of events.

From this it follows that nothing **non-spatiotemporal** can be a cause. Causes require changes; changes occur in time; and what is wholly outside space and time is causally impotent. That is why universals, if there are such things, do no causal work. The point is not that everything known must be known through causation, because the text explicitly rejects the crude thesis that a causal connection by itself mediates awareness. There is always a non-causal component in awareness, even in perception. But causation itself belongs to the spatiotemporal order. Causes are occupants of that order because they are changes within it.

## Why “the cause” is always partial: Mackie’s INUS analysis

Once we see that causes are eventive, the next step is to ask what we ordinarily mean when we single something out as “the” cause. The answer is almost never: a condition that is by itself sufficient. The sentence “Smith’s drunkenness caused the accident” does not mean that drunkenness alone was enough for the crash. It plainly was not. Had Smith been driving a high-performance car on an open country road in daylight, he might not have crashed even if more intoxicated than he actually was. So the cause, as ordinarily cited, is a **partial cause**.

Nor does it usually mean a condition that is absolutely necessary. Smith’s drunkenness was not necessary for his crashing. He might have crashed sober if driving too fast on an icy road. So the ordinary cause is neither sufficient by itself nor necessary without qualification.

J. L. Mackie’s formulation captures exactly this logic. What we ordinarily call a cause is an **INUS-condition**: an **insufficient but non-redundant part of an unnecessary but sufficient condition**.

The analysis proceeds in stages:

1. There was some sufficient condition for Smith’s crash, since he did crash.
2. That sufficient condition was not necessary, because there were many other ways the crash could have occurred.
3. Smith’s drunkenness was not by itself sufficient.
4. But under the operative circumstances—say, a low-performance vehicle, a dark rainy night, a busy street, perhaps a faulty steering mechanism—his drunkenness may have been a necessary ingredient in that particular sufficient set.
5. It is therefore an insufficient but non-redundant part of one sufficient condition, and that sufficient condition is itself unnecessary.

This is what is meant when, in a legal, ethical, or psychological context, we say that Smith’s drunkenness was the cause. We are not identifying the whole cause. The complete cause may be so extensive that, as the text says, perhaps only the entire state of the universe just prior to the event would count. For practical purposes, “the cause” picks out the salient INUS-condition.

This explains why causal discourse is selective without being arbitrary. We isolate what matters **under the circumstances**. The phrase “under the circumstances” is crucial, because it marks the background against which a partial factor becomes non-redundant.

## Aristotle’s four causes and the priority of efficient causation

Aristotle’s famous division into **efficient**, **final**, **material**, and **formal** causes is, on this view, deeply confused except in one case.

An **efficient cause** is straightforwardly coherent: x makes y happen. That is ordinary causation.

A **final cause** is said to be a goal or objective. But a goal, taken per se, does nothing. If the proposition that JMK get in shape is my goal, that proposition itself has no effects. What has effects is my having that goal, my intending to make that proposition true. But my having that intention is simply an event or condition in me, and so a garden-variety efficient cause. Final causation therefore reduces to efficient causation. Either Aristotle is making the trivial point that creatures’ having goals can affect what they do, or he is making the confused claim that propositions themselves cause things.

The more radical criticism concerns **formal** and **material** causes. A formal cause is supposed to be a thing’s form or essence; a material cause is supposed to be the stuff out of which it is made. But the relevant dependence-relations are not causal relations between objects.

Take formal causation first. To say that having three sides is essential to being a triangle is not to identify a cause. It is to say that “x is a triangle” entails “x has three sides.” That is a logical relation between statements. Likewise, to say that consisting of H2O molecules is essential to being water is to say that “x is water” and “x does not consist of H2O molecules” are incompatible statements. Again: logical, not causal.

The confusion arises because Aristotle lets dependence slide between unlike categories. Dependence can be:

- **causal**, in which case it holds between events or states of affairs; or
- **logical/constitutive**, in which case it holds between statements.

It does not hold between objects in the way formal and material causes require. That is why those notions are incoherent. A given triangle-shaped object can cease to have three sides without ceasing to exist; it simply ceases to be triangle-shaped. A puddle can undergo chemical change without vanishing out of existence. The object persists while the description under which it is classified changes. What is essential is essential to being-such-and-such, not to the bare continued existence of the object.

Hence only efficient causation is basic. Final causation collapses into it. Formal and material “causation” are not forms of causation at all.

## Why Hume’s regularity theory cannot succeed

The empiricist pressure against causation tempts one to define causation without invoking any genuine tie—perhaps as nothing but **regular succession**. On a regularity view, to say that E causes E* is, roughly, to say that events like E are regularly followed by events like E*. The difficulty is not merely that this omits an alleged glue. The deeper problem is that it cannot even characterize the right pattern.

It fails in at least three ways.

First, it cannot distinguish **real causation** from **pseudo-causation**. Mere constant conjunction does not tell us which among correlated events is genuinely producing which, or whether both are effects of some common condition. A regularity can register accompaniment without yielding production.

Second, it tends to make **adjacent events** causal simply because they are contiguous in sequence. If causation is no more than one sort of event’s being followed by another sort, then any standing adjacency threatens to become causal. But a succession can be immediate without one event making the next happen.

Third, and most fundamentally, the analysis is **circular**. It presupposes that the world can be described in causally neutral terms of space and time, and then attempts to build causation out of those neutral terms. But space and time, at least as they function in the spatiotemporal world we actually describe, are already causally loaded notions. The text insists on this point repeatedly.

Consider **spatial occupancy**. For a thing to occupy a region R is for that occupancy to alter the trajectories and velocities of other would-be occupants of R. Occupancy is therefore not causally sterile. Similarly, to characterize something as steel is to ascribe malleability and thermal conductivity, both of which are causal properties: how much force is needed to change its shape, how much energy to raise its temperature. Any characterization that says anything substantive about a spatiotemporal thing imports causal content. Purely non-causal predicates such as self-identity or “being such that 1 + 1 = 2” say nothing informative about what a thing is like in the world.

So Hume’s proposed base-level vocabulary—mere sequence in space and time—is not a genuine base. If the notions of spatial location, persistence, and worldly characterization are already causally freighted, causation cannot be reconstructed as a pattern among items first grasped independently of it.

## Why counterfactual theories are also circular

The same defect reappears in a subtler form when causation is analyzed through **counterfactuals**. On that view, E causes E* if, had E not occurred, E* would not have occurred. But this only seems more sophisticated. In fact, the counterfactual relation is itself saturated with causal content.

To assess “Had Smith not been drunk, he would not have crashed under those circumstances,” we hold fixed some features, vary others, and ask what would have happened. That “would have happened” is precisely a causal judgment. Counterfactuals in causal contexts do not replace causation; they redescribe it. Mackie’s own analysis shows why. To say that drunkenness was necessary under the circumstances for the crash is not to eliminate causal structure; it is to specify the role drunkenness played within a sufficient causal set.

The circularity is therefore straightforward:

1. A counterfactual analysis tries to explain causation in terms of what would occur if certain events did not occur.
2. But the truth conditions of those “would” claims depend on what would causally result from the altered circumstances.
3. So the analysis presupposes the very notion it set out to explain.

Counterfactuals are useful in stating causal claims; they do not ground them.

## The incoherence of a causally sterile world

At this point one can see why the picture of a world made up of pure sequence, with causation somehow added afterward, is incoherent. **Persistence** is itself causally loaded. To persist through time is not to remain utterly inert; it is to be a continuing causal sequence. The text puts the point sharply: anything that persists is, for that very reason, a causal sequence.

This rebuts the claim that we never observe causation because we observe only one event after another. If persistence is causal, then whenever we observe anything enduring at all—a rock, a vase, a body of water—we observe a structured continuity of causally connected events. We do not merely infer that there must be causal sequences hidden behind appearances in the attenuated way we infer molecules from looking at water. We knowingly observe things that persist, and in doing so we observe causal sequences.

Likewise, the notion of a thing’s occupying space is causally charged. A body in a region excludes or deflects other bodies. The world of spatially distributed occupants is already a world of interaction. Therefore the imagined Humean world of brute, unrelated sequence cannot even get started. The very concepts needed to formulate it have causal import.

## Causal sequences and the boundaries of objects

Once persistence is recognized as causal, a further thesis follows: a **causal sequence** is a continuous series in which each event causes its successor. This is not an extraneous add-on to objects; it is what objects are, insofar as they persist. Conditions are patterns of constant change, and the continued existence of what we call an object consists in an ordered succession of such internally connected events.

From here, the boundaries of objects are not primitive givens. They are fixed by the continuities of causal sequence. What belongs to one thing rather than another is determined by which events belong to one continuous causal history. That is why dependence-relations, properly understood, run through events and states of affairs, not through objects as bare substrata.

This also clarifies the earlier distinction between condition and event. A living body’s being healthy is not a static fact laid atop a substance; it consists in metabolic events proceeding in the right way. There is no life where there are no metabolic events. The “condition” just is a stabilized causal sequence. To identify the object is therefore to identify an organized causal continuity.

## Causation and evidential meaning

There is an important connection between causation and evidence, but the two must not be identified. The text notes one tempting line of thought: for me to know of a rock, light rays must affect my sensory surfaces; for me to know of Socrates, there must be testimony conveyed by noises or by light reflected from ink marks, and these processes can be traced back to states of affairs involving Socrates. So there is often a **causal nexus** underwriting awareness.

Yet the same passage insists that a causal connection by itself never mediates awareness. There is always a non-causal component to cognition. Thus evidential significance is often supported by causation, but is not reducible to it.

This is exactly what we should expect. An effect can be **evidence** of its cause without being identical with the causal relation itself. Ink marks can be evidence about Socrates because of a causal-historical chain connecting them to testimony and states of affairs involving him. The evidence relation points from effect to cause, whereas the causal relation runs from cause to effect. The two are therefore distinct, though often intertwined. Causation helps underwrite evidential meaning, but evidential meaning is a broader epistemic matter.

## Against reduction to mere sequence: continuity and linkage

This brings us to the most decisive objection to reducing causation to sequence. Even temporal or spatial separation between cause and effect is intelligible only where there is a **continuous chain** linking them. If Smith pulls the trigger and the gun fires, or Jones throws the vase against the wall and the vase breaks, we do not have a bare before-and-after pair. We have an ordered process. The trigger pull initiates a sequence through the mechanism of the gun; the vase’s trajectory terminates in impact and shattering. The connection is not supplied by chronology alone.

A mere sequence view cannot account for action across separation, because separation itself is not enough. There must be intermediate continuity. That is why adjacency is not sufficient, and distance is not disqualifying, for causation. What matters is not mere nearness in time or space but the presence of a continuous causal series in which each event produces its successor. Without such linkage, “earlier than” and “later than” describe only order, not production.

This is also why the empiricist complaint that we never observe anything over and above succession misses the target. What we observe, when we observe the world as inhabited by persisting, space-occupying things, is already continuity of this kind.

## Unobservable causal ties and the electron analogy

The original empiricist complaint was that we do not observe the causal tie itself. We see the rock strike and the window shatter, but not the force that compels the shattering. The reply is simple and sufficient. Unobservability is not by itself an objection. We do not observe electrons or quarks either, yet we have excellent reason to posit them.

So the issue cannot be that causal ties are unobservable. It would have to be that the notion is incoherent, like that of a **square circle**. But the chapter’s argument is that the concept is not incoherent at all. On the contrary, causation is so deeply built into our understanding of persistence, occupancy, malleability, conductivity, health, and every substantive characterization of spatiotemporal reality, that attempts to deny it end by presupposing it.

The opponent says: causation cannot be the glue of the universe because any such tie would itself be just one more occupant of space-time. But this objection fails because what is being denied is already implicit in what the opponent must use. To describe a world of enduring occupants in space and time is already to invoke causally loaded notions. The denial of causation is therefore not an austere empiricism; it is a confusion about the conditions under which anything in the spatiotemporal world can be described at all.

Causation is not an optional metaphysical decoration placed upon an otherwise self-sufficient sequence of events. It is the structure of the sequence itself: event succeeding event by production, conditions as stabilized patterns of event, objects as bounded causal histories, and explanation as the isolation of salient INUS-conditions within that history. Efficient causation is basic; final causation reduces to it; formal and material causation dissolve under analysis. Neither regularity nor counterfactual dependence can replace it, because both borrow causal content from the very world they pretend to analyze without remainder. And the fact that causal glue is not separately observed no more undermines its reality than the unobservability of electrons undermines theirs.

title: What Ethics Is
blurb: A rigorous account of ethics as the analysis of intrinsic value, moral complexity, and the non-binary structure of right and wrong.
body:
# What Ethics Is

## Normative categories and the task of ethics

The first thing to fix is the kind of subject ethics is. Ethics does not begin by discovering a new region of facts, as chemistry discovers compounds or biology discovers organs. It begins with a distinction between two kinds of statements and, correspondingly, two kinds of concepts.

A **descriptive statement** is a statement to the effect that such and such is the case. “Smith is over 6-feet tall” and “grass is green” are descriptive. They say how things are; they do not, as such, register approval or disapproval. A **normative statement**, by contrast, is one that expresses a value-judgment: it says that something falls short of, satisfies, or exceeds some standard or norm. “It is wrong to steal,” “it was evil of Hitler to commit genocide,” “it is commendable to give money to charity,” and “Smith was acting valiantly in saving the drowning toddler” are normative statements.

From this distinction we get the notion of a **normative category**: a category that occurs only in normative judgments. **Good**, **bad**, **just**, **unjust**, **valiant**, **noble**, **wicked**, **depraved**, **commendable**, and **condemnable** are examples. Ethics is the discipline that attempts to clarify the structures of these concepts. To clarify a concept here is not merely to list paradigm cases. It is to state, as clearly as possible, the conditions a thing must satisfy to fall under that concept. Ethics therefore asks: what must an act be like to be praiseworthy? what must an institution be like to be just? what conditions make an act condemnable rather than commendable?

That is why ethics is fundamentally analytic. It is concerned with structure: with the conditions of application of normative categories. If one says that an act is commendable, one is not merely venting approval. One is placing it in a category with a determinate logical structure. Ethics makes that structure explicit.

## Ethics concerns intrinsic rather than instrumental goodness

This immediately requires care with the word “good,” because “good” is ambiguous. Most importantly, there are two kinds of goodness: **instrumental good** and **intrinsic good**.

Something is **instrumentally good** when it has consequences desired by, or advantageous to, the **agent**, the person performing the act. If my sole objective is to make money, then stealing a million dollars from a local orphanage is instrumentally good for me, provided I do not get caught or otherwise suffer for it. In that sense it is useful; it serves my practical interest.

But that same act is not ethically good. It is good only in the strategic, pragmatic, or instrumental sense. Ethics is not interested in that sense. It is not interested in identifying ways for thieves to steal more effectively or for crooked politicians to acquire more power. Ethics is interested in **intrinsic goodness**: goodness that belongs to a thing apart from its usefulness to the agent.

That “apart from” must be taken seriously. Ethics asks which acts and states of affairs are good even when their consequences are disregarded. Thus helping a person in need, where doing so is not to one’s practical advantage, is intrinsically good. Being honest when it would be more convenient to lie is intrinsically good. Playing a musical instrument is intrinsically good. So too happiness, intelligence, benevolence, loyalty, pleasure, life, friendship, compassion, enthusiasm for one’s work and for life, and freedom. The point is not that there is universal agreement on every item in such a list; the text explicitly notes that ethicists differ. The point is that these examples make plain the meaning of intrinsic value: value not reducible to strategic advantage.

It also follows that instrumental and intrinsic goodness are not mutually exclusive. Intelligence can improve one’s strategic position and so be instrumentally good; yet its value exceeds those practical advantages. The same is true of happiness, pleasure, friendship, and honesty. Something can be good as a means and good in itself. Ethics isolates the latter.

## Intrinsic goodness is not identical with commendableness

Once intrinsic goodness is distinguished from instrumental goodness, a second ambiguity appears within intrinsic goodness itself. Some intrinsically good things are **commendable**, that is, **praiseworthy**. Some are not. Ethics therefore cannot treat “intrinsically good” and “deserving praise” as interchangeable.

Consider happiness. Happiness is intrinsically good. The more happiness, the better. But it does not follow that a happy person deserves praise for being happy. Smith may simply be naturally chipper. Perhaps his endocrinal system manufactures happy hormones in abundance. Perhaps he is merely shrewd at avoiding social and professional landmines. Perhaps he is even evil and has discovered how to make himself happy without getting into trouble. In all these cases, the happiness is still a good thing, but it is not necessarily praiseworthy.

The rabbit example sharpens the point. The happiness of a rabbit is a good thing. But rabbits, given their cognitive limitations, are not capable of acting in a praiseworthy manner. Their happiness is intrinsically good without being commendable. Likewise, Smith’s musical talent may be intrinsically good, and the happiness it brings him may be intrinsically good, but if the talent came naturally and required no effort or choice on his part, he does not deserve praise for having it. One cannot deserve praise for the occurrence of something over which one has no control.

By contrast, Jones’s labor for a charity, undertaken with no practical benefit to himself, is both intrinsically good and commendable. So the category of intrinsic goodness divides:

1. intrinsically good and commendable, and
2. intrinsically good and not commendable.

This matters because moral evaluation is more articulated than simple talk of “good things.” Ethics must distinguish the goodness of a state from the praiseworthiness of what brings it about or embodies it.

## Moral badness and commendableness/condemnableness are non-privative and non-binary

The same structure appears on the negative side. Unhappiness is intrinsically bad. Yet a person grieving a loved one does not, simply for that reason, deserve censure. Indeed, failure to grieve the death of a beloved child or spouse would itself be monstrous. Still, some intrinsically bad things are **condemnable**: causing another to suffer for no good reason is both intrinsically bad and worthy of censure.

This prepares the way for a deeper thesis. Moral attributes are not **privative**. A **privative property** is a property a thing has by lacking something: to be cold is to lack heat, to be dumb is to lack intelligence, to be poor is to lack money, to be sugar-free is to lack sugar. A **positive property** is one a thing has by possessing something extra: to be hot, smart, rich, or sugary is to have something.

Now, **commendable** and **condemnable** are positive in this strictly logical sense. For an act to be commendable is not for it to lack condemnableness. For it to be condemnable is not for it to lack commendableness. Each is the presence of something. Condemnableness is like poisonousness: not morally positive, but logically positive. Commendableness is also logically positive. Since neither is the absence of the other, both can be present in the same act.

That is why moral reality is not binary. People resist saying of a single act that it is both good and bad, commendable and condemnable, because they wrongly suppose badness is merely the absence of goodness. It is not. A rock lacks goodness, but it is not thereby bad. To be bad one must have something extra. Hitler was bad not because he merely lacked something, but because he possessed ill-will and a willingness to act on it.

The moral world therefore does not divide neatly into saints and ghouls, heroes and monsters. That simplification may be psychologically easier, but it is not faithful to the actual structure of acts.

## One act can be both right and wrong in different respects

The moral complexity of acts becomes vivid in the examples. Suppose I am playing the piano, doing so very well, and taking pleasure in it. Surely that is intrinsically good.
