But suppose I am thereby waking my very sick roommate, who needs sleep, and I am aware of the harm I am causing. Then the very same act is condemnable. It is wrong, yet also intrinsically good.

Likewise Green, motivated solely by loyalty to Smith, savagely beats Jones for insulting Smith. The act is commendable as loyalty and courage; it is condemnable as excessive and unnecessary violence. No paradox arises, because the commendable and the condemnable are not contraries in the sense of one being the mere absence of the other.

From here we can understand the claim that **right** means least bad and **wrong** means least good. Since acts can contain both good-making and bad-making features, practical judgment does not typically search for a morally pure option. It compares mixed options. The **right** act is the one that is, all things considered, least bad; the **wrong** act is the one that is, all things considered, least good. This explains how an act can be right while still containing a real wrong-making element.

So if one steals in order to save one’s children, the act may be right because a weightier obligation governs the case. But the wrong involved in stealing is not thereby cancelled or erased. The theft remains a genuine wrong-making feature. The point of saying the act is right is not that it has become morally immaculate; it is that, among the available alternatives, it is least bad. Ethics therefore resists the fantasy that a stronger reason annihilates a weaker one. It outweighs it; it does not retroactively make it unreal.

## Legality, morality, intention, and informed judgment

Several distinctions follow.

First, **legality** is not morality. The categories belong to different structures. A law may forbid what is instrumentally advantageous; it may permit what is morally base; it may prohibit what is morally required in a tragic case. To ask whether something is legal is not yet to ask whether it is just, commendable, or right. Ethics concerns the latter categories.

Second, the goodness of an act is not the same thing as the goodness of the agent. The source’s examples already establish this. Happiness, talent, and the rabbit’s pleasure can be good without being praiseworthy. Conversely, an act can produce or embody something good while not being commendable in the agent, because praise and blame track what is under the agent’s control and, above all, the agent’s **intention**. Jones working for charity with no practical benefit is praiseworthy because of what he knowingly and purposively does. Green’s assault is commendable in one respect because it is motivated by loyalty rather than self-interest. Intention fixes praise and blame because commendableness and condemnableness concern not merely what occurs, but how the agent stands to it.

Third, judgment itself can be condemnable when made without sufficient information. If normative judgment is the application of concepts under determinate conditions, then careless application is itself a moral fault. To call an act noble, wicked, just, or depraved without knowing the relevant features is not analytic rigor but negligence. The non-binary structure of morality makes this especially important: because acts commonly have mixed properties, premature judgment is apt to miss what is really there.

## Ethics analyzes concepts; it does not add facts to the sciences

At this point the nature of ethics as a discipline can be stated more sharply. Ethics adds no new facts to the sciences. It does not compete with psychology, sociology, biology, or law by discovering an extra layer of empirical information. Rather, it analyzes the structures of concepts such as “good,” “bad,” “just,” “commendable,” and “condemnable.”

This does not make ethics trivial or empty. On the contrary, conceptual structure determines what follows from what. If we fail to distinguish intrinsic from instrumental goodness, we may call successful theft “good” and think we have said something ethical when we have said something merely strategic. If we fail to distinguish intrinsic goodness from commendableness, we will praise people for talents or temperaments over which they had no control. If we treat condemnable as privative, we will suppose that wherever praise is deserved blame cannot also be deserved. And if we think rightness means moral purity rather than least badness, we will misunderstand tragic choice.

The sciences tell us what is the case. Ethics clarifies what it is for what is the case to satisfy, violate, or exceed a norm.

## Descriptive and normative statements differ in logical role

That is why the distinction between descriptive and normative statements is not superficial. Descriptive statements say how things are. Normative statements register the satisfaction or violation of a standard.

“Smith is over 6-feet tall” places Smith under a measurable descriptive category. “Smith was acting valiantly in saving the drowning toddler” does something else: it measures Smith’s act against a norm and says the act satisfies it. “Grass is green” describes. “It is wrong to steal” evaluates by reference to a standard. “It was evil of Hitler to commit genocide” is not a report of color, shape, or height; it is the placing of an action under a normative category whose conditions ethics seeks to articulate.

The distinction also explains why ethical analysis cannot be replaced by mere accumulation of facts. Facts alone do not tell us whether what they describe satisfies or violates a norm. They are necessary to informed judgment, but not sufficient for conceptual clarity.

## Moral laws can be categorical without being exceptionless in application

A further consequence of the non-binary structure of moral attributes is that moral obligations have a dimension of **weight**. They are not binary. They come in degrees, and some are stronger than others.

The source’s examples are straightforward:

1. If I promise to meet you for lunch, I have an obligation to show up.
2. My obligation to show up to the classes I am paid to teach is stronger.
3. The President’s obligation to serve the interests of 300 million constituents is stronger still.

This means a moral law can hold **categorically**—that is, genuinely and not merely hypothetically—while still being overridden in a particular case by a weightier obligation. “Do not steal” can be a real moral law; yet in a circumstance where stealing is required to meet a stronger obligation, the prohibition is overridden, not destroyed. The outweighed obligation remains in force as an obligation; it simply does not determine what, all things considered, one ought to do in that case.

This is precisely why the right act can still contain a wrong. A stronger duty does not cancel a weaker one as though the weaker one had never existed. It defeats it in practical determination. Hence moral residue: the act is right as least bad, but not free of every condemnable aspect.

## Intrinsic goodness is independent of consequences and practical interest

We can now give a more exact account of intrinsic goodness. An act is intrinsically good when its goodness does not depend on consequences or on the agent’s practical interests. This is stricter than saying merely that it happens to have no useful consequences. The point is logical dependence. If the act would still be good even when consequences are set aside, and even when it is not to the agent’s advantage, then its goodness is intrinsic.

The earlier examples fit this pattern. Helping a person in need, where doing so is not to one’s own advantage, is intrinsically good. Honesty when lying would be more convenient is intrinsically good. Playing a musical instrument is intrinsically good, even though psychologists have discovered that it also promotes neural plasticity and is therefore instrumentally good as well. Freedom, in its several forms—freedom from external physical coercion, emotional freedom from internal psychological compulsion, and intellectual freedom consisting in being able to figure things out for oneself rather than slavishly relying on hearsay—is treated as intrinsically good because its value is not exhausted by usefulness.

If one makes practical interest the test of goodness, ethics collapses into strategy. The orphanage thief would then count as acting well whenever theft prospers. Intrinsic value blocks that collapse.

## The goodness of the agent tracks intention; the goodness of the act tracks normative structure

The final distinction gathers the preceding ones together. The goodness of an **agent** tracks intention; the goodness of an **act** tracks conformity to normative structure.

An act may be intrinsically good though not praiseworthy in the agent, as with natural happiness or musical talent. The state is good; the agent is not thereby commendable. Conversely, an act may be mixed in its normative structure—commendable in one respect, condemnable in another—while the praise or blame due to the agent depends on what the agent intended. Green’s attack on Jones is commendable insofar as it manifests loyalty and courage and condemnable insofar as it manifests excessive violence. To understand the act, we analyze its structure. To assess Green, we must ask what he meant to do and from what motive.

This is why intention fixes praise and blame. Praise is not owed for what merely happens through one, or in one, or to one. It is owed for what one intentionally does when one acts under a commendable motive and in a way that bears the relevant normative structure. Blame, similarly, attaches where intention aligns with condemnable features. Meanwhile the act itself is evaluated by the standards ethics clarifies: whether it is intrinsically good or bad, whether it is commendable or condemnable, whether it is right as least bad or wrong as least good.

Once these distinctions are kept in view, ethics appears neither mysterious nor simplistic. It is the disciplined clarification of normative categories: a study of intrinsic value rather than practical advantage, of positive rather than privative moral attributes, of mixed acts rather than binary fantasies, of weighted obligations rather than crude absolutes, and of the difference between what is good in an act and what is praiseworthy in the person who performs it.

title: Emotivism, Moral Realism, and Flourishing
blurb: A defense of moral realism against emotivism, grounding value in human flourishing rather than sentiment or convention.

# Emotivism, Moral Realism, and Flourishing

## Emotions, judgments, and the failure of emotivism

**Emotivism** is the doctrine that a sincere ethical utterance is not really a judgment at all, but merely an expression of feeling. On this view, to say “Larry is a bad man” is not to state something true or false about Larry; it is just to vent one’s attitude toward him, as one might scowl. Likewise, “stealing is wrong” becomes “boo stealing!” and “giving money to charity is good” becomes “hurray giving money to charity!” If that were right, then there would be no moral truths, because ethical language would say nothing about the world.

The view is false. The first mistake is the claim that moral judgment must be accompanied by a felt emotion. A competent speaker can sincerely say “Cotton Mather was a good man” without feeling anything in particular about Cotton Mather. One can make a moral judgment coolly. Indeed, when one’s judgment is driven by immediate sentiment, it is, to that extent, not an unbiased ethical judgment.

The deeper mistake is to suppose that if emotion is involved, what is present is mere feeling rather than cognition. Hume’s discussion of artistic judgment shows why that is too crude. One may judge a musical work good even when hearing it gives one no pleasure, because one knows that this lack of pleasure is due to an irrelevant, person-specific factor. The example is Smith the composer: you know Smith is marvelous, but you detest him. Hearing one of his works is torture. Yet you know that, were it not for your hatred of Smith, the work would be exquisitely pleasurable. So you judge it good. The judgment is not identical with your present feeling. It rests on a view about what would give pleasure once irrelevant distortions are set aside.

The same structure holds morally. People often judge as moral things that give them no pleasure and as immoral things that they themselves found pleasurable. The condemned prisoner may praise the government for imprisoning him even though prison will make him miserable. He can do this because he sees that, absent his abnormal circumstances, such punishment would make people safer and let them sleep easier at night. So the judgment is not reducible to current feeling.

The lesson is that emotions themselves, when ethically relevant, are not brute gusts of approval or disapproval. They embody a view about value; they are **doxastic**, that is, belief-like. They present something as good, bad, harmful, healing, conducive to flourishing, or obstructive of it. And because they contain this value-content, they can be correct or incorrect. If my revulsion at Larry embodies the thought that he is vicious and destructive, then the emotion is assessable: it fits Larry if he is such a man, and it misfires if he is not. Emotivism treats emotion as non-cognitive noise. The chapter’s argument instead shows that moral responses contain judgments about what benefits or damages beings like us. That is why they are answerable to fact.

## Moral realism and the factual component of ethical claims

From the failure of emotivism, the path opens directly to **moral realism**, the view that ethical claims have a factual component and are capable of truth and falsity. If “x is good” were just “hurray x,” disagreement in ethics would be like one person cheering and another booing. There would be no contradiction, only opposed noises. But our actual moral practice does not work that way. We argue, correct, retract, and accuse others of error. That makes sense only if ethical claims purport to describe something.

The book’s analysis states what that something is. Morality is fixed by facts about our **psychological-biological structure**: the relatively stable anatomy, physiology, and psychology with which beings like us come into the world. Because these structures are what they are, certain things damage us, and certain things are necessary for us to flourish. Morality is to be understood in terms of these needs. What damages us is immoral. What prevents us from flourishing is immoral. What heals us is moral. What facilitates flourishing is moral.

This is realism, but not a mysterious realism floating free of human nature. Moral truths are facts about what augments or damages creatures with our structure. They are therefore objective without being arbitrary. The analogy with biology is decisive. There were no biological truths about humans before there were humans; still, it does not follow that biology is subjective or conventional. In the same way, even if there were no moral truths before there were creatures with our structure, it would not follow that morality is invented by opinion or legislation.

The realist consequence is immediate:

1. Ethical claims depend on facts about what helps or harms creatures with our structure.
2. Facts of that sort are not made true by approval, custom, or decree.
3. Therefore ethical claims are not mere opinion but fact-involving judgments.

So when one says “Larry is a bad man,” one does not merely report one’s distaste. One says, in effect, that Larry’s conduct or character damages people, impedes flourishing, or manifests a structure hostile to the conditions under which beings like us thrive.

## Flourishing as the sole non-derivative good

Once morality is tied to our needs, the central value comes into focus: **flourishing**. Flourishing is the actualization of one’s abilities under conditions suitable to a being of one’s kind. It is not mere survival, not mere pleasure, and not mere obedience. It is being augmented rather than diminished; being enabled to become what one has the powers to become.

The book’s strongest claim here is exclusivist: the one thing with **non-derivative moral value** is flourishing. A thing has non-derivative value when it is good in itself rather than good only because it serves something else. By contrast, something has derivative value when it matters only as a means or condition.

Why elevate flourishing to this unique place? Because all moral assessment in the text is organized by the distinction between damage and augmentation, obstruction and actualization. To say that something is good is to say that it heals, facilitates, enables, or fulfills the capacities and needs built into our structure. To say that something is bad is to say that it frustrates, damages, or deforms those capacities. Flourishing is thus not one value among others; it is the standard by reference to which others get their value.

This has an immediate consequence for altruism. **Altruism** is not intrinsically good as an isolated form of self-sacrifice. It is good when, and because, it facilitates flourishing—one’s own, another’s, or both. If an apparently altruistic practice systematically damages people or crushes their powers, then its moral prestige evaporates. The book’s framework does not allow us to praise sacrifice simply because it is sacrifice.

## The worthless life of Smith and the better life of Brown

The distinction between flourishing and conventional moral respectability becomes stark when we compare the self-effacing “moral” life with the life of a flourishing scoundrel. The source gives us Brown, and the key point pairs him with Smith as the figure of self-effacement. The point is not that scoundrelliness is admirable; it is that a life can be conventionally moral yet worthless if it mutilates the self, and another life can be morally compromised yet superior as a life because it realizes powers.

Brown is despicable. His motives are hate and ill-will. In wartime he performs acts that, from the standpoint of consequences for the liberal democracy he serves, are beneficial. Yet his conduct has no moral worth, because his intention is not to do the right thing. He delights in hurting people. If he discovered that his work improved the human condition, his love of the work would diminish; if he discovered it worsened the human condition, that love would intensify. So Brown’s motives are corrupt.

Still, the chapter’s wider argument refuses the easy inference that the “moral” life, understood as relentless suppression of self-assertion and ambition, must therefore be better as a life. Great accomplishment typically requires aggression, narcissism, and self-interest in some degree. A legal or ethical order that eradicated all such tendencies would leave “no heroes, only zeros”: no Beethovens, no Einsteins, no Freuds, no Mendelssohns, no Emily Dickinsons, no Madame Curies, no Emily Brontes; no geniuses, no innovators, no creators—only milquetoast do-gooders and innocuous squares.

That is the decisive comparison. A person like Smith, if “moral” means endlessly self-effacing, harmless, compliant, and drained of all aggressive energy, may lead a worthless life precisely because he does not flourish. Brown, if taken as the flourishing scoundrel, may have the better life in the prudential sense that his powers are more fully realized, even though his motives are morally despicable. Moral worth and the worth of a life are not identical. The book insists on that separation because otherwise morality would become a machine for praising self-nullification.

## Why self-mutilating ethics is incoherent, and why flourishing is not indulgence

An ethical system is incoherent if it commands beings to destroy the very capacities in terms of which their good is defined. If morality is fixed by our needs as creatures with a certain structure, then a code requiring the mutilation of one’s true self undercuts its own basis. It treats as virtue the frustration of the powers whose fulfillment constitutes flourishing.

This is why a world in which all anti-sociality, all aggression, all self-interest, and all narcissism were legislatively stamped out would be not morally ideal but supremely immoral. It would prevent flourishing. It would also annihilate **autonomy**, because a world in which it is not even possible to act immorally is a world in which one has no real options. Since people cannot flourish without a certain amount of freedom, such a world would be both lifeless and coercive.

Yet flourishing must be distinguished sharply from **self-indulgence**. The source makes the distinction through Brown. It is often to one’s practical advantage to act immorally; and many immoral acts are enjoyable. But enjoyment does not itself constitute flourishing. Brown’s sadism gives him satisfaction, but it is not therefore good. Why not? Because the standard is not “what this individual happens to enjoy” but “what augments rather than damages beings with our structure, setting aside individual-specific distortions.” Brown’s pleasures are tied to injury, terror, and degradation. They do not actualize a healthy human capacity; they damage others and reflect a disordered psychology.

So the distinction runs as follows:

- **Flourishing** actualizes abilities and sustains the conditions under which beings like us can thrive.
- **Self-indulgence** gratifies appetite or ill-will without regard to damage, deformation, or the frustration of flourishing.

That is why the rejection of self-effacing morality does not collapse into a celebration of vice.

## Moral judgment without occurrent feeling

The denial of emotivism has a further consequence. Because emotions are essentially value-beliefs, one can sincerely judge “x is good” without any occurrent feeling at all. The point is not merely that emotion and judgment can come apart occasionally; it is that ethical judgment is not constituted by a felt episode.

The evidence is already before us. One may say, coolly and sincerely, that Cotton Mather was a good man. One may grudgingly concede that an act by someone one detests was the right thing, while wearing a frown. One may praise a punishment that will oneself suffer. In each case the judgment is intact even though the affective profile is absent or hostile.

This becomes intelligible once we recognize that the core of the judgment is belief about value: a belief that this act heals rather than damages, facilitates rather than obstructs flourishing, or answers appropriately to the needs of beings like us. A person can entertain such a belief in a detached way. Ethical cognition is therefore not hostage to sentiment. Sentiment may accompany it, distort it, or oppose it; but the judgment itself has propositional content.

## Supervenience: moral facts fixed by descriptive facts

The realist structure is tightened by the doctrine of **supervenience**. To say that moral truths supervene on psychological and biological truths is to say that two situations cannot differ morally without differing in their non-moral, descriptive features. Once the physical, physiological, and psychological facts are fixed, the moral facts are fixed too.

This matters because it blocks the idea that morality floats free of the world or is projected onto it by attitude. If two cases are alike in every descriptive respect—same capacities, same vulnerabilities, same harms, same benefits, same restrictions of freedom—then they must be alike morally. Otherwise morality would be arbitrary.

The source makes the point with direct force: moral truths are truths to the effect that certain things damage people and others augment them. If morality is fixed by what our psychological-biological structure needs, then any complete specification of that structure and of the relevant conditions suffices to determine the moral status of acts affecting it.

This supervenience relation also explains why ethical disagreement is often genuine but not decisive against realism. The existence of many moral codes does not show that all are right. Some are simply false because they misidentify what damages and what facilitates flourishing. The Nazis had a moral code. It was a bad one. Its precepts were false. Disagreement is perfectly compatible with objective truth; biology too admits error.

## Altruism’s derivative value

Now the place of altruism can be stated precisely. **Altruism** has value only insofar as it facilitates the flourishing of others. It is not a basic good in its own right. The reason is now familiar: if flourishing is the sole non-derivative good, then every other moral notion derives its worth from its relation to flourishing.

This is not a downgrading of concern for others. On the contrary, concern for others matters exactly because others are beings with the same sort of psychological-biological structure: vulnerable to damage, in need of healing, capable of augmentation, and possessed of powers that can be actualized or thwarted. Helping them has value because it contributes to their flourishing.

The derivative status of altruism also explains why some apparently altruistic demands are immoral. If a code requires people to obliterate their own capacities, to live as permanent instruments for others, or to prevent excellence wherever self-assertion is involved, then the code turns altruism into a weapon against flourishing. Once that happens, altruism ceases to be good. It has severed itself from the sole source of its value.

## Why a world of milquetoast do-gooders would be immoral

The book’s most provocative claim follows naturally. A world of entirely compliant, selfless, morally sanitized people—a world of milquetoast do-gooders who never act on self-interest—would be immoral. The reason is not that murder, theft, and cruelty are needed for color. The reason is that such a world would block genius, autonomy, and flourishing.

The argument proceeds in stages:

1. Great accomplishment often requires aggression, narcissism, and self-interest in some degree.
2. A system that made all immorality impossible would suppress those traits wherever they appear.
3. It would thereby eliminate the conditions for innovation, creativity, conquest of intellectual territory, and the realization of exceptional powers.
4. It would also strip people of freedom by removing the option of acting otherwise.
5. Therefore it would prevent flourishing on a massive scale.
6. Since nothing is more evil than preventing people from flourishing, such a world would itself be immoral.

That is why the chapter insists that there would be no Beethovens or Einsteins in such a world. The point is not biographical gossip about these figures, but a structural thesis about human excellence: it is often inseparable from traits a simplistic moralism would censor. An order that prized harmlessness above flourishing would give us bureaucratic vacancy in place of human greatness.

## Against opinion, culture, and legislation: moral truth grounded in human nature

All of this culminates in a final rejection of **moral conventionalism** and **moral nihilism**. Moral truth is not made true by opinion, culture, or legislation. A legislature can create legal rules; it cannot create moral truth any more than it can legislate biological fact. Opinion may track moral truth or fail to track it. Culture may embody wisdom or falsehood. Laws may facilitate flourishing or obstruct it. None of these constitutes the source of morality.

The source offers the right formulation. Let **PBS** abbreviate our psychological-biological structure. Moral principles are conditional truths of the form: if there were creatures having PBS, then treating those creatures in certain ways would be wrong, and treating them in certain other ways would be right. This secures both objectivity and dependence on nature. Morality does not pre-exist all possible creatures in abstraction from their constitution; nor is it invented by those creatures. It is fixed by what they are.

Hence moral truth is grounded in the fixed capacities and vulnerabilities of human nature: our proneness to damage, our need for freedom, our susceptibility to terror and injury, and our capacity for the actualization of powers. What heals and augments beings like us is morally favored. What maims, stunts, terrorizes, or suppresses their flourishing is morally disfavored. Where coercion is necessary to prevent greater damage, it may be justified; where intervention causes greater harm or greater abridgment of freedom, it becomes immoral even if aimed at stopping wrongdoing.

The overall position is therefore internally unified. Emotivism fails because moral judgment is not mere feeling but contentful, belief-laden assessment. Moral realism holds because ethical claims are made true or false by facts about damage and flourishing. Flourishing is the only non-derivative good, and altruism matters only through its service to it. A self-effacing life may therefore be worthless, and a flourishing but vicious life may, as a life, be better. Ethics cannot coherently command self-mutilation, yet flourishing is not mere indulgence. Moral facts supervene on descriptive facts about our psychological-biological structure. And because those facts are not made by opinion, culture, or law, moral truth is objective without being detached from human nature.

# Utilitarianism, Hedonism, Egoism, and Kant's Ethics

## Hedonism and egoism: the mistake about what moves us

The first confusion to remove is the psychological one. **Psychological hedonism** is the doctrine that human beings always seek pleasure, that whenever a person acts, he acts in order to experience pleasure. Parallel to it is **psychological egoism**, the doctrine that one can never act except self-interestedly, that the sole intention in performing any act is to benefit from it. These views look hard-headed, but they rest on a failure to distinguish two things: acting **in order to bring about** a result and acting while **knowing** that the result will occur.

The physician case makes the distinction exact. A doctor performs a lifesaving emergency procedure without anesthetic. He knows the patient will feel pain, but he does not operate **in order to inflict pain**. We know this because, were anesthetic available, he would use it. The pain is foreseen, not intended. That distinction will matter later in moral theory, but it already defeats the hedonist psychology. From the mere fact that Smith knows composing music brings him pleasure, it does not follow that he composes in order to bring himself pleasure.

Why, then, does he compose? The answer given in the text is stronger than the mere denial of hedonism. Smith, a latter-day Mozart, composes because he sees value in composing. And because it has value, doing it gives him pleasure. The order of explanation runs from value to pleasure, not from pleasure to value. Unless Smith valued the act of composing, it would not bring him pleasure at all. If he regarded composing as a waste of time, he would not like doing it. Pleasure here is not the object sought; it is the reflective accompaniment of an activity believed to be worth doing.

This is why the comparison between Beethoven and the heroin user is decisive. There are indeed cases in which people act with the objective of experiencing pleasure: drinking alcohol, doing drugs, taking vacations, watching TV. The author explicitly says that he watches TV because he likes it, not because he thinks it has value. That is precisely why such acts are regarded as base when made central. No one thinks ill of Beethoven for devoting himself to composition, though he enjoyed nearly every minute of it. We admire him as dedicated to his craft. But we revile the party boy who spends his nights doing cocaine and his days sleeping off its effects as empty and dissolute. The difference is not that one feels pleasure and the other does too; both do. The difference is that Beethoven acts in order to do something valuable, whereas the cocaine user acts in order to feel good.

The chapter strengthens the point with two thought experiments. Mother Teresa helps the poor because she sees value in doing so, and for that reason helping them gives her pleasure. X, by contrast, undergoes cranial surgery and acquires a peculiar side effect: giving money to poor people now causes him exquisite pleasure in a strictly causal way, as heroin causes pleasure. He does not value the poor, and if hurting them produced comparable pleasure, he would do that instead. Likewise, Y thinks composing is a waste of time and does not even like music, but he has a knack for composition and gets a huge surge of pleasure from doing it. Y’s relation to composing is like the heroin user’s relation to heroin. Beethoven’s is not. In Beethoven the pleasure is mediated by perceived value; in Y it is merely caused.

So psychological hedonism and psychological egoism are false. People often pursue what they regard as worth doing, and the pleasure or benefit they derive depends on that prior valuation. Even apparent self-interest is parasitic on recognition of value. If you do not see value in being on the Supreme Court, then being on it would mean nothing to you, and you would not regard it as in your interest. Our egocentrism is real, but it is not morally empty in the way psychological egoism claims.

## Ethical hedonism and egoism: false because they would mutilate a human life

Once psychological hedonism falls, **ethical hedonism** becomes visible in its full absurdity. Ethical hedonism says that people have an obligation to pursue their own pleasure and no other obligations. **Ethical egoism** says one ought never to act in a manner that is not self-interested. These doctrines are not merely false; they are dehumanizing.

The decisive objection is again Beethoven. Ethical hedonism would say that Beethoven’s obligation was to have a good time. But Beethoven’s central activities were not undertaken simply in order to have a good time. He worked because he valued the work. If one forced him to abandon his compositions in favor of idling, amusement, or direct pleasure-seeking, one would not be liberating him; one would be eviscerating his life. The doctrine therefore implies that the Beethovens of the world ought to stop doing what they love in the serious sense of “love”: not mere liking, but valuing. It would require titans to become munchkins.

That is why the chapter says ethical hedonism looks liberating only superficially. Less superficially it is cruel. It treats the joy attached to serious activity as interchangeable with the joy attached to cocaine or vacuous diversion. But it is not interchangeable. Beethoven’s joy is valuable because it arises from engagement with something valuable. Jones’s joy in cocaine is not. Pleasure has great value, but it lacks an important kind of value when detached from worthwhile activity.

The same verdict applies to ethical egoism. If all one ought ever to do is what is self-interested, then activities whose worth lies in what they are, not merely in what they do for the agent, become morally unintelligible. Yet the very fact that something can count as in one’s interest depends on its independent value. Egoism therefore borrows the very standards it pretends to replace. It says “pursue your good,” but what makes anything your good is that you already see it as worth having or doing.

## Kant’s two categorical imperatives and their failure

Kant enters at this point because he too thinks morality is categorically binding. A **categorical imperative** is a rule that one should follow no matter what: unconditional rather than hypothetical. Kant offers two formulations.

The first says, roughly, that an act is moral if it would not be **self-defeating** were everyone to act similarly. The second says that an act is wrong if it treats a person as an object rather than a subject, and right if it treats a person as a subject rather than an object. The second is the autonomy-based formulation: **autonomy** is self-determination, a person deciding how he will live; **heteronomy** is others deciding how he lives.

Kant thinks these formulations are equivalent. They are not. The text’s counterexample is simple: in a world of con-men, the smart con-men could still con the less smart con-men. So acts of using people need not be self-defeating even if universalized. Conversely, some morally good conduct could not be universally successful. Physicians heal people, and healing is good; but not everyone could successfully be a physician, since someone must grow crops, build roads, and enforce the law. Therefore the universalizability test and the autonomy test come apart. Kant’s claim of equivalence fails.

Both formulations also go wrong by forbidding lying, manipulating, and similar acts even in circumstances where catastrophe can be averted only by such means. The text’s examples are uncompromising. If you must steal from Smith to save your children’s lives, and there is literally no alternative, then stealing is the right thing to do. If torturing one person is the only way to prevent a nuclear device from detonating in the middle of a city, then torturing may be far less wrong than allowing many innocents to die. A theory that simply says “never lie,” “never manipulate,” or “never wound” mistakes a real moral consideration for an exceptionless action-guiding algorithm.

The underlying confusion is that Kant conflates the **good** with the **praiseworthy**. To refrain from lying or manipulation can be admirable; to be the kind of person who needs strong reason before resorting to such acts is morally important. But it does not follow that in every circumstance the good outcome is the one in which no such act occurs. Sometimes the right act is the lesser evil. One may be justified in doing what remains bad in itself because not doing it would be worse. A principle can hold categorically without dictating the outcome in every conflict.

## Utilitarianism: a truth and its ruinous consequences

At this point the attraction of **utilitarianism** is obvious. It captures a genuine truth: helping is good. Saving lives, relieving suffering, making the world better—these are not accidental moral considerations. Any plausible morality must account for them, and utilitarianism does so directly by evaluating actions in terms of their consequences.

But that truth is not the whole truth. The familiar fatal counterexamples are enough. If killing one healthy person and distributing his organs would save several others, the transplant case would favor the killing. If framing an innocent person would prevent widespread unrest or produce better overall results, the theory would favor framing. Yet both are morally monstrous. Their monstrosity consists precisely in sacrificing a person as though he were merely a repository of utility, an object to be used.

The natural retreat is **rule-utilitarianism**: do not evaluate individual acts by direct consequences; instead adopt rules whose general acceptance would maximize good consequences. But this either collapses into act-utilitarianism or into deontology. If the rules are allowed exceptions whenever breaking them produces better results, then one is back to act-utilitarianism. If, on the other hand, the rules are held firm even when better results would follow from violating them, then one has ceased to be a consequentialist in spirit and has become a deontologist, someone who holds that certain kinds of acts are wrong independently of outcome. Rule-utilitarianism cannot stably occupy the middle ground.

## Consequentialists and deontologists: the real disagreement

This does not mean consequentialists and deontologists aim at different worlds. They do not. Both want a world in which rights are not violated, people are not manipulated, and autonomy is secure. Their disagreement is about how to achieve that world.

The consequentialist thinks the route to the best moral order is to maximize good outcomes, even if particular rights-violations must sometimes be committed along the way. The deontologist thinks that systematically respecting certain constraints is itself essential to securing the kind of world we want. On this picture the disagreement is not over whether murder, coercion, or deceit are generally bad; everyone agrees they are. The disagreement concerns whether moral principles operate as side-constraints, weights, or direct maximizing criteria.

This reframing matters because it prevents the usual caricature. The deontologist is not indifferent to outcomes; he too wants fewer rights-violations. The consequentialist is not positively in favor of violating rights; he believes such violations are sometimes instrumentally necessary to minimize them overall. The dispute is therefore strategic and structural, not a dispute about whether human beings matter.

## Double effect: intended and merely foreseen results

The distinction between intending and merely foreseeing an effect now returns in its proper moral form as the **doctrine of double effect**. The physician who performs a painful emergency procedure without anesthetic causes pain, but not in order to cause pain. The pain is a foreseen side effect of saving the patient’s life. That makes him morally different from the sadistic physician who withholds available anesthetic out of a desire to make the patient suffer.

The doctrine marks a morally serious difference. An intended bad effect is part of one’s plan; a merely foreseen bad effect is not. The doctor would eliminate the pain if he could do so without losing the life-saving benefit. The sadist would not. So an action can have two effects, one good and one bad, and be assessed partly by whether the bad effect is a means or aim, or only an unavoidable accompaniment.

This doctrine also helps explain our judgments in hard cases. When the lesser evil is chosen, remorse remains fitting because the bad effect remains bad. The obligation not to wound, deceive, or steal has not vanished; it has been outweighed. That is why one can be justified and yet regretful.

## Kant’s legal model of morality

Kant’s deeper mistake, on this reading, is to model morality on legality. Law aims to determine, in a publicly specifiable way, what outcome is permitted, forbidden, or required. Kant seeks something analogous in ethics: a moral law that dictates the outcome of action by a test or formula. But morality is not like legality in that respect.

The Smith case shows why. The principle that stealing is wrong can hold categorically even when stealing is the right thing to do because it is the lesser of two evils. If one had no obligation at all not to steal from Smith in those circumstances, then one’s remorse at bankrupting a good man would have no objective basis; it would be a hallucination in emotional form. But the remorse is appropriate. You did the right thing and still did something bad. The moral principle survives defeat in deliberation; it is not extinguished by being outweighed.

Legality has trouble with that structure because law typically seeks a final verdict. Morality often gives us competing verdicts with different weights. To say “stealing is wrong” is not always to say “never steal”; it is to say that stealing always counts against an act, even if in some cases stronger obligations count more heavily. Kant misses this because he assumes a moral law must dictate action in the way a legal statute does.

## Rationality and autonomy

What, then, remains genuinely valuable in Kant? His second formulation points toward it: **autonomy**. The text presents autonomy as self-determination, the condition in which one decides how one will live rather than having that determined by others. At bottom, autonomy and **rationality** are the same kind of thing seen in different domains. Rationality is deciding how to think; autonomy is deciding how to live. In each case what matters is authorship by the subject rather than imposition from outside.

This identity explains why treating persons merely as objects is so central a moral wrong. To manipulate, deceive, coerce, or dominate someone is not simply to produce a bad state of affairs. It is to displace that person’s status as a self-directing center of thought and life. Heteronomy is thus not just dependence; it is subjection to another’s will in a way contrary to one’s own authorship.

## Why Kant’s argument from universalization fails

Kant wants to show that morality is rational by showing that immoral principles fail when universalized. But his argument equivocates on **universalize**. There are at least two ideas in play:

1. everyone acting on the same principle, and
2. a principle being one that any rational agent could endorse as such.

Kant slides from the second to the first. From the fact that some act would be self-defeating if everyone did it, he infers that the act cannot be rationally willed. But the inference is invalid. Con-artistry may remain effective for the more skillful in a world full of con-artists. Medicine remains good though it cannot be everyone’s occupation. So “cannot be universally practiced successfully” does not imply “irrational,” and “cannot be rationally endorsed as respecting persons” is not the same test as “would fail if universalized in behavior.”

Because of this equivocation, Kant’s attempt to identify morality with self-interest also fails. He believes that what is immoral will, when universalized, undermine itself and thus reveal itself as contrary to reason. But since the universalization test misfires, the bridge from rationality to morality collapses.

## An autonomy-based principle as the better approximation

The better approximation to moral truth is therefore not the self-defeat test but an autonomy-based principle: acts are morally bad insofar as they undermine persons as subjects, and intervention is justified only to prevent greater violations of autonomy.

This principle preserves what is right in deontology without the rigidity that makes Kant’s system untenable. It explains why manipulation, lying, stealing, wounding, and killing are categorically bad: each is a form of imposing on persons rather than dealing with them as self-directing beings. It also explains why such acts may nevertheless be justified as lesser evils. One may override one person’s autonomy to preserve the autonomy of a million others. The wrongness remains; the balance shifts.

That is why the doctor may cause pain to save a life, why stealing from Smith may be right when the alternative is letting one’s children die, and why forbidding all such acts without regard to consequence is morally obtuse. A moral principle can be categorical in the sense that it always applies as a reason, without being absolute in the sense that it always settles the decision.

The resulting picture rejects hedonism and egoism because value is prior to pleasure and self-interest. It rejects ethical hedonism and egoism because they flatten human excellence into mere gratification. It rejects Kant’s first imperative because universal self-defeat is neither necessary nor sufficient for immorality. It qualifies his second by treating autonomy not as an exceptionless rule but as the central moral value whose protection can sometimes warrant tragic infringements. It grants the consequentialist insight that helping is good and outcomes matter, while denying that persons may simply be used whenever the numbers favor it.

The core moral reality is not pleasure, not self-interest, and not the legalistic application of an inflexible law. It is the value of persons as autonomous subjects and the permanent moral significance of what we do to them, even when, in a world of conflict, the right act is only the least wrong one.
